en: Ūṃ, salutations to Śrī Śiva.
[In the *Śrīmad-Vedāntasāra-Vīraśaiva-Cintāmaṇi*]
The commencement of the Uttarakhaṇḍa.
[First Section] Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
To you, the embodiment of the glorious mantra, to Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness.
Salutations to the venerable Guru-Nātha, the embodiment of Brahman in its six stations. || 1 ||
Now the Vīraśaiva scripture is commenced.

Here, the qualified candidate is specifically the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) who is devoted to the practice of Vīraśaivism; [he attains his goal] by means of the direct realization of Śiva obtained through devotion to Śiva.
The sole purpose is supreme liberation, which consists of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Śiva through the union of the *liṅga* and the body (*aṅga*).

The subject matter is the knowledge expounded in the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*) and the one hundred and one stages (*ekottaraśatasthala*). The relationship between this subject matter and the scripture of the Vīraśaiva Siddhānta is that of the object and its means of cognition (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*).

Thus, the meaning is that the scripture consists precisely of these fourfold connections (*anubandha*). Now, having previously in the first section described the common duties for all Śaivas— such as Vīraśaivas, Śuddhaśaivas, Miśraśaivas, and others— the specific duty of the Vīraśaivas is now being defined.

This is the meaning. For the Vīraśaivas, who maintain the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), [this is so] because of the statement regarding the dissolution of the soul into the *liṅga*.
In the *Śāṅkarasaṃhitā*:
"That Śambhu, whose limiting adjunct is *māyā*, is Sadāśiva in the form of the *liṅga*."
Having avidyā as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), it comes to possess the nature of the limbs [of the body]. || 3 ||
In the Kāmikāgama it is said: "The Liṅga should indeed be Śiva himself; the Aṅga (the body) should truly be the Self."
For the perfect union of those two, Śiva and the Self, is indeed their true conjunction.
Union alone is liberation in the form of sāyujya, and there is no other.
And for the Vīras, O Maheśvarī, liberation is attained in a single birth.
For other Śaivas as well, liberation occurs within three births.
Thus, in the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā,
regarding the reality of the meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam*, which are mutually contradictory in their distinction as the *liṅga* (the signifier) and the *aṅga* (the signified).
Having abandoned the denoted meaning produced by limiting adjuncts, [one realizes] that which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
That cognition which perceives Śiva as being non-different from the indicated object is [the right view].
That is declared as "relationship" (saṃbandha) by those who know the Vedānta scriptures.
In this context, the meaning of the term *vīraśaiva* is stated in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, in the words of Reṇuka addressed to Agastya,
and also in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* of the *Śaivapurāṇa*.
The knowledge produced by the Vedanta is proclaimed as "Vidyā."
Because he delights in knowledge, he is called a "hero" (vīra). || 8 ||
It should be performed by the Śaivas and Māheśvaras, both internally and externally, in due order.
Śiva and Maheśvara do not differ from one another at all in this world. || 9 ||
Regarding the etymological derivation of the term Vīraśaiva:
in whatever manner they may differ, Śaivas and Māheśvaras are not distinct from one another.
Those men who take refuge in Śiva and are devoted to the sacrifice of knowledge are known as Śaivas. || 10 ||
Those on earth who are devoted to ritual sacrifices are declared to be Māheśvaras.
Therefore, the Śaivas should perform [the rites] inside, while the Māheśvaras should do so outside.

Thus, by this [verse], the Vīraśaivas are those devoted to the worship of the Jñānaliṅga situated in the center of the heart-lotus, while the Vīramāheśvaras are those attached to the worship of the Kriyāliṅga situated in the center of the lotus-palms of their hands. || 12 ||
Furthermore, in the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi:
"Because there is a special delight in knowledge (vidyā), which is of the nature of Śiva."
Therefore, these highly fortunate ones are remembered as Vīraśaivas. || 13 ||

Thus, by this [verse], the Vīraśaivas are those who are devoted to the practice of that knowledge (*vidyā*) which is produced from the "head of the Vedas" (*vedaśiras*), as established by the statement of the *Sūta-saṃhitā*: "knowledge born of the Vedāntic sentences. || 14 ||

In the *Uparibhāga* of the *Śāṅkarasaṃhitā*, it is stated: “Because he delights in *vidyā* and abandons *māyā*—which is to be discarded—like a dog, by this etymological definition (*nirukta*), he is remembered as a *Vīramāheśvara*.
By this, it is meant that those who are intent on delighting in *vidyā* and whose nature is to mock or transcend *māyā* are called *Vīramāheśvaras*.

Furthermore, regarding the term *vīraśaiva*, it is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*) meaning "that which is both *vīra* and *śaiva*. The word *vīra* means "especially praised" (*viśeṣeṇa stuta*).
[This is derived from] the root *īra-* with the prefix *vi-*.

It is derived from the verbal root *stu* (to praise) with the suffix *ghañ*, applied according to the rule "in the sense of a non-agent kāraka and when it is a name," resulting in *stuti*; furthermore, by the rule of vowel lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*), the form *stutiḥ* is established. Alternatively, in the sense of "one who bestows (*rāti*) or destroys (*hanti*) the contradictory meanings produced by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)," the root *rā* is used in the senses of "giving" (*dāna*) and "cutting" (*chedana*).

From the root *rā* (to give) with the prefix *vi-* as an attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*; furthermore, by the rule *anyeṣv api dṛśyate*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs due to the prefix, resulting in the form *vi-rā-ka*. Alternatively, in the sense of "one who specifically bestows (*rāti*) the desired fruit," the suffix *ka* is applied to the root *rā* (to give) with *vi-* as an attendant word, according to the rule *ig-upadha-jñā-prī-kiraḥ kaḥ*.

Furthermore, by the addition of the suffix *ka* according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*, by the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule *ato lopa iṭi ca*, and by the lengthening of the vowel in the prefix according to the rule *anyeṣvapi dṛśyate*, [the form] is established. Moreover:
In the Vīrāgama, it is said: "He alone is this [reality] within this entire world."
Because he is distinguished [by these qualities], he is therefore called a hero (vīra). || 16 ||
That which has a connection with Śiva is called Śaiva; thus it is esteemed by the wise.
Because of the union of both, it is known as Vīraśaiva. || 17 ||

Regarding this point, in the *Śāṅkarasaṃhitā*, in the chapter on the Determination of the Six Stages (*Ṣaṭsthalanirṇaya*), it is said: "Animals are superior in intelligence to worms, insects, and birds."
Humans are superior even to animals; among them, the twice-born are the most excellent.
Among the twice-born, the Brahmins are superior; among the Brahmins, those whose intellects are fixed on sacrifice are superior.
Among those whose intellects are fixed on ritual acts, the renunciants are superior. || 19 ||
Among them, the wise are superior; among the wise, those who worship Śaṅkara are the best.
Among them, O fortunate one, the most excellent are those who are united with my own form and limbs.
A person who possesses knowledge of the six stages (ṣaṭsthala) is superior to those who merely touch the limbs of the Liṅga.
Therefore, there is nothing superior to him in all three worlds in any way whatsoever. || 21 ||
He is always to be saluted and worshipped by those who desire to conquer the cycle of worldly existence.
"What is the use of much speaking, my child? I am indeed that very person; of this there is no doubt."
Thus has been explained in brief the entire knowledge for determining the site.
This is to be kept secret among all scriptures; I have spoken it to you out of affection for you.
Regarding this matter, which is to be personally realized, all the Vedas and all the scriptures [bear witness].
All the arguments in the Purāṇas culminate in this. || 24 ||
By this, it is stated that he is called a Vīraśaiva, who is declared to be distinguished among all the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas. || 25 ||
In the *Viśeṣārthaprakāśikā*,
the word *vi-* here has the sense of "optionality" (*vikalpa*), and the word *ra-* has the sense of "devoid of" (*rahita*).
The Śaiva path free from conceptual construction is known as Vīraśaiva. || 26 ||
That which is the supreme state, non-dual and without conceptual construction, is indeed one alone.
That is called Vīraśaiva, and not the other which is conceptual (savikalpaka). || 27 ||

Thus, the designation "Vīraśaiva" belongs only to those who are devoted to the knowledge of Śiva—the realization of the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva)—which is taught by all the Upaniṣads. || 28 ||
In the Śiva-āgamas, such as the Kāmika,
the term "Vi" denotes Vidyā, which brings about the realization of the identity between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva).
Those Śaivas who take delight in her are considered Vīraśaivas. || 29 ||
Thus it has been stated. Such etymological explanations (nirvacana) exist in many ways within the Śaiva Āgamas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas;

however, they are not written here for fear of excessive prolixity. It is determined that I, being a worshiper of the [nine] planets and devoted to the Dahara-vidyā, am indeed the primary qualified candidate for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā).

Because of the union with the *prāṇaliṅga*. Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement: "If one is devoid of the external sacrifice (*bāhyayāga*), the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) will not be accomplished," and from the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*: "When there is a longing for the contemplation of the internal *liṅga*, no [longing] arises for the external. [Therefore,] having unified the *iṣṭaliṅga* and the *prāṇaliṅga*...

Based on the statement from the *Śivarahasya*, "one should worship [thus]," Vīraśaivas must perform external worship preceded by internal worship, and internal worship preceded by external worship. || 30 ||
Likewise, in the *Uparibhāga* of the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*:
"Having placed that very *liṅga*, the symbol of the Supreme Self, in the center of the lotus-pedestal of his hand..."
A person should worship [the deity] with a single-minded focus through ritual offerings distinguished by their internal and external varieties. Thus:
he who, having placed his chosen *liṅga* upon the seat of his own hand, directs the movement of his mind toward absorption in it...
O dear one, he whose soul is free from desire for the multitude of external activities—he indeed is a Vīraśaiva. || 32 ||
The Exposition on the Eligibility for the Knowledge of Brahman.
Thus, in that very chapter concerning the description of the Karapīṭha, Skanda said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear the supreme [teaching] which is beneficial to all living beings."
Some, however, declare that the worship of the *liṅga* upon a pedestal (*pīṭha*) is indeed praiseworthy.
Some were experts in the Śiva Āgamas and devoted to the worship of the prāṇaliṅga.
Having established the vital breath (prāṇa) within the liṅga, one performs the worship of Śiva upon the palm of the hand.
O God, they praise the supreme; tell me which of these two is the principal.
O Śaṃkara, you ought to sever this great doubt of mine.
The Lord said:
"Well asked by you, my child; I shall explain this in its entirety."
The essence of the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, which is secret and captivating.
In whomsoever devotion has been firmly established, even if he be an outcaste, he is the best among the twice-born.
One who knows the four Vedas is dear to me, but one devoid of devotion is not dear.
That devotion should be known as twofold, according to the distinction between external and internal.
The external [form] is gross, while the internal is subtle; it is directly honored by Vīramāheśvara.
Upon a lion throne in a pure, most beautiful place, adorned with jewels.
That which is the worship of the Śiva-liṅga is called external devotion.
Having established the vital breath (prāṇa) within the liṅga, one should establish the Śāmbhava liṅga within the vital breath.
If one makes the mind incorporate the body and does not think of anything at all; || 40 ||
This is called "internal devotion" by the Śiva-yogins.
The life of that person in whom she resides is like a rotten seed. || 41 ||
The perception of saṃsāra continues only until the exhaustion of the enjoyment of prārabdha karma.
That man should be known as liberated while living (jīvanmukta), a hero and a devotee of Maheśvara. Thus [it is said].
In the lotus-navelled one; Śiva, endowed with omniscience and other perfections, is the supreme cause.
One should not bestow the knowledge of non-duality without firm steadfastness.

Based on such scriptural authorities as these, it must be stated that he alone is qualified for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). [Objection: But surely all people have the qualification for the meditation upon Brahman by means of the *praṇava*, since that meditation requires only renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) as its qualification, as in the texts:
"The ascetics, through the yoga of renunciation, are of pure being" and "With 'Om,' one should join the Self."

Therefore, because the word "uparata" (withdrawn) conveys the idea of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) in the phrase "peaceful, self-controlled, withdrawn," it is established that only a person characterized by such renunciation possesses the qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, according to the statement, "one should see the Self in the Self alone. Thus, one should perform the hearing [of the scriptures] only after having renounced.

If that is so, then for the sake of realizing That, one should approach a Guru alone, carrying fuel in hand— a teacher learned in the Vedas and established in Brahman; and to him who has approached him properly, whose mind is perfectly tranquil and who is endowed with self-restraint,
that wise teacher should truly declare that Truth by which one knows the Imperishable Person.
For, by the statement in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, "the knowledge of Brahman," there is seen a contradiction with renunciation (saṃnyāsa) in the case of one who carries fuel in his hand.
In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, following Yājñavalkya’s instruction of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) to Janaka, there is an establishment of Janaka’s qualification for that knowledge;
for we see the renunciation of a knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*) when it is said that Yājñavalkya went forth as a wandering mendicant, even though Janaka was a householder.

Because the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman is observed [in various cases]; for it is well known in the Purāṇas that even householders such as Janaka and others who possess the knowledge of Brahman, as well as celibate students (brahmacārins) such as Vāruṇi, Śvetaketu, and Nācikaeta, have attained the renunciation of the wise (vidvatsaṃnyāsa) through the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self.

Since the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is well-known from the Chāndogya, Taittirīya, and other Śrutis, the right to this knowledge belongs not only to renunciants (saṃnyāsins), but rather specifically to those who have transcended the stages of life (atyāśramins) and are endowed with tranquility, devotion, and other such qualities. And thus:

In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, following a set of six questions—beginning with "The exponents of Brahman say: What is the cause? Is Brahman born? From what are living beings born? By what do they live? and so forth—the discourse concerning the knowledge of Brahman is undertaken across six chapters;
and at the conclusion, the knower of Brahman, Śvetāśvatara, [speaks].
The Knower proclaimed this supreme purifier, honored by the assembly of sages, to those who have transcended the stages of life.

This supreme secret of the Vedanta was imparted in a former age; it is not for one who is not tranquil, nor for one who is not a son, nor indeed for one who is not a disciple. "To him who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and as for the Divine, so for the Guru—to him these meanings have been told, and they are revealed to the high-souled one."
Thus, because of the qualification of the person entitled to the knowledge of Brahman. || 45 ||
In the Kaivalya Upaniṣad, at the beginning: Then Aśvalāyana, having approached the blessed Parameṣṭhin, spoke to him.

"Teach me, O Blessed One, the most excellent knowledge of Brahman, which is ever practiced by the virtuous and kept secret, by which the wise man, having long since cast off all evil, attains the Puruṣa who is higher than the high.
To him, he (the teacher) said:
And know that the Grandfather [Brahmā] attained it through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation— not by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth,
but by renunciation— since scripture declares that faith, devotion, and meditation alone are the causes for eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman.

In that very same place: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of the Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation and are of pure being—they all, at the time of their final end, are liberated from the supreme immortality in the world of Brahman. (47)
Thus, even after the procedure for renunciation has been set forth.

“Having restrained all the senses and having bowed with devotion to one’s own guru while abiding in the ‘beyond-the-āśramas’ (atyāśrama),” [and] because of the qualification of the person entitled to the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) as stated: “one who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī) should mutter [the mantra] either constantly or repeatedly. || 48 ||

Similarly, in the *Muṇḍaka*, immediately after the injunction for renunciation (*sannyāsa*) situated within the section concerning the ascetic (*yati*), at the time of the conclusion regarding the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*):

"One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the 'head-vow' (śirovrata) has been performed according to rule," because from this it is understood that the performance of the head-vow is a specific, mandatory qualification for the recipient.

For in that very same place, by the statement "this is not for one who has not undertaken the vow," there is a prohibition against those who have not taken the vow having the right [to perform it]. || 49 ||

Furthermore, in the *Atharvaśiras*, within the section on the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), it is stated: "Having taken ashes with [the mantra] beginning 'Agni' and having rubbed them, one should touch the limbs. This is because of the injunction regarding the vow:
"Therefore, this is the *Pāśupata* vow for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (*paśu-pāśa*). (50)
And in the Kālāgnirudropaniṣad, regarding the rule for applying the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with mantras, it says: "One should draw three lines; this is the Śāmbhava vow.

Since this prescribes the rule for the vow pertaining to the knowledge of Brahman, the practice of the *atyāśrama* (the state beyond the stages of life) is mandatory even for renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*).
Thus it is said in the fourteenth chapter of the Kūrma Purāṇa: "Then, in the meantime, seeing the great sage approaching..."
The one named Śvetāśvatara, the most excellent among the great Pāśupatas. || 52 ||
His entire body was smeared with ashes, and he was clad in a loincloth for covering.
His body emaciated by asceticism, he wore a pure sacrificial thread.
And having thus favored King Suśīla, who was endowed with virtuous conduct, [he departed].
He accepted as his disciple one whose impurities had been destroyed by ascetic penance.
Having caused the wise man to perform the entire procedure for renunciation (saṃnyāsa), [he should proceed].
Then, likewise, one should perform the knowledge of the Lord and the vow prescribed in one's own Vedic branch. || 55 ||
It is the essence of all the Vedas without exception, that which effects liberation from the bonds of Paśu.
It is known as Atyāśrama, practiced by Brahmā and the other gods.
Having looked toward his disciples dwelling in that hermitage, he spoke.
[He saw] Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, who were entirely devoted to the practice of celibacy. || 57 ||
Having studied only the branch set in motion by me here, the yogins [attain their goal].
They dwell together, meditating upon Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe.
The sage proclaimed the great mantras beginning with "Agnir" and so forth.
Now, since the mantras beginning with "atha agniḥ" are recited in the *Atharvaśiras*,
and because the wearing of ashes is intended by the Purāṇas through these seven mantras ending with "tasmād vratam etat pāśupatam," [it constitutes] both the *atyāśrama* and the *pāśupata-mahāvrata*.

Because it is understood that they share a common application, and because the qualification for the fruit of Brahma-knowledge and that fruit itself— as delimited by this result— are recognized through the two statements concerning liberation (*kaivalya*) in the *Muṇḍaka*,
[it follows that] the *Muṇḍaka*, *Kaivalya*, *Atharvaśiras*, *Kālāgnirudra*, and *Śvetāśvatara* Upaniṣads...
It is understood that there is a unity among the well-established Śirovrata, Pāśupatavrata, Śāmbhavavrata, and Atyāśramavrata.
Thus it is said in the Sūtasamhitā, in the Jñānayogakhaṇḍa, in the fourteenth chapter.
The Lord said:
Alternatively, having taken white ashes with Atharvaṇa mantras, [one should apply them].
And the wise have declared that the vow consists of smearing all the limbs with ashes.
O Sage, those who are established in the Upanishads of the Vedas declare this to be Pāśupata.
Some call it the head-vow (śirovratam), and others likewise call it the beyond-the-stages (atyāśramam).
Some call that the *vrata*, while others call it the *Śāmbhava* or the *Aiśvara*.
The greatness of this vow is established in the concluding portions of the Āgamas.
It removes all sins, is meritorious, and illuminates all knowledge.

Thus, since this [observance] is a qualification for one entitled to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), and since it is prohibited that "one who has not performed this vow is not entitled" even to the entitlement for Vedic study (*adhyayana*) in the absence of such a vow,
the previously cited statement from the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* establishes the entitlement of one who has performed the *śirovrata*.
Since the author of the *Sūtasaṃhitā-vyākhyāna* has expressed his agreement with the view that it pertains to the *pāśupata-vrata*,
it is established that the vow of wearing the *tripuṇḍra* and performing the *uddhūlana* is necessarily a qualification for one who is entitled to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). || 63 ||
As it has been said in the Sūtasamhitā:
O best of sages, the knowledge of Vedānta has been declared to you.
By those twice-born ones who have indeed performed the Pāśupata vow with devotion, [the goal is attained].
"Instruction should be given only to them; such is the teaching of the Vedas. (64) Thus it is said.

The author of this commentary, Mādhavācārya, [explains] that the phrase "vedānuśāsana" (the instruction of the Vedas) is intended by the concluding statement of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the head-vow has been performed according to rule."
From this demonstration, it is determined that the Śirovrata, the Pāśupata vow, and the Śāmbhava vow have a single purpose;
otherwise, the Śirovrata, which is specified as a qualification for the seeker in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*,
would be understood as excluding the others.

Because the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣadic statement, supplemented by the Kūrma Purāṇa and others, is understood to prescribe a stage of life (atyāśrama) that excludes all others, and because the Pāśupata vow is likewise understood to be independent [of other means], there is no deciding factor (*vinigamaka*) for the cognition of one over the other;
thus, [both are] unimpaired (*adṛṣṭa*).

Because there is the fault of falling into eightfold alternatives, it is established that for the sake of avoiding that, there is both the necessity of performing [the rite] as a single office and its oneness. || 65 ||
Thus it has been said in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
Smearing the body with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be respectfully regarded as constituent parts of knowledge.
The best of sages declare that [it] resides in the Atharvaśiras.
O wise ones, by whom the Pāśupata vow has been correctly practiced.
His knowledge shall arise, and by that, there is liberation from the bonds.
The smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are solely as limbs of knowledge.
The best of sages, who are the direct branches of the tree of absolute liberation, proclaim this.
Smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are solely limbs of knowledge.
The best of sages, followers of the Śvetāśvatara branch, declare this.
This is the dharma of the stage of life which has been joyfully practiced by them.
For them alone is the knowledge of Śiva, which is the cause for the eradication of saṃsāra.
Thus, according to the injunctions for vows found in the Śrutis and Purāṇas, such is the nature of the *atyāśrama*.
In the Skanda Purāṇa, within the Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā, in the thirteenth chapter.
The five-syllabled supreme vidyā leads to the attainment of the light of Śiva.
The syllable Om is the Praṇava, the subtle one, the supreme seed of all sciences.
Therefore, one should purify all principles without exception by means of the *praṇava*.
When one should contemplate oneself as Śiva, enumerating those qualities.
One should lead the Self into this body of Śivabhūti by means of the Haṃsa.
Having taken up the ashes of the Śiva-fire with the mantra, one should purify them. || 73 ||

The meaning is that [it arises] from the *virajā-homa* performed in a fire consecrated according to the method of the Śaiva Āgamas, such as the *Kāmikāgama*, by means of the [mantra] "Śivāgnibhasma. In that very same [text]:
"One should dust the body with ashes while reciting the seven verses beginning with 'agniriti'; one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) while reciting 'triyāyuṣaṃ jamadagneḥ'."
The intervals between the head, forehead, ears, neck, arms, thighs, and the region of the navel are each six finger-breadths.
One should contemplate within oneself Śambhu, the Lord, the supreme Śiva, peaceful, accompanied by Umā.
They declare this to be the conduct of the hermitage of one whose limbs are covered in ashes and who has manifested all-encompassing radiance.
This is the highest stage of life among all four stages of life.
That which is an animal, and its state as an animal, one should abandon through this vow.
"O King, there is no means of exit from the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) in any of the scriptures;

rather, liberation is attained here either through the Pāśupata vow, by dying at Kāśī, or by the smearing with ashes arising from the Virajā-homa performed by oneself"— such scriptural authority establishes the Pāśupata [practice] consisting of the smearing of ashes produced from the aforementioned Virajā-homa.
For a person who is steadfast in the *ātavrata* and endowed with the two kinds of devotion previously mentioned,
there is— preceded by the purification of the *tattvas* through their drying up and so forth by means of the five-syllabled mantra joined with the *praṇava*—
