Only they possess the qualification [for this], by virtue of the power of Śiva-initiation. || 168 ||
By the authority of such statements, it must be said that activity proceeds from speech and cessation proceeds from speech. || 169 ||
Furthermore, in the Bhṛgusaṃhitā:
A Caṇḍāla is always present, but not so at all times.
The Śūdra-status of the Śūdra has passed away, whereas that of the Brāhmaṇa is otherwise.
In the sixty-third chapter of the Mānavīya-saṃhitā within the Āditya-purāṇa:
"Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even one born of the lowest caste..."
A devotee of Śiva is always worthy of worship; he is the most excellent of all Brāhmaṇas. || 171 ||
In the *Liṅgasāra*, it is said: "Whether woman, man, eunuch, outcaste, or one born of a twice-born lineage,"
There is no distinction of caste regarding the Linga-worship; all are remembered as attendants of Rudra.
Just as the water from the mountain streams of a city attains oneness upon reaching the Gaṅgā.
By the power of initiation and yoga, even a Śūdra or others may attain the state of Śiva.
The Śūdra-status of the Śūdra has departed, and the twice-born status of the Brāhmaṇa likewise.
In one who is perfected by the Śiva-consecration, no distinction of caste exists. || 174 ||
According to the subtle tradition, this Śūdra is indeed one perfected by the purificatory rites of Śiva; he is indeed a twice-born (dvija).
He by whom a distinction is made between the [two] genders shall go to the Raurava hell. || 175 ||
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"He who reviles devotees by deed, mind, or speech..."
O Sage, there is no deliverance from hell for that deluded soul.
This is well known in such Purāṇas and Āgamas. || 177 ||
In the Laiṅgya [Tantra], it is said that the central piṇḍa, situated in the midst of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ārka (twelve), bestows sons.
The remains of the offerings to Śiva are declared in the Vedas; what need is there for further elaboration? || 178 ||
In the Śaiva Purāṇa,
it is said that this entire world of moving and non-moving beings has arisen from the *piṇḍa* of Rudra.
"Out of delusion alone, he does not recognize that he is like the son of a courtesan, O dear one. || 179 ||
In the Jābāla branch [of the Veda] it is said: "They eat what has been taken by Rudra; they drink what has been drunk by Rudra;

they smell what has been smelled by Rudra. Therefore, learned Brahmins of tranquil mind consume only the *nirmālya* (the remains of an offering); one should eat only the *nirmālya*, one should partake only of the *nirmālya*."
Because of the observation of injunctive statements. || 180 ||
In the Śaiva-saṃhitā,
Vyāsa said:
One who is possessed of fickleness of tongue and devoid of the purificatory rites of Śiva.
If one who enjoys the grace of Śiva should go to the Raurava hell, [it would be a contradiction]. || 181 ||
In every respect,
for those who lack purification through Śiva-initiation, the enjoyment of pure objects leads to fault.
As it has been said in the Kāmikāgama:
Though impure in soul, one who is pure [in mind] may, out of greed, think: "That which has been eaten by me is supremely purifying."
For by consuming it, a Śūdra goes to destruction, just as one does through the study [of the Veda].

On the basis of such scriptural authorities, since those who are uninitiated and devoid of devotion to Śiva— those wicked Brahmins consumed by the curse of the nine sages— are unworthy of enjoying the grace of Śiva,
it is stated that only one who enjoys the grace of Śiva and is devoted to Śiva is truly a Brahmin. || 184 ||
In another text:
"The Brahmin born from the *rudrapiṇḍa* [should worship] Śiva, the Lord of All, as his Guru."
Through delusion alone he does not recognize his father, just like the son of a prostitute. || 185 ||
It should be stated that "Rudrapiṇḍa" refers precisely to Śiprasāda. || 186 ||
Likewise, in the Skanda [Purāṇa]:
"Those who are born from the *rudrapiṇḍa* and those who recite the sequence of the Vedas..."
Those who know the Śrī Rudra, which is to be recited as Brahman, are remembered as true Brāhmaṇas. || 187 ||

Based on such scriptural authorities, it is determined that only those who possess the knowledge of Śiva— having been born from the *piṇḍa* (sacramental body) produced by the grace of Śiva— are true Vīramāheśvara Brāhmaṇas.

For this very reason, although Viśvāmitra was born of a Kṣatriya and was a partial incarnation (aṃśa) of Rudra, he attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa through ascetic penance; whereas Paraśurāma, though born of a Brāhmaṇa and a partial incarnation of Viṣṇu,
performed the duties of a Kṣatriya in his activities due to the exchange of the *caru* offerings between the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava rites.
It is heard in the Harivaṃśa.
In that regard, long ago, there was a confusion of sacrificial oblations between Bhṛgu and the followers of Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Indeed, in the Vaiṣṇava portion of the Jagatī meter, the son of Jamadagni was also born.
Viśvāmitra was the portion of Śiva, while Gādhi, the joy of the Kuśikas, was his [portion].
And he begot a son whose nature consisted of austerity, knowledge, and tranquility.
Having attained the tranquility of a Brahman-sage, he has thus reached the state of a Brahman-sage. || 190 ||
In the *Bhāgavata*, this account— caused by the mutual exchange of the sacrificial offerings (*caru*) between the Brāhmaṇa and the Vaiṣṇava—
is stated somewhat cryptically due to its nature as a Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa.
Thus, the origin of the Brāhmaṇas is established as being from the Brāhmaṇa alone.
Because the birth of a Brāhmaṇa from anything else is impossible. || 191 ||
And Rudra’s status as a Brāhmaṇa is heard in the *prapada* mantra of the Sāma Veda branch.
"Among the gods you are a Brāhmaṇa; I am a Brāhmaṇa among men. Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa pursues a Brāhmaṇa, saying, 'I pursue you! || 192 ||
Regarding this matter, in the Parāśara Purāṇa it is stated: "Therefore, for a Brahmin, a connection with Śiva alone is indeed appropriate."
All the gods are of mixed origin, and Purandara is a vṛṣala.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) is indeed a Vaiśya, while Hari is the supreme Kṣatriya.
The Blessed One Rudra is a Brāhmaṇa, the highest of the high among all.
For the state of being Brahman belongs to Rudra; his status as a Brāhmaṇa is not born of causes.
Indeed, in this world, a brahmin always seeks refuge with another brahmin.
One should take refuge in the Great Brahman, the Lord, and not in another. || 195 ||

Thus it is well known in various Purāṇas; for this very reason, according to the principle found in the Yajurveda and the Ṛgveda— "He who sacrifices beyond his own deity falls away from his own deity, does not reach the higher one, and becomes worse off"—
it is proper for a Brāhmaṇa to honor only a Brāhmaṇa, otherwise he becomes worse off.
The meaning is that [he] becomes so, because Rudra is a Brāhmaṇa, because he is the cause of the origin of Brāhmaṇas, and because he is to be meditated upon by Brāhmaṇas.
It is indeed proper that those who harbor hatred toward the devotees of Rudra should be excluded from the community of Brahmins. || 196 ||
Thus it has been said:
One should know that a son who hates his father is of another's seed.
One who constantly hates the Brahmins, him one should know as "another-seeded" (of perverted nature). || 197 ||
In the Mahābhārata: By birth one is born a Śūdra; by action one is called a twice-born (dvija).
A Brahmin who knows the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras knows Brahman; he is a true Brāhmaṇa. || 198 ||
A Brahmin who upholds the four Vedas but is devoid of devotion to Śiva is not a true hero in this world.
Indeed, there is no one equal to a Śūdra who is endowed with devotion to Śiva. || 199 ||
Though he was a devotee of Śiva, a brahmin, and devoted to the study of the Vedas, [he fell].
He alone is said to be Śiva; this is the truth, there is no doubt. || 200 ||
The specific distinction for Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva is the recitation of the Vedas.
For those devoid of devotion to Śiva, there is the howling of dogs, jackals, and crows.
The teaching of the Vedas to Brahmins who are devoid of devotion to Śiva.
A creation equal to the braying of donkeys would become a destruction. || 202 ||
The teaching of the Vedas to twice-born men who are devoid of devotion to Śiva.
Just as water in a broken jar becomes entirely useless, so too does this [teaching] become futile. || 203 ||
Even one of low birth, of evil conduct, a sinner, or guilty of a minor offense—
He should mutter the five-syllabled mantra; once purified, he may perform the recitation of the Vedas.
The viewing of the Śiva Āgamas by Brahmins who have not been initiated.
O Great Goddess, this is evil; this is the truth, there is no doubt about it. || 205 ||
And even the Vedas have issued forth from the lotus-face of Brahmā.
The scriptures consisting of the knowledge of Śiva have emerged from my mouth. || 206 ||
O Śivā, I am the creator of the universe, the four-faced one, and the maker of all.
Therefore, the Śiva-āgama [should not be disclosed] to twice-born men who have not been initiated.
Recitation may be a cause of sin [for others], but for those who have been initiated, it yields great fruit.
Having obtained the permission of the Guru, O Śivā, one should study the divine scripture.
In the Gāruḍapurāṇa, in its latter section (Uttara-bhāga), [there is mention] of those belonging to the lineage and characterized by the wearing of the *liṅga*.
For those who possess knowledge and are devotees of Śiva, the status of being a Śūdra does not exist at all.
In the Namaka, the Camaka, and the Vedic Pañcabrahma-mantras;
Only they possess the qualification [for this] by virtue of the power of Śiva-initiation. || 210 ||

On the authority of such statements as these, only those who are born through the initiation (dīkṣā) of Śiva and are devotees of Śiva are true Brāhmaṇas; they alone are entitled to the performance of Vedic mantra-rituals,
such as the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads along with mantras, and the recitation of the *namaḥ* and *camaka* hymns.
It should be stated that they are "those who lack qualification. But who, then, are those lacking qualification for Vedic injunctions and for the recitation of the Vedas?
To this, it is replied: || 211 ||
In the Āditya Purāṇa,
in the Mānavīya Saṃhitā, in the seventh chapter, the words of the sage Dadhīci:
And all these brahmins, who were hostile toward Maheśvara—
May they be excluded from the Vedas, their minds struck down by sin.
All those devoted to the practices of heretics go to hell. || 212 ||
In the Sāmbapurāṇa, during the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, these are the words of Dadhīci:
In the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the smearing with ashes, and the consecration with Vedic mantras, [these are the requirements].
May you and likewise those born of your lineage turn away from this. || 213 ||
O twice-born ones, in the tantras outside the Veda, such as the Pāñcarātra and others, [this is not found].
"You would all become initiated, O lowest of Brahmins, in every respect. (214)
And you are marked upon your limbs with the conch, the discus, the mace, and other such symbols.
Out of faith, you would become outcasts from the Vedas, the lowest of the twice-born. || 215 ||

Thus, in the Skanda, Liṅga, Śiva, Kūrma, Padma, Āditya, Parāśara, and other Purāṇas, there are nine sages who pronounced curses upon the brahmins: Bhṛgu, Dadhīci, Gautama, Vīrabhadra, Nandīśvara, Dūrvāsas, Brahmā, Kaṇva, and Upamanyu.
They are recited. || 216 ||
Dadhīca, Gautama, Kaṇva, Upamanyu, Bhṛgu, and Vidhi.
Dūrvāsas, Vīrabhadra, and Nandin are the ones who inflict curses in the Kali age. || 217 ||
Thus, those who are scorched by the fresh curse of the Sage, who revile Śiva, and who are the lowest of Vaiṣṇava Brahmins— whosoever they may be— they alone are determined to be outside the Veda.
That has been explained in many ways in the preceding chapters; it should also be kept in mind here.
Furthermore, if it is asked in which Vedic [traditions] there is eligibility for the Vīramāheśvaras who bear the *liṅga*, it is said in reply: || 218 ||
In the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* of the Śaiva [Āgama], in the second part (*uparibhāga*), within the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Upamanyu,
in the chapter titled "The Description of the Conduct of Devotion" (*bhaktyācāranirūpaṇādhyāya*).
The words of Śiva addressed to the Goddess; likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, a scripture of Vīraśaivism, the words of Reṇuka addressed to Agastya in the section on devotion (*bhaktisthala*).
The ritual of worshipping Śiva is to be understood as external; it is not called sacrifice (yāga) and so forth.
The emaciation of the body for the sake of Śiva, such as the Kṛcchra and other penances, is not our considered view. (219)
Japa is the practice of the five-syllable mantra or indeed the practice of the Praṇava.
The practice of reciting the Rudrādhyāya and other such texts does not constitute the study of the Vedas and so forth.
Meditation is the contemplation of the form and other attributes of Śiva; it is not the contemplation of the self and so forth.
Knowledge is the understanding of the meaning of the Śiva-āgamas; it is not the cognition of other objects. || 221 ||
Thus, this fivefold Śivayajña has been proclaimed.
He who worships Śaṅkara with these five sacrifices,
Endowed with supreme devotion, he is indeed called a devotee. || 222 ||
O lady of excellent hips, upon the arrival of the Hero, asceticism, sacrifice, recitation, and the like come to an end.
O lady of excellent hips, the oblation offered into the mouths of heroes is never exhausted.

Thus, based on authoritative statements such as "this alone is the sacrifice for the Vīraśaivas," the Vīraśaivas [employ] Vedic mantras in their procedures for the wearing of ash and rudrākṣa beads— beginning with fire— and for the worship of the Śivaliṅga, specifically the five-syllabled mantra, the praṇava, and the Śatarudrīya.

Regarding the phrase "the practice of the Rudrādhyāya and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (ādi), it is implied that the Vīraśaiva, though born of the Brāhmaṇa caste, possesses eligibility for the Upaniṣads which expound upon Brahman;
however, it must be stated that the Śruti pertaining to the Karmakāṇḍa is to be avoided by him. || 224 ||
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, in the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Upamanyu:
"What is the use of saying much more here? All devotees are qualified."
Therefore, he is indeed superior even to my five-syllable mantra. || 225 ||
And this six-syllabled mantra, beginning with Oṃ, is superior to all mantras.
He is the bestower of all goals upon all devotees of Śiva without exception. || 226 ||
In the Candrajñānāgama,
there is the commitment (samaya) and the distinction [of the practitioner] through the initiation of yoga and liberation (yoganirvāṇadīkṣā).
And for those belonging to the four castes and stages of life (or those established in the four castes and stages), the six-syllabled mantra is indeed their duty.
Of men who behave improperly and who have not studied the Vedas, the twice-born.
And the instruction of the six-syllable mantra must not be given, O Maheśvarī.
In the sixty-third chapter of the Mānavīya-saṃhitā:
"Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even one born of the lowest caste..."
A devotee of Śiva is always worthy of worship; he is the best among all Brāhmaṇas. || 229 ||
In the *Vajrasūcī Upaniṣad*, there are these eight alternatives: among those castes, who indeed is a Brāhmaṇa?

Is it the living soul (*jīva*), the body, the birth (*jāti*), the duty (*dharma*), the action (*karma*), the caste (*varṇa*), scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), or righteousness (*dhārmikatva*)? Thus are the eight alternatives.
Having thus explained the absence of true Brāhmaṇahood among these eight types of alternatives, it was stated that "one who knows Brahman is a Brāhmaṇa.

Therefore, based on the Purāṇic statement, "Those who know Śrī Rudra, who is the referent of the word 'Brahman,' are remembered as Brāhmaṇas," one who is born from the initiation (dīkṣā) of Śiva, who is learned in the Śiva-śāstra, who possesses knowledge of Śiva, and who is a devotee of Śiva [is a true Brāhmaṇa].
"O Brahmin, it should be said thus. || 230 ||
In the Mahābhārata and elsewhere it is said:
"By birth one is born a Śūdra; by action one is born a twice-born (dvija)."
A Brahmin is one who studies the Vedas; a Brāhmaṇa is one who knows Brahman. || 231 ||
Thus it has been said. In the sixty-third chapter of the Mānavīya-saṃhitā within the Āditya-purāṇa, Sūrya said:
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even one born of the lowest caste;
A devotee of Śiva is always worthy of worship; he is the most excellent of all Brāhmaṇas. || 232 ||
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā of the Śaiva Āgama, in the latter section, within the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Upamanyu.
Likewise, in the Śivadharmottara and elsewhere.
For this eightfold devotion exists even in a barbarian.
He is a lord of Brahmins, a sage, glorious, an ascetic, and a scholar.
Keeping all of this in mind, it was stated by the Paramahaṃsa Ācāryas in the *Vajrasūcī*:
I shall proclaim the Vajrasūcī, the treatise that pierces ignorance.
Censure is an ornament for those devoid of knowledge, but it is a blemish for those who possess the eye of wisdom. || 234 ||
If there is doubt regarding the status of a Brahmin in this body, then those of the past and future are also included.
Therefore, the bodies of ancestors must not be burned by their sons; for that reason, it is not so.
If there is doubt regarding the Brahminhood of a living being, he [should treat him] together with all other living beings.
He moves in the form of a swan, neither externally nor internally.
If there were doubt regarding Brahminhood based on birth, that would not apply here in this land.
In this context, what is the caste of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Vasiṣṭha, Agastya, and the others?
If there is doubt regarding one's caste as being Brāhmaṇa, [the proof lies in] those born from the mouth, the arms, the thighs, and the feet.
White and other such colors are equal; therefore, they do not exist as one [in a single entity]. || 238 ||
If there is doubt regarding his status as a Brahmin in terms of dharma, then [the signs are] such things as being addicted to sleep and food.
For all those phenomena are indeed equal; therefore, they are not distinct.
If there is a doubt regarding the status of a Brahmin through action, then action such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and so forth [is required].
Therefore, that Brahminhood is not common to Kṣatriyas and the other castes. 240.
If there is a doubt that Brahminhood consists in scholarship, then [the same would apply] to Kshatriyas and others.
Indeed, that scholarship which arises from the study of all the scriptures does not exist [in him]. 941.
And if there should be a doubt that brahminhood consists in being righteous, [then...]
Therefore, Kṣatriyas and others are certainly not devoted to the true dharma of sacrifice and so forth.
Śiva [is the referent] because of Vedic scriptural passages such as, "Among the gods, you are the Brāhmaṇa."
Among the gods, one may be a Brāhmaṇa; among men, one who is devoted to Him is a Brāhmaṇa.
In the *prapada* mantra of the Sāmaveda: "Among the gods you are a Brāhmaṇa; I am a Brāhmaṇa among men. Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa approaches a Brāhmaṇa; I approach you. (244)
In the Parāśara Purāṇa, it is said:
"All the gods are of mixed origin, but Purandara is a Vṛṣala."
The Grandfather (Brahmā) would be a Vaiśya, and Hari, the Supreme, would be a Kṣatriya. || 245 ||
The Blessed One Rudra is a Brāhmaṇa, the highest of all.
Indeed, in this world, the Brahmin always seeks refuge with the Brahmin.
One should take refuge in the Great Brahman, the Lord, and not in another. || 246 ||
In the Yajurveda: "He who sacrifices beyond his own deity falls away from his own deity; he does not reach the higher one and becomes worse off. (247)

The meaning of this is explained: that brahmin who, having bypassed or transgressed his own deity Śiva, worships or honors another deity—he indeed falls away from his own deity; becoming the lowest of men and an offender, he does not attain the supreme goal, nor does he go to the highest state.
He will certainly become more wicked than the most wicked. || 248 ||
Furthermore, in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad]:

"O Prācīnayogya, worship Brahman as having space for its body, whose self is truth, who delights in the vital breaths, whose mind is bliss, who is enriched by peace, and who is immortal"— in this passage,
Brahman alone is the true nature, characterized by the power denoted by the word "space."

Having assumed the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) consisting of the power of vital breath (prāṇa-śakti), and having experienced the bliss of objects perceivable by the mind, you shall become the ancient nectar enriched by the qualities of samādhi;
meditate on this— meaning, being of what kind, that is, being a fit candidate through ancient deeds.
The causal efficacy of past actions as a basis for qualification was stated by Śiva in the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*:
"Not by all ascetic practices, nor by all yogas, nor even by all meritorious deeds and all sacrifices..."
"Through all gifts and every means offered to me throughout infinite births, [devotion is attained]. (250)
Thus, it has already been stated that those worthy of the ancients possess the qualification for devotion to Śiva. || 251 ||
Moreover, in the Skanda-purāṇa:
"They resemble serpents, have uneven eyes, possess a luster like coral-red,
are interspersed with women, have matted hair on their heads, and are adorned with crescent moons."
The gods, eternally blissful, of constant grace, with glistening dark-blue throats, and bearing axes as Rudra does—they shall become your devotees. (252)
Thus, it must be stated that Nandīśvara and the other hosts of Pramathas are indeed Rudra-hosts who are Vīramāheśvara devotees. || 253 ||
If it is asked who those Rudras are, it is stated in the Śukla-yajus and the Vājasaneyi [Saṃhitā].
Countless thousands are neither remembered nor seen.
In the Śatarudrīya, [it occurs] in the Avatāna mantra.

Those thousands upon thousands of Rudras who are well-known from such Vedic texts as "The Rudras who are upon the earth," and who have assumed forms through the divine play of Supreme Śiva— all these are forms of Rudra; likewise, those liberated by the Pāśupata vow,
or those liberated by dying at Kāśī, the site of the Pāśupata, all of them are forms of Rudra.
Thus, both those who have been liberated from beginningless time and those liberated at the beginning are specific manifestations of the form of Rudra. || 254 ||
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
And those who are the lords of Śambhu’s attendants do not return to the surface of the earth.
Having enjoyed pleasures as they desired, they shall attain union with Śiva. || 255 ||
If it is asked: "Since those who are thus liberated are free from returning [to saṃsāra], by what cause do they become devotees?"—it is said in reply: || 256 ||
In the Āditya Purāṇa, the words of Dūrvāsas addressed to Indra:
All the lords of the Gaṇas assume forms at will and act according to their own desires.
"The liberated rejoice together with Śiva and go to the state of Śiva. || 257 ||

On the basis of such scriptural authority, it must be stated that devotees, free from the subjection of karma, act by their own will for the welfare of the world and for the purpose of establishing the dharma of Śiva. || 258 ||
The words of Śiva to Kumāra in the latter part of the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā.
For whenever a decline of the Śaiva dharma occurs,
At that time, this incarnation of Gaṇeśa occurred upon the surface of the earth. || 259 ||
My child, these leaders of the Gaṇas have descended to the surface of the earth at my command;
having been born into all various castes, they shall remain devoted once again to the worship of the Liṅga.
Having established themselves in the supreme state of Vīraśaiva for the welfare of men in this world, they shall wander about wearing the five mudrās, and at the end, they will all come to me.

In the *avatāna-mantra*, "Homage to them; may they be gracious to us," the Rudras are heard to be the bestowers of happiness. Therefore, for the welfare of the world in the Kali Yuga, Nandīśvara and others become the ancient and modern devotees (*bhaktas*) beginning with Basaveśvara.
The teachers beginning with Revanasiddha are the *ācāryas*; those beginning with Allama Prabhu and Deva are the *jaṅgamas*.

Their life stories are well-known in the scriptures and Purāṇas composed by Vīraśaiva teachers, such as the Somanātha-bhāṣya and the Basava-purāṇārādhyacaritra; they should be consulted therein. || 261 ||
In that very context, there is the statement of the Sage Sūta: "O Gaṇeśas, whenever there occurs a decline among those in the mortal race who possess the unity of Prāṇa and Śiva..."
Descending to the surface of the earth at those various times, they indeed act together to establish the Dharma.
When there was a decline of the Dharma, as malevolent hosts arose among various families on earth— those who reviled Śaṅkara, were devoid of virtue, and were destroyers of that Dharma.
"Training themselves in the entire path of the auspicious Dharma and establishing these worshippers of the Liṅga here, they shall all once again attain union with Śambhu. (263) Thus it is said.
In another text: those Rudras who, descending from the world of Rudra and assuming human form, [act] for the welfare of the world.
They perform various kinds of charming movements; homage to those who worship the Three-Eyed One. || 264 ||
Devotion belongs only to the liberated one; it never belongs to the bound one.
Liberation occurs only for the devotee, never for the non-devotee.
In the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā:
"Having become Rudra, one should worship Rudra; one who is not Rudra should not worship Rudra."
He who is connected with the body of the Prāṇaliṅga is Rudra; there is no doubt in this matter. || 266 ||
In the Skanda [Purāṇa],
it is said that the Brahmin is the "earth-god" (bhūsura), while the mobile [deity] is the "earth-rudder" (bhūrudra).
Between the two, Suras and Rudras, Rudra alone is distinguished as superior. || 267 ||
In the Śivarahasya,
the two forms of Nīlakaṇṭha are indeed described as both the moving and the unmoving.
The bearer of the *liṅga* moves about in a mobile form, such as that made of clay and other materials, which is itself immobile.
In the Śivadharmas, it is said that the liṅga is of two kinds: the stationary and the mobile.
Through the disparagement of the mobile, the immobile becomes fruitless. || 269 ||
In the *Uttaravātula*, it is said:
"Therefore, one should offer the *prasāda*, the *nirmālya*, and likewise the *pajjala* to the *liṅga*."
One should offer it to the mobile liṅga; listen, O Six-faced One, to how this is done in every respect. || 270 ||
In the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā.
The water used for washing the feet of one who is established in the Prāṇaliṅga as his very body [is sacred].
"For the sake of purifying the sins of the ignorant, that holy place belongs to Śikhivāhana. (271)
In another treatise:
Likewise, one should smear upon one's own body the remains of the food offered once to the worshipper of the Liṅga.
He becomes a vajra-body and rejoices together with Śiva. || 272 ||
In the Anuśāsana Parvan of the Mahābhārata,
[it is stated that] by anointing one's feet with the remnants of Dūrvā grass left over from a meal.
The imperishable Viṣṇu suddenly attained the state of possessing a vajra-body.
In the Skanda [Purāṇa]:
By consuming gruel, one is purified; by smearing the feet and the rest of the limbs [with clay], Viṣṇu [is pleased].
Thus, at that time, he was joined with a boon in the form of a curse by the sage. || 274 ||
In the Śaiva-saṃhitā of the Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa, within the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini,
it is stated that both Viṣṇu and Paraśurāma were initiated by Śiva.
They were both devotees who partook of the water used for washing his feet and the remains of the offerings.
Vasiṣṭha also became most venerable through the power of that grace.
Through the cultivation of serene faith, the great sage Viśvāmitra was born. || 276 ||
Pāṇini, Kaṇāda, Kapila, Gautama, and the others.
Through the cultivation of serenity, through meditation, through worship, and even through dhāraṇā;
Having been born as those who perform the act of seeing, they cause the three worlds to hear [the teaching]. || 277 ||
Neither by means of a great stationary linga nor by means of a great mobile one.
Homage again and again to him for whom faith has arisen in two ways. || 278 ||
Furthermore, in the Liṅgasāra and elsewhere it is said:
"A woman devoted to the worship of the Liṅga who is affected by the impurity of menstruation or childbirth..."
Just as the sun and fire, so too shall he become pure as ten million fires. || 279 ||
In the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā:
"O child, there is no birth-impurity for one who is joined with the body of the Prāṇaliṅga."
That which arises from birth and that which arises from death exist in the ultimate sense. || 280 ||
Lineage, caste, and other such qualities are attributes of the body, not of the self.
Because it is inward-facing, because its nature is consciousness, because it is full, and because it is of the nature of Śiva. || 281 ||
Thus it is well known in the Basaveśvara Purāṇa: "Iṃbyamma, Uvvā, Caṅgalā, and the illustrious Basava, the sun of the learned."
They are avoided by those who have been born for a month, by the remnants of a funeral meal, and by those in a state of ritual impurity (sūtaka). || 282 ||
In another text it is said:
"By means of pride in [one's] caste and stage of life, a man becomes a slave to the Veda."
"Free from conceit, he abides in the summit of the Vedas. || 283 ||

In the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā: For him who possesses this knowledge of the Supreme Self, which pertains to the connection between the Liṅga and the Aṅga, there shines forth the inner self as composed of the meaning of the three words— pure, eternally blissful, and ever-existent.

That person, whose heart is filled with devotion for the lotus feet of Śrīkaṇṭha, having abandoned the remainder of the collection of actions pertaining to other objects—whether enjoined or prohibited—should practice [the path]. (Liṅgasāra, verse 284).
Whether a woman, a man, a eunuch, an outcaste, or one born of a twice-born lineage;
There is no distinction of caste in the worship of the Liṅga; all are remembered as attendants of Rudra. || 285 ||
This is well known in the Śaiva Āgamas and Purāṇas, and so forth.
In the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā:
"The one who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī), being connected with the Prāṇaliṅga, [wears] a ring of sacred ash."
One should carry a patched garment, a water-pot, an alms-bowl, and a staff. || 286 ||
In that very same place, in another section,
one should maintain equanimity toward the patched garment known as patience and the pouch of ashes.
O child, [take] the water-pot of compassion and the beautiful staff of knowledge.
One should beg for the alms-bowl of dispassion and the alms of devotion. || 287 ||
Such accounts of the deeds of the Vīraśaivas, who are free from all objective appearances (nirābhāra), are well known in the Śaiva Āgamas and Purāṇas.

On the basis of such scriptural authorities as these, it must be stated that the Vīraśaiva alone, who transcends all castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), is the "one beyond the stages" (atyāśramī) and thus possesses the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā). || 288 ||
In the fifth chapter of the Muktikhaṇḍa of the Sūtasamhitā:
"The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant..."
And he who transcends the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī)—the wise one is superior according to this sequence. || 289 ||
O Lotus-eyed One, even a householder is superior to one who dwells in the forest and to an ascetic.
One becomes a guru solely through the power of the excellence of one's knowledge, and not otherwise. || 290 ||
O Hari, even those in the stage of forest-dwellers and likewise those who have renounced the world [attain this].
One becomes a guru only through the power of the excellence of knowledge, and not otherwise. || 291 ||
The Guru who transcends the castes and stages of life is declared to be the authority for all.
Even he would not be superior to me, O Supreme Person, as I have said. (292)
One who transcends the castes and stages of life is said to be the direct teacher of even teachers.
He whose conduct regarding caste and stage of life has dissolved through the vision of his own Self.
Having transcended all castes and stages of life, he abides in his own self.
The man who, having transcended his own stages of life and social classes, abides in the Self alone.
Thus he is declared by those who know the meaning of all the Vedas to be one who has transcended the [ordinary] castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī). || 294 ||
Indeed, it was stated by Śaṅkarācārya in the *Manīṣāpañcaka*:

"That consciousness which manifests most clearly in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, which is woven through the bodies of all beings from Brahmā down to a tiny ant, is the witness of the world."
"He who possesses the firm wisdom that 'I am indeed That, and not the visible object,' whether he be an outcaste or a twice-born, he is my teacher"—this is my conviction. || 295 ||
From such scriptural authorities as these, it is determined that the Vīraśaiva alone, who transcends the [ordinary] castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī), is the most excellent of all. || 296 ||

Furthermore, at the conclusion of the *Atharvaśiras*, beginning with the words: "This is to be meditated upon; let that speech speak; that is the internal grasping; this path is stretched out," and so forth.
By the passage ending with "O Rudra, they say there is oneness in Rudra," the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga* and its wearing are declared. || 297 ||
In the subsequent [section]: "The fierce, eternal, and ancient [deity] bestows through austerity the desired vigor;
that vow is this Pāśupata," and the wearing of the chosen *liṅga* is also mentioned. || 298 ||

In the subsequent passage, beginning with "Agni," it is stated that one should take the ashes, rub them [on the body], and touch the limbs; thus, this Pāśupata vow for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa) is established, and the wearing of ashes as a limb of its worship is declared. || 299 ||
The meaning of this, however, should be examined in detail in the section on the wearing of the *liṅga*.

In this context, by way of the illustration of wearing the internal and external *liṅga* and the application of ashes, one should perform the observance of all the practices of the Vīramāheśvaras, such as the wearing of *rudrākṣa* beads and so forth. || 300 ||

Furthermore, at the conclusion of the *Atharvaśikhā*, which forms part of the collection of various Upaniṣads within the trunk of the Veda consisting of the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan, it is said: "One should meditate upon the Lord who is to be meditated upon;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra are born from Him, as are all the senses together with the elements."
"The Cause, indeed, the Cause—Śambhu, endowed with all sovereignty and the Lord of All—is to be meditated upon in the midst of space.
Thus, "Īśāna, Śiva alone is to be meditated upon as the maker of auspiciousness; having abandoned everything else"—with these words, the Ātharvaṇī [Upaniṣad] concludes.

Having established the fundamental tenet of the Vīraśaiva doctrine— that the attainment of supreme liberation (niḥśreyasa) is caused by meditation directed exclusively toward Śiva through the abandonment of other deities— he taught that for those seeking liberation, "Śiva" refers to meditation focused solely on Śiva to the exclusion of other gods. Thus, he refuted the systems of others and established the Vīraśaiva position characterized by exclusive devotion to the Liṅga.
Having itself stated its own conclusion for the sake of certain realization through its state of being free from doubt, the Atharvaśikhā comes to its end. || 301 ||
"In this matter, the excellent Śikṣā of the Atharva Veda concludes thus:"
The *Atharvaśikhā*, the crest-jewel of all the Vedas, declares: "It is indeed thus."
This is well known in various Purāṇas, such as the Sūta-saṃhitā.
This has been explained in detail in its preceding section. || 302 ||

Thus, it should be understood that this very Śruti is the root source for those Āgamas and Purāṇas of the Vīraśaivas which, through the renunciation of other deities, establish exclusive devotion to the Liṅga alone. || 303 ||
Therefore, at the conclusion of all the Upaniṣads of every Vedic branch, it is the Vīraśaiva doctrine alone that is taught in the *Atharvaśikhā*;

for this very reason, one who is devoted to the head-vow (*śirovrata*) known as Pāśupata, who wears the internal and external *liṅga*, who smears himself with ashes, and who is solely intent upon Śiva [is the true practitioner].

The Vīramāheśvara alone is the most excellent; he alone is the one qualified for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā)—this is the ringing proclamation of the Vīraśaiva Siddhānta in various Śruti, Purāṇas, and Śivāgamas, and there is no hope for others regarding their own established tenets. 304.

"Furthermore, because of the statement in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*, 'The Atharvaveda is known as the fourth [Veda] and indeed that which transcends the fourth,' the Vīraśaiva doctrine is understood from the concluding statements of the fourth Veda; moreover, it is the first among the branches of the Vedas,
consisting of the collection of various Upaniṣads contained within the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvaṇa."
Since the meaning of the introductory passages is appropriately determined in accordance with the concluding statement that identifies [the Self] as the crest-lock of the Vīraśaiva,

and since there is no such evidence for other [doctrines], and because the Vīraśaiva system remains preeminent at the end of all the Vedas, it is established without obstacle that the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself; for him, there is no [return].
Based on the scriptural statement, "The vital breaths cause [the soul] to depart; they dissolve right here," liberation is indeed identity with the essential nature (svarūpa). || 305 ||
Furthermore, as stated in the Anubhavasūtra: "In both worlds—regarding matters pertaining to this life and the next—devotion remains with its full majesty, even without coming and going. (306)

Some [attain] the state of Śiva along with their vital breaths; some with their own bodies; some with their wives, their children, their homes, and their circles of kinsmen; and others with their villages and countries.
Having gradually abandoned all of this, including their attendants and others, some go forth by themselves as devotees. (307)
Some devotees, possessed of attachment toward objects such as the vital breaths and so forth, attain oneness with Śiva together with their companions.
Some, being skilled in detachment, having abandoned those sense objects, go of their own accord to that auspicious state. || 308 ||
In the Śivadharmottara, it is said:
"The primordial abode of Umāpati resembles ten million moons."
Endowed with all desires, it is pure, eternal, and inexhaustible. || 309 ||
Having attained this divine state, they are freed from all afflictions.
They are omniscient, all-pervading, pure, and perfectly complete. || 310 ||
They perform their duties with complete purity and are endowed with supreme sovereignty.
Both with bodies and without bodies, they always move according to their own will.
Those men who have attained the supreme state are devoted to the yoga of knowledge.
For them there is no return again to the terrible cycle of saṃsāra. || 312 ||
Thus, this is well known from such passages. Furthermore, in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, it says: "The passionless ones depart by way of the door of the sun."
In the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa it is said: "He attains union with Brahman, equality of power, and residence in the same world."
Thus, for those who have reached the world of Śiva, there is no returning again.
"Those who are liberated rejoice together with Śiva and go to the state of Śiva," according to the words of the Purāṇas.
In that very same [text]: "They attain unity with Brahman; therefore, it must be stated that liberation is indeed unity with Śiva, who transcends the paths (adhvan). || 313 ||
In the Anubhavasūtra,
the Śiva-āgamas spoken by Śiva range from the Kāmika to the Vātula.
Among them, this great scripture known as the Vātula is the most excellent of all. || 314 ||
In the great tantra known as the Vātula, according to its division into the eastern and northern sections.
In that which is named "The Northern," two parts have been fully described.
This is the Śivasiddhānta Tantra known as the Tantrottarapratīpa.
There, the Lord of Gods spoke to the Goddess concerning the determination of the six locations (ṣaṭsthala).
And by means of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Itihāsas, as well as the scriptures such as the Śivadharma and others.
The Śivasiddhāntatantra, which provides a definitive exposition on the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), is now being told.
By means of the Śiva-āgamas, which contain the secrets of Śiva’s non-duality and are of ultimate truth.
The Śivasiddhāntatantra, which provides a definitive exposition of the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), is now being told.
By all the sentences of the Upaniṣads and by the Purāṇas whose purpose is the latter [part of the Vedas].
And by all the scriptures of the Gītā, which are the ancient great thoughts.
The Śivasiddhāntatantra, which provides a definitive exposition on the six locations (ṣaṭsthala), is now being told.
Through the word of the guru, through one's own experience, through reasoning, and through valid means of knowledge.
It is called the Śivasiddhāntatantra, the determination of the six locations (ṣaṭsthala). || 320 ||

Thus, in the *Śivācārakathana*, which is an extraction of the essence of the conduct of the Vīramāheśvaras— the quintessence of the Vedas, Vedāntas, Śiva-Āgamas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Gītā, Śāstras, and ancient sayings.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Establishment of the Eligibility for the Knowledge of Brahman," in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the *Śrīmad-Vedāntasāra-Vīraśaiva-Cintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Niṣṭhuraśrīman-Nañjanācārya. Śrī.
Śrī.
Salutations to Śrī Śiva.
We shall explain how [this work] establishes the identity of the meaning of the Vedas and the Śaiva Āgamas.
Now, it may be argued that because this Vīraśaiva system is rooted in the Śaiva Āgamas and Tantras such as the Kāmika, it is not Vedic;

for those who follow a doctrine taught in non-Vedic Tantras have no authority [to practice] Vedic rites. Rather, its purpose is the induction of those who have strayed from the Vedic path into the Tantric path. Therefore, the Vīraśaiva system, being based upon that, is non-Vedic.
This is what is stated: || 1 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, the words of Reṇuka and Gaṇeśa addressed to Agastya:
O great sage, [this is] from the Sāṃkhya and other systems that abide in only a portion of the Veda.
The Śaiva Tantra is distinguished because it conforms to all the Vedas. || 2 ||
This is declared to be the Śaiva Tantra, known as Siddhānta, spoken by Śiva.
Because it embodies the meaning of all the Vedas, its authority is always equal to that of the Vedas themselves.
The Āgamas have been proclaimed in many ways by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
"Namely, through the divisions of Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula. (4)
Therein, he defines the various divisions of the Śaiva Āgamas.
Among them, the Śaiva tradition has four divisions; everything therein is definitively established.
The left, the right, and the mixed—these are known as the Siddhāntas. || 5 ||
Having there stated the characteristics of the Vāmā and other Āgamas, he shows that the Siddhānta is in agreement with the Vedas.
That which is called Vāmā is predominant in power (śakti), while the Dakṣiṇa is of the nature of Bhairava.
The Siddhānta, which is beyond the seven Mothers and is a synthesis, is in accordance with the Vedas. || 6 ||
Anticipating the question of what those treatises on established tenets (siddhānta-śāstra) are, they are now being defined.
The Śiva-āgamas, beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Vātula, were spoken by Śiva.
These are to be known as the established tenets, accompanied by their subdivisions. || 7 ||
With the doubt as to in what manner the Siddhānta scripture is in agreement with the Vedas, it is now examined.
In that very same [text].
The Śiva-āgama, known as Siddhānta, is so called because it proclaims the dharma of the Vedas.
Because it contradicts what is outside the Vedas, it is said to be "not approved by the Vedas. || 8 ||
He demonstrates the causal unity of the two Vedic systems established by Śiva.
In that very same [text]: "The Vedas and the Siddhānta are one, because they both establish the same meaning."
The wise should know that the validity of these two is always equal. || 9 ||

In the *Tātparya-saṃgraha*, it is stated: "Even while asserting that 'the Vedas are authoritative,' people understand your divine scripture to be authoritative; by this very statement, the authority of both the Vedas and the Āgamas must be fully acknowledged."

Based on the authority of the Vedic scripture, "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to all," the validity of the two Vedic doctrines established by the great seer Śiva is indeed unimpeded; having thus stated the identity of these Vedic doctrines, in that [context]...
The Siddhānta demonstrates the Vīraśaiva doctrine as the exposition of the identity of the meaning of the Vedas and the Śaiva Āgamas. || 10 ||
In the great tantra named Siddhānta, beginning with the Kāmika, as proclaimed by Śiva.
The supreme Vīraśaiva doctrine has been taught in the northern region. || 11 ||
In accordance with such statements as these, the resolution is now examined.

Furthermore, it is common to the scriptures that establish the superiority of Śiva that the Lord (pati) is the Supreme God, the individual soul (jīva) is the bound one (paśu), and everything insentient other than those two is the fetter (pāśa); moreover, the knowledge of this triad is the cause of liberation. || 12 ||
Thus it is stated in the Sūtasamhitā, in the fourth chapter of the Muktikhaṇḍa: "Beings beginning with Brahmā and ending with the immobile are proclaimed to be bound souls (paśus)."
I am their lord, O God; I am remembered by the wise as Paśupati.
O lotus-eyed one, I bind those bound souls with the noose of Māyā.
O fair-eyed one, I am the liberator of all those animals.
"The virtuous and eternal Śruti declares me alone to be the liberator. || 14 ||
In that very same place, in another section, the Lord of the World [taught] the Great Tantra consisting of three subjects and four chapters.
He spoke to the daughter of Himavat those dharmas which are the sole means for attaining liberation. || 15 ||

Among those, some Śaiva Āgamas expound the three categories of *paśu*, *pāśa*, and *pati*; some expound the supreme reality (*paratattva*) of Śiva; some expound the Supreme Brahman as the triad of forms (*trimūrti*);
and some expound the thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattva*).

Some [of these scriptures] expound the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), while others expound the Śaiva conduct (śivācāra), such as the wearing of ashes and rudrākṣa beads, the worship of the liṅga, the praṇava, the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara-mantra), and festivals dedicated to Śiva; since these Āgamas are rooted in the perceptible Veda (pratyakṣa-vedamūlatva), [they are authoritative].
Because validity is established, there is no burden in postulating invalidity;
for those [passages] that convey three distinct meanings—such as "So many indeed are the animals, both bipeds and quadrupeds; therefore Rudra is the lord of animals"—one should know the Lord.
The severing of all fetters through the exhaustion of the afflictions is the abandonment of all evil.

"By the practice of churning with knowledge, the wise man burns away the fetter," and "This is the Pāśupata vow for the sake of liberation from the fetters of the bound soul"— since such statements are heard in the direct Veda, the Śaiva scripture is based upon this kind of technical definition.
It is indeed Vedic. || 16 ||

For this very reason, the Rāmānuja system— which employs the technical categorization of the three principles of consciousness (cit), unconscious matter (acit), and the Lord (īśvara)— is indeed non-Vedic because it lacks a foundation in Vedic terminology; it is merely a pretense of being Vedic and should therefore be disregarded.

This is because it is rooted in the non-Vedic Pāñcarātra Tantra, and because it contradicts the Vedas by enjoining practices such as the wearing of ashes and rudrākṣa beads, which are well-known from direct perception and numerous Vedic scriptures.
The five forms of Brahman, namely Sadyojāta and the others,

are thus established by the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta found in the Nārāyaṇa-praśna of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka within the Yajurveda, as well as by the statements of the Bṛhajjābāla and other Upaniṣads.

The Śaiva Āgamas that expound this [reality] also possess authority because they are rooted in direct perception and the Vedas. Those [texts] which expound the supreme reality of Śiva state: "Śiva alone is the absolute," "the cessation of the manifold world, auspicious and non-dual, is the fourth," and "Rudra is indeed one; there is no second to him."

Because it is heard in various Upaniṣads of different recensions— such as in the *Bodhāyana*— that "Rudra is superior to all," by means of the negation of anything else, [he is] the proponent of the thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattva*).
By means of the twelve mantras beginning with prāṇa and apāna found in the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad, may Prakṛti, Rāga, Kalā, Vidya, Niyati, Kāla, Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara,
Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva— along with myself— be purified by the will of Paraśiva; I am light, stainless, and free from sin.
Because it is rooted in the *viraja* mantra with the exclamation "bhūyāsaṃ svāhā," it pertains to the scriptures that expound the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*)—

those which teach the sixfold division of the path as: "phoneme (*varṇa*), word (*pada*), mantra, aspect (*kalā*), world (*bhuvana*), and principle (*tattva*)"— and thus it belongs to those [scriptures] that expound the path.

The validity [of this] is established because it is rooted in the mantra, "O Lord of the paths, you are the end of the best of paths," which accords with the Vedic statement, "He attains the further shore."

The bathing with ashes, the smearing of ashes, the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and the wearing of rudrākṣa beads are well-known through hundreds of scriptural passages in various Upaniṣads of diverse recensions, such as the Atharvaśiras, Kālāgnirudra, Bṛhajjābāla, Bhasmajābāla, Rudrākṣajābāla, and Kātyāyana.

The wearing of the *liṅga* is well-known in the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, and other scriptures; it is to be seen in the subsequent section [of this work] in passages such as "Oṃ is Brahman. The *praṇava* (the syllable Oṃ) is traditionally taught in such texts; however, the five-syllabled mantra, "namaḥ śivāya," is found in the middle of the *Śatarudrīya* hymn, specifically within the eleventh section (*anuvāka*) of the *Yajussaṃhitā*.

The practice of festivals for the worship of Śiva and so forth is well-known; one should praise that [tradition] because the Śaiva Āgamas are rooted in the Mantras and rooted in the Bodhāyana Sūtras, and thus their Vedic character is established.
Therefore, the Śaiva doctrines, which have the same meaning as those [Sūtras], are indeed Vedic. || 17 ||
Furthermore:
The fool who is intent on reviling Śiva and who censures the scriptures of Śiva.
Has any atonement for that ever been seen by anyone, even in any scripture? (18)
In this context, "Śiva-śāstra" refers to that scripture which establishes Śiva as not attainable through other means of knowledge;
namely, the Vedas and the Śaiva Āgamas, which, because they were composed by the eternally existent, omniscient Lord who is self-established, are independent [of other authorities].
Its validity is unimpeded. || 19 ||

However, since the Purāṇas and Itihāsas serve as supplements to that [Veda], their authority is to be understood as being like that of the Smṛtis, on the basis of having the Veda as their source; such is the distinction to be observed. || 20 ||
And for those heroes who have undergone the Śiva-consecration, who possess knowledge and righteousness, and who are virtuous.
It is declared to have twenty-eight divisions and is remembered as Śaiva.
Thus it is stated in the Āgamas, the Vedas, and the Vedānta Upaniṣads.
But the great Dharma of Maheśvara is declared to be eternal for the sake of liberation. || 22 ||
But surely, in the Kūrma Purāṇa it is said: "Others follow the left-hand Pāśupata conduct and take refuge in the Pāñcarātra. (23)

If it is argued that because [the text] prohibits Vaidikas from following Tantric practices through such statements as "ityādi," the authority for Vaidikas lies only in the Dharma propounded by the Vedas and not in what is stated in the Tantras—[we reply: no. || 24 ||

If one accepts that a "Vaidika" is simply one who performs the conduct prescribed by the Vedas, then the injunction would be rendered purposeless with respect to him, since he has already been a performer of Vedic-prescribed acts prior to the injunction. Furthermore, if his status as a performer were established solely by the force of the injunction, there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*):

his status as a performer of Vedic-prescribed acts would depend upon his engagement with the injunction, and his engagement with the injunction would depend upon his status as a performer of Vedic-prescribed acts.

Even in the position that the Tantrikas have the authority for the dharma taught in the Tantras because it possesses Vedic character by virtue of being performed by those authorized by the Vedas, the same defect applies;
furthermore, [this would mean] that the Vaidikas lack authority for the dharma taught in the Tantras.
Since mantras such as the Praṇava, Gāyatrī, Śrīrudra, Puruṣasūkta, Pañcākṣara, Tryambaka, and Jātavedasa— along with their ancillaries (aṅgas), enclosures (āvaraṇas), mudrās, purascarana rites,
and ritual applications— are absent from the Vedas, the worship of these [mantras] along with their ancillaries would necessarily be prohibited; yet this is not an acceptable conclusion.

Furthermore, since in Vedic works such as the *Prapañcasāra* composed by Śaṅkarācārya and others, the description of the procedure for hearing [the scripture] pertains exclusively to that which is declared in the Tantras; and moreover, because it is prescribed by direct Vedic revelation in the passage: "This [mantra] of Soma and Sūrya establishes the universal liṅga, the pure mantra of the hand."
Since the various auxiliary rites— beginning with the selection of the site for the installation of the *liṅga* and ending with the consecration of the temple (*vimāna-pratiṣṭhā*),

as well as the chariot festivals (*rathotsava*) and so forth— as taught in the Śaiva Āgamas such as the *Kāraṇa* and *Kāmika*, are absent from the Purāṇas, it would follow that they should not be performed; yet this is not an acceptable conclusion.

And the substratum turns away from Śiva, the Supreme Self. || 54 ||
"In its own glory"—thus says the Vedānta, which is self-evidently authoritative and speaks the truth.
