Therefore, the Supreme Lord is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
He himself is always the Liṅga; no other Liṅga exists for him.
For those ignorant ones who have immersed themselves in the ocean of saṃsāra and whose minds have made their very selves [the object of] their intellect,
O bulls among the twice-born, for the sake of cultivation in accordance with the ripening of the mind. || 57 ||
Of the god Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is without support.
O wise ones, the support is imagined as if real through the consecration by mantra. || 58 ||
Others, the most learned in the Vedas, say that the *liṅga* is so called because it is a place of dissolution (*layana*).
Nevertheless, the Lord Maheśvara himself is the Liṅga. || 59 ||
This [universe], while dissolving, dissolves indeed into the true Brahman.
The Supreme Brahman does not dissolve, because its essential nature is eternally real.
O best of the twice-born, [this applies] to unreal things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like.
Dissolution is observed neither in the case of reality nor in the case of a fragment of mother-of-pearl. || 61 ||
And everything that is inauspicious, other than Śiva, dissolves into Śiva.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, the Liṅga is itself the imperishable Hara.
Other yogis and brahmins as well proclaim [this] of Śiva.
And in this body, which is the substratum, there are the signs of the Supreme Self.
In the fourth chapter of the Brahmagītā.
There exists a God, self-established, the witness of everything in every way.
He is the direct liberator from saṃsāra for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra. || 64 ||
And by him, the minds of all were impelled with constancy.
When there is an object, that which is the vital breath (prāṇa) moves, and speech also speaks.
The eye sees forms, and the ear likewise hears sound.
But by that very Self through which all things [exist], they are indeed impelled.
They proceed incessantly, directed toward their respective objects.
And its capacity to set [the world] in motion is also due to illusion (māyā), not by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva). || 67 ||
And the existence of the sense faculties is not at all considered to be intrinsic.
O best of gods, his [body] becomes as heated as a red-hot iron ball. || 68 ||
The Lord Maheśvara himself has superimposed both the sense of hearing and the self [upon one another].
Having entered it, Hara bestows the faculty of hearing upon the ear.
The Supreme Lord, having entered the mind which is superimposed upon the self, [perceives it].
Established in sattva, his mind bestows [the fruit] according to the rule.
Having attained the state of speech for speech, Hara assumed the nature of breath for breath.
In this way, you grant the eye of insight through the very practice of restraint.
But for the other imagined sense-faculties, Maheśvara is the cause.
Having assumed each respective form, he indeed bestows [the fruit] according to the rule.
In that regard, there are the eye, speech, the mind, and those other [senses] as well.
They do not go [into dissolution] within the Supreme Self, whose intrinsic nature is self-luminous.
That deity is other than what is known, and likewise other than what is unknown.
And likewise by speech, by mind, and by sight. || 74 ||
O best of gods, [this is true] even by means of the ear, the breath, or any other [sense].
"It is impossible to make it an object of experience; this which I have spoken is indeed the truth. (75)

On the basis of such scriptural statements, the consciousness of Śiva, though undivided, appears within the six substrates— the sense organs, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and so forth— gradually assuming, through those respective limiting adjuncts (upādhis),
the forms of the Great Liṅga, the Prasāda-liṅga, and the Cara-liṅga, corresponding to the aspects of Śiva, Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta.
The sixfold Liṅgas— namely, the Liṅga, Śivaliṅga, Guruliṅga, Ācāraliṅga, and those called Liṅgāhvaya— are the supreme state of Śiva.
Its detailed elaboration is to be seen in many ways throughout the preceding and subsequent chapters. || 76 ||
Furthermore, in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], in the Brahmavallī:
"He who knows Brahman— truth, knowledge, infinite, hidden in the cave of the heart within the supreme heaven— he attains all desires through the wise Brahman."

From this very Self, indeed, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, the person—beginning thus with the succession of the five sheaths (pañcakośa), it concludes with: "Bliss is its Self, Brahman is the tail, the support."
It is stated that Brahman is denoted by the words "space" (vyoma) and "bliss" (ānanda). In that very same [text]:
From which words turn back, along with the mind, unable to reach it.
It has been said: "The knower of Brahman as bliss fears nothing whatsoever. (78)
In that very same [text], by the passage beginning "From fear of Him the wind blows," etc., His very sovereignty of command which cannot be transgressed is declared.
In that same [text], starting from "That is one human bliss" (*sa eko mānuṣa ānandaḥ*), there is the presentation of blisses increasing by a hundredfold.
By the passage ending with "That is one bliss of Brahman," it is stated that bliss has Brahman as its presiding subject. || 80 ||
In that regard, in the Bhṛguvallī, beginning with the words, "From which indeed these beings are born," and so forth.
Ānanda knew that Brahman is bliss; indeed, from bliss alone these beings are born, by bliss they live once born, and into bliss they enter at their passing away.
This is his knowledge, belonging to Bhṛgu and Varuṇa, in the highest heaven.
In this context, it is stated that the words "Ānanda" (Bliss) and "Vyoma" (Space) have the same meaning. || 81 ||
In that very same Brahmavallī.

"He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate. He created all this, whatever exists here. Having created it, He entered into that very thing," and so forth; by such passages, His status as the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe and His nature as the inner controller of all have been declared. For who indeed could breathe, if this bliss were not in the ether?
For this, Ānanda, is indeed the meaning of the phrase "he goes": || 82 ||

If Śiva-Śakti, who is denoted by the term "Space" (Ākāśa) and whose nature is consciousness and bliss, did not exist, then which living being in the world would perform movement such as exertion, or which living being would even perform mere locomotion? For bliss, through the medium of enthusiasm, is the cause of activity; it is the repository of all and the essence of all.
The intention of the word "what" (kiṃ) is that [the world] is established as being endowed with bliss; thus it is stated in the *Brahmagītā*.
In the absence of this supreme bliss, even though it is the very nature of the selves, it does not manifest for them.
O gods, which man truly lives, or who indeed acts perpetually? (84)

In the Taittirīya, however, it says: "O Prācīnayogya, meditate upon Brahman as having space for its body, whose self is truth, who delights in breath, whose mind is bliss, who is the essence of peace, and who is immortal"—
thus [it refers] to the Power denoted by the word "space."
It has been stated that [Brahman] is to be meditated upon as the body of the Supreme Brahman; therefore, it must be said that Brahman, whose body is space, is the Liṅga. || 85 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, in the section concerning the Great Space (*mahākāśasthala*).
Consciousness alone is the supreme goal, whose essential nature is eternal bliss.
That which the sages, freed from all doubt, call the supreme ether.
The supreme space is unmanifest, characterized by the bliss of awakening.
They say the Liṅga is composed of light, wherein yogins dissolve.
Just as luminous bodies shine individually within the elemental ether.
In that same way, the cosmic eggs shine especially in the supreme ether. || 88 ||
Based on such scriptural authorities as these, it should be understood that Śiva alone, whose essential nature is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), is the Liṅga.

Furthermore, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad it is said: "All these beings indeed arise from space alone; they dissolve back into space; for space is greater than these, space is their ultimate resort. Thus, the fact that the power whose nature is the conscious space (cidākāśa) is the material cause of the universe has been stated.

Thus, this nature of Śakti— well-known through many such scriptural passages, denoted by the term "Ākāśa" and consisting of the form of consciousness-bliss— is [discussed] in the first section (*pūrvakhaṇḍa*) within the investigation into the non-duality of Śiva as qualified by Śakti, in the *Kūrma-vākya*, *Bhavānī-vākya*, and *Praṇava-vākya*...
This has been explained in detail through the words of Vyāsa, Śuka, and Śaṅkarācārya;
that should also be kept in mind here. || 90 ||
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, in the latter part, in the chapter on the Origin of the Liṅga within the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Upamanyu.
Relying upon the complete meaning of the Atharvaśikhā, it is said: Kṛṣṇa said:
What is this that is called the *liṅga*, and how is Maheśvara the possessor of the *liṅga* (*liṅgin*)?
And how does he possess the nature of a sign? Why is he called Śiva in this context? || 91 ||
Upamanyu said:
The unmanifest is declared to be the subtle body (liṅga), which is imperishable and the source of the three guṇas.
That which is the beginningless and endless material cause of the universe.
That very thing is the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), illusion (māyā), and has the nature of space (gagana).
From that very source, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings has arisen.
That which is impure, pure as it were, pure, and both pure and impure—thus it is threefold.
Then Śiva, Maheśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha [arrived]. || 94 ||
And by the command of Śiva, the elements and those born from the senses dissolve.
Therefore, Śiva, as the possessor of the Liṅga, shall then command the Liṅga.
For it is from that very source that the universe, once born, undergoes dissolution.
By this alone its status as a sign is established, and not by anything else whatsoever.
And the liṅga is the body of Śiva and Śivā, because it is presided over by them both.
Therefore, Śiva along with Ambā is worshipped there eternally. || 97 ||
The pedestal of the linga is the Great Goddess; the linga is the Lord Maheśvara.
Therefore, by the worship of that alone, the two gods themselves are truly honored. || 98 ||
In ultimate reality, the state of possessing a subtle body does not exist for those two.
Since those two are pure by their own nature, the body is [pure] only through metaphorical designation. || 99 ||
This very material cause of the six paths, known as Pure Māyā, the Śiva-tattva, which is the nature of Śiva’s eternal substratum, must be called the Great Liṅga (mahāliṅga). || 100 ||
It should be understood that this very Mahāliṅga is the pedestal (pīṭha) for the previously mentioned Niṣkala Śiva-liṅga, whose nature is Cidambaram;
thus it is stated in the preceding section. || 101 ||

In the *Liṅgasūkta* of the *Bāṣkalasaṃhitā*: "Seeing both Brahmā and Viṣṇu engaged in battle, bound by enmity through the quality of passion (*rajas*), Agni Jātavedas stood between them as Sthāṇu Rudra, the protector of the world; seeing Sthāṇu, they ceased their combat."

"Viṣṇu, desiring to see the boar, set out for a great distance; having submerged himself in the earth, Brahmā quickly flew up to heaven as a vulture"—by such passages, it is stated that [the Lord] is "exceedingly radiant beyond the worlds. (102)
Therefore, it has been stated at the beginning of the Ṛgveda: "I praise Agni, the domestic priest. (103)
In this matter, according to the *Kāraṇāgama*: "Fire is his ash; for there is no other [fire] than the one whom I praise as the domestic priest (*purohita*)."
Śambhu is the consumer of the Ṛgveda, the sky-goer, the one born of Yoga, and fire; such is the Vedic revelation. || 104 ||
The words of the Lord to the Goddess in the Kāśīkhaṇḍa:
O noble lady, you alone are the Jyotirliṅga, and I am the Liṅgin, Maheśvara.
Therefore, O beloved, behold this very light known as Avimukta.
O Jābāli!
Kuru-kṣetra is indeed the unliberated, the sacrificial ground of the gods for the gods.
"It is the abode of Brahman for all beings," so it is said in that very same place.
"This infinite, unmanifest Self is established in Avimukta."
And its supreme location is between the eyebrows and the nose.
The junction of the eyebrows and the nose is the junction of this world and the world beyond.
In the Mānava Purāṇa: "Vārāṇasī is situated at the junction of the eyebrows and the nose."
Therein lies the field of Avimuktaka, where Rudra is eternally present.
In the Liṅga, in the form of light, he is directly named Viśveśvara. || 208 ||
So it is in the Puruṣasūkta, in the Mantropaniṣad, and likewise in the Śivasamkalpa.
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent as the sun, beyond the darkness. 109.
In the Mahāliṅga Purāṇa.
The Liṅga-form is the light of Śiva, situated above darkness.
That very same supreme unmanifest [reality] is adorned with a circle of light.
That is the imperishable, the supreme light; that is the highest step of Viṣṇu. || 110 ||
In the Śivadharmaśāstra.
Within the center of the liṅga is the entire universe, the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving.
There is nothing superior to that which is external to the *liṅga*; therefore, one should worship the *liṅga*. || 111 ||
In the Reṇukāgama.
In the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, in the Liṅganirṇaya section, and in the Kāmikāgama.
They call the unmanifest the subtle mark (liṅga), the root cause of the worlds.
The view that Maheśvara is the possessor of a *liṅga* is inconsistent with reason.
He is indeed Śiva himself, the stainless one, consisting of the bliss of consciousness.
It is called the *liṅga* and nothing else, from which the origin of this universe proceeds. || 113 ||
Others, likewise, say that the knowledge born from the Vedānta texts is the *liṅga*.
The Śruti declares that the supreme Liṅga, consisting of light, is of the nature of Śiva.
By its light all this shines forth; of this there is no doubt.
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon, nor lightning, nor fire. || 115 ||
There are no stars when the supreme Self shines forth as the Great Liṅga.
Therefore, the Liṅga is the Supreme Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Through meditation on "one's own form," that state is produced. || 116 ||
In the Kāmikāgama, it is said:
"The pedestal is the supreme Śakti; the liṅga is Paraśiva himself in person."
Through the union of Śiva and Śakti, the universe is called that Liṅga.

Therefore, it is stated in the preceding section that within the Vedas— which consist of a collection of various Upaniṣads belonging to the branches (śākhās) of the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvaṇa— the Liṅga alone is propounded at the beginning, middle, and end. || 118 ||
Thus, it is well-established that [the term] is synonymous with the names "Brahman" and "liṅga"; enough of this excessive detail. || 119 ||

Thus, in the *Śivācārakathana*, which is an extraction of the essence of the conduct of the Vīramāheśvaras— the quintessence of the Vedas, Vedāntas, Śiva Āgamas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Gītā, Śāstras, and ancient sayings— [ends here].
In the *Śrīmad-Vedāntasāra-Vīraśaiva-Cintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Ācārya Annaṅga Niṣṭhura Śrīman, in the Uttarakhanda,
the fourth chapter, titled "The Synonyms and Names of the Word Brahmalinga," is complete. Śrī.
Śrī.
We shall now explain the sequence of the compassionate grace of the Guru for those seeking liberation.
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* of the *Reṇukāgama*, in the section concerning the *piṇḍa*:
"When the cage of sins has been destroyed by merits accumulated over many births..."
The embodied soul with a purified internal organ is designated by the term "piṇḍa" (the body). || 1 ||
In this conceptualized phenomenal world produced by Śiva and Śakti.
Abounding in merit, with sins destroyed, he is a pure-souled one known by the name Piṇḍa.
The wise know that Śiva alone is directly composed of consciousness and bliss.
He is free from conceptual construction, without support, devoid of qualities, and beyond phenomenal proliferation. || 3 ||
The connection with beginningless ignorance arises from a portion of that [Self], and these are designated as "jīvas."
They are established within the various distinctions of birth, such as gods, animals, humans, and so forth. || 4 ||
The illusory Maheśvara, dwelling within their hearts, is their impeller.
Just as water [appears] in the moonstone, and fire in the sunstone. || 5 ||
Just as the sprout is established within the seed, so Śiva abides within the self.
The nature of the self and the nature of the Lord are both imagined within the one Brahman.
Just as the state of being the original image and the state of being the reflection are both conceived in the sun;
Through the differentiation of the three qualities within the Supreme Reality, which is of the nature of consciousness.
The state of being an enjoyer, the state of being an object of enjoyment, and the state of being an impeller are all merely imagined.
The eternal power, consisting of the three qualities, is established in Brahman.
From the imbalance of those [humors], there arises the designation of the three types of entities within that [body].
The Brahman-consciousness, whose limiting adjunct consists of the supreme reality (paratattva), is the Lord (Īśvara).
That which consists of a certain degree of sattva and rajas is called the "experiencer."
That which has the quality of darkness (tamas) as its ultimate limiting adjunct is called the "object of enjoyment" by the wise.
The enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—these three are known as the fundamental realities.
It is imagined within the indivisible Brahman-consciousness through the differentiation of qualities.
In this context, the impeller is Śambhu, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose limiting adjunct (upādhi) is pure.
All those who possess mixed attributes are known as bound souls (paśus) and experiencers (bhoktṛs). || 12 ||
The unmanifest is said to be the object of enjoyment, having the nature of pure tamas.
Śambhu is the omniscient impeller, while the individual soul (jīva) is said to be possessed of limited knowledge.
That which is utterly hidden consciousness is called the insentient unmanifest.
It is further designated as "with substrate" (upādhi) due to the distinction between the pure and the impure. || 14 ||
The supreme Māyā, which causes delusion, has pure adjuncts and resides within its own substrate.
Even so, the impure limiting adjunct (upādhi), which is the locus of ignorance, causes delusion. 15.
Due to the differentiation of the power of ignorance, living beings are said to be of many kinds.
By the power of his illusory energy (māyā-śakti), the Lord, the Sovereign, assumes manifold forms. || 16 ||
The Great Lord is omniscient, the creator of all, and eternally liberated.
He is a doer of little, a knower of little, bound, and possessed of an eternal body. || 17 ||
Living beings, deluded by ignorance, are devoid of the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman.
They wander through saṃsāra in accordance with their own karma. || 18 ||
Due to the distinctions among various types of birth, such as gods, animals, humans, and so forth.
For embodied beings indeed revolve according to the sequence of the wheel's rim. || 19 ||
Karma alone is the cause of the diversity of birth, lifespan, and experience.
The Supreme Lord is the witness and the impeller of these embodied beings.
Of these beings who wander perpetually, constrained by the machine of karma.
Śambhu is the impeller of embodied beings and the one who shows the path to their welfare.
Through the ripening of his own karma, the latent impressions of his impurities have been utterly destroyed.
By the grace of Śiva, this living being has become pure-minded.
When the individual soul (jīva) possesses a pure internal organ due to the ripening of pure karma, [it attains liberation].
Through the compassion of Śiva, the divine devotion becomes fully manifest.
This living being in its final body is designated by the term "piṇḍa" (the physical aggregate). || 23 ||

"Because of the statement, 'In this regard, due to the connection with beginningless ignorance, those who are portions of Him are designated as individual souls (jīvas),' it is stated that all individual souls are portions of Śiva."
For this very reason, it is said that living beings possess the nature of Śiva. || 24 ||
In the Haṃsa Upaniṣad, it is stated that one should meditate upon the Self as the Haṃsa within the heart: Agni and Soma are its wings,
Oṃkāra is its head, the Bindu is its third eye, Rudra is its face, and Rudrāṇī its feet—
thus described is the form of Śiva as qualified by Śakti.

In accordance with the intended meaning expressed by Bhagavatpāda— that "I worship that indescribable, auspicious pair, moving within the minds of the self-restrained (yamins), which has the nature of the swan to be meditated upon as the object of worship in the heart"—
it is perceived as the manifestation of the very nature of Śiva qualified by Śakti. || 25 ||
Bodhāyana also said: "He who should say 'Haṃsa, Haṃsa,' [knows that] 'Haṃsa' by name is Sadāśiva."
Then one should meditate upon oneself in the form of Rudra, as three-eyed and five-faced.
Thus, the nature of the swan as being identical with Śiva has been stated. || 26 ||
In the seventh chapter of the *Brahmagītā*, it is stated:
"If the individual soul thus perceives its own form as Śiva with firm conviction..."
He always performs the play of delight within his own self alone, and nothing else.
In that very same [text].
In the divine city of Brahman, within the ether, Śiva is directly established.
Consisting of mind, the leader of the body of vital breaths, he is established within every heart-lotus.
By the knowledge of that, they are completely liberated from whatever appears as the nature of the body of bliss.
The knot of the heart is broken, and all doubts are severed.
And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both higher and lower is seen.
In that regard, [it is explained] in the sixth chapter.
He who has been described as the "small ether" is the Supreme Lord.
He is eternal, existing as distinct from the specificities of the body and so forth. || 32 ||
The states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep which appear to embodied beings—
Even for her, the Great God himself, the Lord, is the witness as one who is distinct.
In that [Self], she both shines and does not shine by way of being superimposed as a form. || 33 ||
In that very same [text].
Therefore, Śambhu is by his very nature the support of all and the pervader of all.
This self is supreme and all-pervading; it is never [attained] by means of all meritorious deeds.
O gods, such a witness is not struck down by sins; he is free from death and free from old age.
Free from sorrow, free from desire for victory, and free from thirst, he is characterized by truth and other such virtues.
O bulls among the gods, he is likewise one whose desires are true and whose resolve is true.
This is because of the authority of such scriptural statements as these.
The individual soul, established in itself, becomes liberated through the knowledge of Śiva. || 36 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"In this wheel of Brahman, the Haṃsa wanders, perceiving himself as distinct from the Impeller."
By this, being delighted, he attains immortality. || 37 ||
In that very same [text].
The self, being powerless, is bound by its state as an enjoyer; but by knowing God, one is released from all sins.
"The Knower and the Unknower, the two unborn ones—the Lord and the Non-Lord; for the one who is unborn is indeed joined with the object of enjoyment for the sake of the enjoyer.
And the infinite Self is of universal form and is a non-doer. When one perceives these three as 'This is Brahman'—" || 38 ||
In that very same place.
There is one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form.
For one unborn soul, taking delight, lies along with her; another unborn soul abandons her once she has been enjoyed.
Two birds, inseparable companions, dwell upon the same tree.
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit of the pipal tree, while the other looks on without eating.
Upon the same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by a sense of powerlessness.
When he perceives the Lord as distinct and beholds His majesty, then, freed from sorrow, he rejoices. (39)
And in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, beginning with "Two birds," it says: "When he perceives the golden-hued one, the agent, the Lord,
the Person who is the source of Brahman."
Then, the wise one, having shaken off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equanimity. || 40 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad]:
"Having known the God, there is the abandonment of all evils; with the afflictions exhausted, there is the abandonment of birth and death.
Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace. (41)
By the authority of such statements as these, the attainment of liberation by the individual soul through the knowledge of Śiva occurs. || 42 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad]: "Having made one's own body the lower fire-drill and the syllable Om the upper fire-drill..."
By the practice of churning through meditation, one beholds the Divine like something hidden.

Oil is in sesame seeds, clarified butter in curd, water in flowing streams, and fire in flint-stones; even so, this Self is perceived within the self by one who beholds it through truth and austerity as the all-pervading Self, like clarified butter contained in milk. That Brahman, whose root is the knowledge of the Self and austerity, is the supreme secret teaching (upaniṣad).

“Having known the unborn, eternal, and pure God through all principles, one is released from all sins”—thus it is said in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad. Indeed, this Self is established in the divine city of Brahman, within the ether.
Consisting of mind, the leader of the body of vital breaths, it is established by others having fixed their hearts upon it;
through the knowledge of that, the wise behold the immortal form of bliss which shines forth. 45.
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, and all doubts are cut away.
And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both supreme and non-supreme is seen.
In the supreme golden sheath is the stainless Brahman, devoid of parts.
That pure light, the light of lights, those who know the Self know it to be such. || 47 ||
Brahman alone is this immortal reality in the east, in the west, in the south, and in the north;
it extends below and above; Brahman alone is this entire universe, this most excellent. Thus [ends the section]. 48.
And in various branch Upaniṣads as well.
Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being.
Free from sorrow, he beholds Him—the Lord of majesty, the Creator of desire—through the clarity of the elements.
The meaning is: "the element of the Supreme Lord. || 49 ||
In the seventh chapter of the *Brahmagītā*:
"Two birds, known as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśa*), dwell together in this body."
Of those two, the individual soul (jīva) experiences the fruit of karma, not the Great Lord (maheśvara). || 50 ||
The distinction between these two, imagined through māyā, manifests of its own accord.
Just as space is divided into the space within a jar and the great space. || 51 ||
The individual soul, which is imagined as being distinct from supreme consciousness, is itself imagined as having the form of Śiva.
Śiva is directly the imagined [form], and the conscious individual soul is always [Śiva] by his own nature.
For the nature of both Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) is always pure consciousness alone.
That being so, how can there be equality in that which is pure consciousness alone and devoid of differentiation?

If it is argued that the wearing of the *liṅga* should not be practiced because it was not mentioned by the authors of the Sūtras such as Bodhāyana and Āpastamba, we reply to this as follows.
In the *Caturvedatātparya-saṃgraha*, that which is known through direct Vedic revelation is celebrated in the Purāṇas and has been extensively set forth by the sage Bodhāyana.
"Even the procedure for the vision of all goals has been forgotten by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras, like the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) at the end of worship"—

it follows that the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras [have neglected] the worship of Śiva, which is well-known from various Vedas, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas, just as they have neglected the sacred thread.
Just as that was forgotten, it should be understood that the wearing of the *liṅga* has likewise been forgotten by them.

It must be stated that the wearing of the *liṅga* should be performed by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), because it is well-known in direct perception, the many Vedas, the Āgamas, the Purāṇas, and the Itihāsas. || 2 ||

Furthermore, because it removes the ignorance of one who is veiled by ignorance, bestows knowledge, and makes known the hidden reality, it is called a *liṅga*; therefore, the wearing of the *liṅga* must be performed. || 3 ||

Furthermore, since it is heard that the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras expound the rules for the constituent parts of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), what fault is there in their not stating that the wearing of the *liṅga*— which is taught in the Upaniṣads— is a constituent part of knowledge (*jñānāṅga*)? Such is the wearing of the *liṅga*.
It is enjoined by direct Vedic revelation itself. || 4 ||

"This [mantra] of Soma and Sūrya establishes the universal Liṅga; it is the purifier of the hand"—thus is the wearing of the Liṅga (liṅgadhāraṇa) described.

Here, having prescribed the installation of the Liṅga by means of the statement "he establishes the universal Liṅga," when there arises the expectancy as to what the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for that installation of the Liṅga is, [the text specifies] "the mantra of the hand" (*pāṇimantra*).

Because "pavitram" (purifier) is a qualifying attribute of the *liṅga* (the sacred thread), its wearing on the hand and other parts of the body is enjoined. It is called *pāṇimantra* because it protects (*trāyate*) through meditation (*mananāt*) upon the hand; thus, just as the *yajñopavīta* is described as "the supreme purifier" (*paramaṃ pavitram*), so too is this [thread] a purifier at the time when impurity might arise during acts such as ritual purification (*śauca*) and sipping water (*ācamana*).
From the injunction regarding the *pavitra* [ceremony], it is understood that it should be worn at all times; thus it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
