If the vow of the Prāṇaliṅga is broken, no expiation is prescribed.
Therefore, one should hold it with great care, lest one’s life be lost.
The meaning is that, based on such statements from the Purāṇas and Āgamas, [this practice] should not be performed out of negligence.

Thus, for those Vīraśaivas who are exempt from [ordinary] expiatory rites, there exist Āgamas and Purāṇas that prescribe the relinquishment of life— consisting of the contemplation of oneness with the Liṅga— in the event of the loss of the Liṅga or the loss of their vow.
It should be understood that the Veda alone is the root source. || 15 ||
In another work: "O God, salutations to you, the Brahman, the teacher, the great-souled one."
The refutation of that [view] is indeed by Death alone, because it is produced by the universe.
O supreme teacher, may there be for me no rejection [of this teaching], but rather its firm retention.
It is well known in the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas, and has been heard by me with my own ears.
"This liṅga of mine, which is the refuge of Śiva, was carried away by me from that person. || 17 ||

In another passage: "Oṃ! May there be retention for me, may there be no forgetting; may I be a retainer of what is heard in my ears; may it not be cast away from me or from such-and-such a person—Oṃ!"
"Oṃ" means the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga, which is the Supreme Brahman; the rest has been explained.
Regarding this matter, there is an elaboration in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Oṃ is the Supreme Brahman, Maheśvara in the form of the Liṅga."
In all states and at all times, even for half a moment. || 19 ||
O best of the twice-born, desiring both enjoyment and liberation without separation [from the deity].
One should maintain [the mind] fixed upon these five locations with a concentrated mind.
And that divine form was whispered into his ear by the Guru.
One should constantly recite the five-syllabled king of mantras, which is established in the Vedas. || 21 ||
"In this matter, may I be a bearer [of the Veda]," so says the Śruti in the Ṛgveda.
This hand of mine is the Blessed One; this [other] hand of mine is even more blessed.

"This is my universal remedy; this is the auspicious touch. This is the mother, this is the father; this has come as the restorer of life. This is your crawling-place, O Subandhu; come forth, leave the snake!"

The meaning of this is as follows: "This is my hand; this is my hand. [Regarding the term] *bhagavān*: he possesses *bhaga*, therefore he is *bhagavān*. Thus, is the word *bhagavat* a designation for one who is worthy of worship? "This is my most venerable one (*bhagavattara*); this is my most venerable hand. The suffix *-tara* exists here in the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*).

Therefore, this hand is thus distinguished: "This hand of mine is the universal medicine. This hand is the universal medicine—that is, the physician for the disease of existence, the illusory manifestation (*māyā-prapañca*) of the universe. This is the "auspicious touch" (*śivābhimarśana*); the word *abhimarśana* does not merely denote physical contact, but rather—
He touches from all sides and all around, thus he is Abhimarśana;
because he touches every limb of the Liṅga-form with the tips of the branches of his own palms, he is Śivābhimarśana.
This is the mother, this is the father, this very hand is the father, this is the life-sustainer—this very hand indeed.

"Jīvātuḥ" means a life-restoring medicine; according to Amara, "jīvātuḥ" is a life-saving drug. This "prasarpaṇam" of yours—*prasarpaṇam* meaning procreation, which signifies the generative organ (*liṅga*)—is adorned with the excellence of the Vedas, known as the Supreme God, and is fully embellished as the source of procreation. (As stated in the *Śrī Rudra Bhāṣya*).
Because it is defined as that which brings forth [the world] by being the cause of the universe.
In the *Yajurveda*: "For your glory, O Maruts, they honor you; O Rudra, that birth of yours which is beautiful and wondrous (*citra*).
Regarding the phrase "that supreme station of Viṣṇu which was established," it is said: "The secret name is 'the name of the cows' (*gonāma*). Here, "birth" (*janima*) is a name for a *liṅga*;
"wondrous" (*citra*) means "to be admired" or "to be honored. Therefore, "gliding forth" (*prasarpaṇa*) is a name for a *liṅga*.
Subandhu means one with a beautiful bond; that is to say, one who is a kinsman to those in distress.
The address to him is "O Subandhu. This crawling of yours is a sign [of your devotion].
"Come" means "approach"; "nirahi" means "reside here forever. The meaning is that you must never be released from my hand. || 22 ||
Regarding this point, it is stated in another treatise: "This hand of mine is the Blessed One; this [other hand] of mine is even more blessed."
"By the constant touching of Śiva and by the wearing of the Śivaliṅga. || 23 ||

In the Ṛgveda: "Your filter is stretched out, O Brahmaṇaspati; as the Lord, you encompass its limbs on every side. That which is uncooked does not reach it, nor does the one whose body is not heated; only those who are purified and strong partake of it."
The meaning of this is as follows: in the vocative "Brahmaṇas-pate," the use of the nominative case is a Vedic anomaly; [he is] the Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings.
"May Brahmā, the sovereign of Brahmā, the lord of Brahmā, the auspicious Śiva, be ever propitious to me"—thus from the mantra "Sadāśivom."
This Lord is Brahmaṇaspati; that Brahman is called the Liṅga.
For that [place] is renowned as sacred; by contact with it, the body becomes pure. || 25 ||

Based on the corroborative statements of the Skanda Purāṇa, Brahmaṇaspati—the supreme Śiva, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and stainless (nirañjana)—is called this "liṅga" which is the very nature of Brahman. The use of the word *ta* (it) instead of *etad* (this) is an archaic Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), as seen previously. That very liṅga is [the subject].
It is known as "pavitram" (purifying) because it specifically protects one from falling into the ocean of hell; this is well-established and renowned.

To address the question of what connection this *liṅga* has with the protection of persons from the ocean of hell, he says: "The Lord of all" (*viśvataḥ prabhuḥ*). Here, by that word "all" (*viśva*), the bound souls (*paśu*) existing within the universe are meant.
They are perceived. || 26 ||
From Brahmā down to the stationary beings,
[all belong] to the trident-bearing God of gods.
Those who are subject to the power of saṃsāra are proclaimed to be like cattle.
Because he fell upon them, Śiva, the Lord of Gods, is remembered as Paśupati.

The meaning is that, because of this statement, due to their falling [at his feet], and because the relationship of master and servant between him and that Liṅga is established by its very nature, it is entirely appropriate for this Liṅga to provide protection for those animals. || 28 ||

He explains the very manner of that protection: "He seeks out the limbs" (*gātrāṇi paryeṣati*). The limbs (*gātrāṇi*) are the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, the sense organs, and the internal organ—all these constituent parts.
Having cast away the objects such as sound and so forth through his own conjunction with them, he himself abides within those sense organs and [withdraws] them.

Having first accepted objects such as sound and so forth, and then having given those objects back to them in their purified form, you seek out [the Self]; "you seek out" (*paryeṣi*) is the second-person singular verb form used by way of transposition from the third person.
For this very reason.
Whatever pleasure arises from the senses, that has been offered to Śiva.
That various grace is to be experienced through the medium of those respective sense organs.
The *iṣṭaliṅga* is in the external limb, while the *prāṇaliṅga* is likewise within.
The liṅga of existence is forever well-established within this very limb of the Self.
And the Liṅga is established in the limbs of the heart according to the proper sequence.
"Likewise, the subtle body (liṅga) is established sequentially within the limbs of the organs of action. || 31 ||

From the statement of the *Vātula-āgama*: "Because learned Brāhmaṇas of tranquil mind eat only what has been eaten by Rudra, drink what has been drunk by Rudra, and smell what has been smelled by Rudra,
[they partake of] the *nirmālya* alone."
And because of the Vedic revelation: "They eat only the *nirmālya*; one should resort to the *nirmālya* alone; one should consume only the *nirmālya*. || 32 ||
Thus,

it should be understood that this very Śruti is the root source for all the Āgamas and Purāṇas which establish the worship, dedication, and focused attention upon the Yoga of Brahman in its six stages, characterized by the union of all limbs and the Liṅga. || 33 ||

He states that for those devoid of mastery over the senses and lacking austerity, there is no attainment of the supreme state due to the absence of union with the *liṅga*, based on the Taittirīya statement: "Seek to know Brahman through austerity."
Because of the statement in the Brahmopaniṣad: "The knowledge of the Self has austerity as its root."
In the phrase "ataptatanuḥ," the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative.
Since there is no body apart from the sense organs such as the ears and eyes, the word "body" (tanu) here refers to the sense organs.
"Untormented" means not restrained; thus, one whose body and senses are untormented is "untormented in body and uncontrolled in senses," which means he is ignorant.
The "raw" (āma) person—one devoid of Śiva-initiation due to the absence of the digestion of impurities—does not attain that Liṅga; he does not reach it.
To the question of who, then, does attain that Liṅga? [the text responds:]...

Based on the statement from the Yajurveda, "O Rudra, that body of yours which is auspicious, not terrible, and which destroys evil," he says that only those who are disciplined and have become free from sin through the initiation of Śiva attain [this state].
"Those who have taken refuge" means those who have taken refuge in the auspicious dharma (*śivadharma*);
whatever persons there may be who carry that [dharma] and bear its emblem (*liṅga*), they alone, in brief, attain the *liṅga*, and no others.
The meaning is that those devoid of austerity, devoid of the purificatory rites of Śiva, and lacking the wearing of His liṅga, do not attain the supreme state. || 34 ||
Regarding this matter, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Brahmaṇaspati is indeed the Lord; that Brahman is called the Liṅga.
For that is renowned as the sacred purifier; its Lord himself is omnipresent.
Through contact with that, it itself makes the limbs pure.
Indeed, one whose body is unheated and who is devoid of the refinement of raw matter is truly a kingless man. || 36 ||
Devoid of initiation, one shall not directly attain the supreme liṅga.
Those who rely on the Śiva-dharma, who are peaceful, and who are devoted to the worship of Śiva. || 37 ||
Those who always carry the liṅga go to the supreme state.
Otherwise, O Goddess, it is not possible to attain me; such is the sacred revelation (śruti).
Regarding this matter, it is stated in the Kāśīkhaṇḍa:
The supreme, stainless sky, free from all impurity, is situated within the body.
That which transcends birth, death, and old age is declared to be pure. || 39 ||
Because it protects one excessively from falling into the ocean of hell.
That which is the purifier among all purifiers is that Liṅga, the light of the Lord.
Through contact with that, it will indeed make his limbs pure.
O Goddess, this supreme jyotirliṅga is identical with you.
The supreme abode of Śiva-bliss is difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined their selves.
Those who have always taken refuge in the Liṅga carry it with constant devotion.
All of them attain me alone in this matter; of this there is no doubt. || 42 ||

In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, in the section concerning the wearing of the *liṅga*, there is a statement by Reṇuka and Gaṇeśa addressed to Agastya: "O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is Aghora and the destroyer of sin..."
Since he is praised with the Yajus mantras, therefore Śiva is free from all evil.
The Linga is declared to be Brahman, and its Lord is Brahmaṇaspati.
For that is renowned as pure; by contact with it, the body becomes clean.
He says "Ṛk": "The filter is spread out for you, O Brahmaṇaspati."
Therefore, that pure Śaiva liṅga, which is free from all affliction, should be worn.
Indeed, one whose body is unheated, who is without sovereignty, and who is devoid of the refinement of raw material [is such].
One who is devoid of initiation shall not directly attain the supreme liṅga.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, he whose body has performed austerity is called Taptatanu.
One who is matured for liberation attains the wearing of the *liṅga*. || 47 ||
He who does not first perform austerity is said to be one whose body has not been refined by heat.
This one is unripe; this one is unrefined; such a person does not attain the fruit of wearing the *liṅga* for the sake of liberation. 48.

This is well known from such sources as the *Atharvaśiras*, in its concluding section. Beginning with "That is to be worshipped" and ending with "This is the Pāśupata vow," the Pāśupata system—consisting of the wearing of the *liṅga* and the application of ashes—is defined. (49)

In that regard, this very [path] is to be meditated upon: "Let speech speak it; let it be grasped within. This path is stretched out by the north, by which the gods, by which the seers, and by which the ancestors reach the supreme station, the ultimate goal."

"In the center of the heart, [is] the Lord of the universe, Jātavedas, the most excellent, [the size of] a mere tip of a hair; those wise ones who behold Him abiding within themselves—for them there is eternal peace, and not for others. (50)
An exposition is now commenced for the purpose of explaining the passage beginning with "That this should be meditated upon."
This very thing should be meditated upon: that small, stainless lotus, the abode of the Supreme, situated in the center of the city.
Even there, that which is within the small, sorrowless space—that is what should be worshipped.
Because of the statement of the Taittirīyas. || 51 ||
The supreme space is unmanifest, characterized by awakening and bliss.
They say the Liṅga is composed of light, wherein yogins dissolve. || 52 ||
Immeasurable and indescribable, it is worshipped by those seeking liberation.
The supreme Brahman is the great Liṅga, beyond the phenomenal world and imperishable.
That very [Self] is within all beings, its range being the three abodes. || 53 ||
According to the statement from the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, that which is under discussion is well-known as the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*).
The meaning is that this very form of the small ether, the *prāṇaliṅga*, is to be meditated upon and worshipped by those seeking liberation.
Let that speech speak; let that very organ of speech, the faculty of speech, speak on the subject at hand.
Let him perform the praise with "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya"; therein lies the inclusion [of all]. 54.
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, in the section concerning the wearing of the *liṅga*:
"The supreme *liṅga* of Śaṅkara is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), the cause of all."
That which is its retention in the mind is described as being immediately thereafter. || 55 ||
Either in the foundation (ādhāra), or in the heart, or continuously in the space between the eyebrows.
After the contemplation of the Jyotirliṅgas, there is the wearing of the Liṅga. || 56 ||

According to this scriptural statement, "that" refers to the aforementioned *liṅga* itself; "the end" means that which resides within the navel, the heart, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), namely the *prāṇaliṅga*; "grasping" means its retention.
"This is the broad path"—
thus it is stated in the Puruṣasūkta, the Śvetāśvatara, the Kaivalya, the Śivasamkalpa, and other Upaniṣads, and there is no other.
"There exists a path for proceeding," because this excludes any other path. || 57 ||
For embodied beings who are fearful and situated within the mouths of the serpents of existence.
"Devotion alone [leads] to Virūpākṣa; there is no other path"—such is the Śruti. || 58 ||
From the corroborative statement, "This path," the meaning is that this path of wearing the *liṅga* is extensive and well-known, as expressed in the verse beginning with "yena devāḥ. || 59 ||

In the Yajurveda, from the scriptural statements: "O Maruts, you grant joy for Your glory," "O Rudra, that birth of Yours which is beautiful and wonderful," "That supreme station of Viṣṇu which has been established," and "The secret name, the name 'Go'," [it is established]. || 60 ||
The great Viṣṇu [worships] the Raudra Liṅga, known as Janimā, which is made of stone.
Having worshipped Cārucitra, he attained the supreme state. || 61 ||
From the statement in the Parāśara Purāṇa.
Viṣṇu always worships a linga made of sapphire.
By that [means], he attained the eternal and singular wonder that is Viṣṇu-hood. || 62 ||
This is because of statements from the Śivadharmottara and other Purāṇas.
The deities, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Sureśa, were filled with supreme joy.
They bear the Śiva-liṅga upon their heads day and night. || 63 ||

This is according to the statement of the *Kāmikāgama*. The meaning is that by means of which path of wearing the *liṅga*, all deities beginning with Hari, Brahmā, and Indra attain the supreme state. [And] "by means of which the sages... [and so forth].
On their necks were the sages beginning with Harakaṇṭha, as well as the Manus.
They always wear the Śiva-liṅga and worship it. || 65 ||
Thus, according to the statement in the Purāṇakāmika Āgama.
In the *Dharmasaṃhitā* of the *Śaiva Purāṇa* and in the *Śaivasaṃhitā* of the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini.
Pāṇini, Kaṇāda, Kapila, Gautama, and the others.
Through the cultivation of serenity, through meditation, through worship, and even through dhāraṇā;
Having been born as those who perform the act of seeing, they cause the three worlds to hear [the teaching]. || 66 ||
Thus, from the words of Vyāsa.

The meaning is that sages such as Bhṛgu, Upamanyu, Devala, Dadhīci, Dūrvāsas, Vasiṣṭha, Kapila, Gautama, Vāmadeva, and others, by means of the northern path characterized by the wearing of the *liṅga*, attain the supreme state; thus it is said, "by which [path] the ancestors [attain it]. || 67 ||
In the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā: All the ancestors in our lineage desire that sons endowed with devotion to Śiva shall be born among us.
They shall become virtuous beings of pure disposition; among them, let even a single one bear the outward mark (liṅga).
By its power, we two shall attain the world of the Lord, partaking in infinite satisfaction.
For in this way, having attained the state of the heavenly world, those ancestors constantly long for oneness with Śiva. (69)

According to this statement from the Śāṅkara-saṃhitā, the meaning is that all the ancestors attain the supreme state by the path of wearing the liṅga on the north [side]. In the middle of the heart— that is, in the center of the heart-lotus—
is the Lord who is the soul of the universe, as subtle as the tip of a hair or the awn of a grain of wild rice (nīvāra).
Jātavedas, whose nature is self-luminous. || 70 ||
In the Taittirīya and the Bṛhannārāyaṇa [Upaniṣads].
The heart, moreover, resembles the interior of a lotus bud and is turned downward.
Below, at the end of a span from the navel, it stands above the *viṣṭi*.
Enveloped by garlands of flames, it shines as the great abode of the universe.
At its end is a subtle cavity; in that, everything is established.
In its center is a great fire, with universal radiance and faces on every side.
By [the passage] beginning with "thus," etc.
In its center, a flame of fire, extremely subtle, is situated pointing upwards.
She was radiant like a streak of lightning situated in the midst of a dark blue rain-cloud. || 73 ||
Thin like the awn of wild rice, yellow, radiant, and resembling a minute particle.
In the center of that crest, however, the Supreme Self is established.
Having thus proclaimed the Supreme Self as the object of worship in the Dahara-vidyā, the immediately following section begins with:
"Homage to Nidhana, homage to Nidhanapati, homage to the Urdhva, homage to the Urdhvalinga," and so on, up to: "Homage to Śiva, homage to Śivalinga, homage to the Ātman."

"Salutation to the supreme Self-liṅga; salutation to the supreme; salutation to the supreme liṅga"—thus is described the nature of the liṅga of Śiva, that is, of the Supreme Self (paramātman), who is the Liṅga of Śiva. Here, the word *ātman* ending in *-ā* is a Vedic form (*chāndasa*). || 75 ||
In this matter, O Lord of Yogins, I shall speak of the definition of the Tāraka-Brahman in the *Yogamaṇidarpaṇa*; listen to that:
"In the midst of fire is the station of the sun, and in the midst of the sun is the moon. (76)
In the midst of that is the sprout, joyful, the heart, possessing a divine form.
He was illuminated by streaks of lightning flashing within a dark blue cloud.
Subtle like a sprout of wild rice, the golden lamp is comparable to an atom.
And at the tip of that self's head, he [visualizes] the Śakti in the form of the Praṇava.
She is endowed with the powers of sound, the point, and the digit, and her form has the appearance of a star.
One should know that above the Śakti is the Liṅga, which has the form of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni).
Resembling ten million suns, it was a mass of radiance like ten million moons.
Indeed, this Liṅga has been described by yogis as the Tāraka-Brahman. || 80 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "The Person, the size of a thumb, the inner self, is eternally seated in the heart of all people. (81)
In the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad: "The Person, the size of a thumb, stands in the middle of the self."

By stating "the Lord of what has been and what is to be," having thus declared the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), it is described that the qualities of the individual soul, such as being the size of a thumb, are merely adventitious (aupādhika).
In that very same [text]: "The person is the size of a thumb, like a flame without smoke."
Based on such authoritative sources as "The Lord of the past and the future," the term *jātavedas* refers to that which resides in the center of the heart-lotus;
its meaning is the *prāṇaliṅga*, consisting of consciousness and having the nature of smokeless fire.
The most excellent, the best, abiding within the self. || 83 ||
Making the self the lower fire-drill and the syllable Om the upper fire-drill,
Through the practice of churning with meditation, one may behold the God as if he were hidden.
Just as oil is in sesame seeds, butter in curd, water in flowing streams, and fire in the fire-drills, so too does the Self arise within the self. || 85 ||
Regarding this point, it is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Brahmopaniṣad and elsewhere, beginning with the words: "Having made the Self the lower fire-drill..."
Thus the Self is grasped within the self by that very being who perceives it through austerity. || 86 ||
In the *Brahmopaniṣad*: "Consciousness resides in the heart; it is the supreme, most pure sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
In the *Īśvaragītā*: "For those engaged in ritual action, [the sacred thread] is in fire; for the wise, it is in water, in space, and in the sun."
For the ignorant, the *liṅga* is in wood and such materials; but for yogis, it is in the heart.
In the Kāmikāgama, it is stated that the supreme, pure, and stainless Liṅga is the eternal Brahman.
That which is designated as Śiva is pure consciousness alone, eternally blissful and unrestrained.
He is the cause of all worlds and even the cause of the Vedas.
The fulfillment of all reality and the crossing over the ocean of birth. || 90 ||
Consisting of light, indescribable, it abides within the self of yogis.
How is it known that in the world there is no great teacher [who is] compassionate? || 91 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, regarding the location of the *bhāvaliṅga*: "Either in the *mūlādhāra*, or in the mind, or in the middle of the eyebrows—[it is] perfectly pure."
The practitioner of yoga should worship the linga in the form of a lamp with substances representing the elements of existence.
The meaning is that, by virtue of such scriptural authorities, the sign of the Supreme Self (paramātmaliṅga) is established within one's own self.
The wise, who possess perfect knowledge, behold that Śiva in the form of the *prāṇaliṅga* through their venerable Guru. || 93 ||
In the Kaivalya Upaniṣad:
"That by which the manifold world of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, is illumined..."
Having realized "I am that Brahman," one is liberated from all bonds.
Whatever is to be enjoyed, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoyment within the three abodes;
I am the witness, distinct from them, pure consciousness alone, the eternally auspicious Śiva. || 95 ||
Within the body, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being.
"Free from sorrow, he beholds Him—the Lord, the Greatness—through the clarity of the element, as one whose will is His own. (96)
In the *Brahmavallī* of the *Taittirīya*, based on such statements as, "He who knows Brahman— truth, knowledge, infinite—

hidden in the cave of the heart, in the supreme ether, he attains all desires through the omniscient Brahman," [Brahman is defined] by means of an indirect definition (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*) characterized by the exclusion of what it is not (*atad-vyāvṛtti*).

The meaning is that they perceive the Supreme Śiva, known as the *prāṇaliṅga*, which is pure consciousness alone, distinct from the visible world, and characterized by an eternally perfect nature of truth, consciousness, and bliss; having known that Lord, they attain ultimate peace.

Based on such statements as, "Having known [the Self], one attains liberation; having known the Lord, one is released from all bonds," it follows that for those who contemplate the internal Liṅga, there is eternal peace; the meaning is that they attain perpetual liberation.
Not for others. || 97 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather...
Then, by not knowing Śiva, there will be an end to suffering. || 98 ||
According to this statement, the meaning is that for others who are devoid of the knowledge of Śiva, whose nature is the *prāṇaliṅga*, there is no eternal liberation. || 99 ||

Furthermore, in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, regarding the section on the nature of the *liṅga*, it is said: "Others likewise declare that the knowledge born from the Vedāntic statements is the *liṅga*. (100)
Thus, in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, within the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*, it is stated:
"Some say that the *liṅga* of Śiva is the knowledge of the supreme Self through the realization of Vedānta.
Therefore, it must be said that the *liṅga* is indeed the very nature of the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Ātman. 101.
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "For this Self is established in the divine city of Brahman, within the ether."
Consisting of mind, the leader of the body of vital breaths, he is established with others having placed their hearts [upon him].
By the knowledge of that, the wise behold the immortal one consisting of bliss which shines forth. 102.
The knot of the heart is rent asunder; all doubts are severed.
All karmas are exhausted when that which is both supreme and non-supreme is seen.
In the supreme golden sheath is the stainless Brahman, devoid of parts.
That pure light, the light of lights, those who know the Self know it to be such. || 104 ||
There the sun does not shine, nor do the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine there.
"From where does this fire come? The lightnings shine"—from such a statement of the Upaniṣad. || 105 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, the Śruti declares that in the place of one's own *liṅga*, there is the supreme *liṅga* consisting of light, whose essence is Śiva.
By its light all this is illuminated; of this there is no doubt. || 106 ||
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon, nor lightning, nor fire.
When the supreme Self shines forth as the Great Liṅga, there are no stars.
Therefore, the Liṅga is the Supreme Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Through meditation on "one's own form," that state is produced. || 108 ||

This is because of such scriptural statements; and because of authoritative evidence from such declarations as: "The supreme Śaiva state is well-known from the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Āgamas, wherein the Brahman known through the Dahara-vidyā, when endowed with the power of Prāṇa, is indeed the Prāṇaliṅga."
This very thing is to be worshipped; by such statements as "let that speech speak" and "that is the internal grasping," the wearing of the *prāṇa*-liṅga is declared. || 109 ||
In that very same Atharvaśiras, further on.
They say that within the vital breaths is the mark of the mind, in which reside anger, thirst, and forbearance.
Having severed thirst—the root of the net of causes—and having reflected with the intellect, one should establish it in Rudra; thus they speak of oneness with Rudra.
The meaning of this is as follows: "In the vital breaths"—that is, within the five vital breaths—"of the inner mind," meaning of the inner heart, "they say there is a sign";
the meaning is that the wise say it is the *prāṇaliṅga*. Within which subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) is anger... [found].

Anger exists, and that which exists is craving; craving is the root of the web of causes, the root of the web of causes for saṃsāra. Having severed craving—which consists of the desire for states such as those of Brahmā and others—by means of dispassion, one cuts it away.
Having reflected with the intellect, having meditated upon it, and having established it in Rudra. || 110 ||
Having established the vital breath (prāṇa) within the liṅga, one should establish the Śāmbhava-liṅga within the vital breath.
Having made the mind incorporate the body, one should not think of anything at all.
This is called "internal devotion" by the Śiva-yogins. || 111 ||
Thus, from a statement in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā.
In that very place: "Having placed the life-force of the disciple into the Śivaliṅga, which is your seat..."
Having established the liṅga within that vital breath, it then becomes a prāṇaliṅga.
Because it has been stated thus: "Having taken the breath of the disciple, one should deposit it there in the *liṅga*."
One should establish that talliṅga within his vital breath with single-minded devotion.
Thus, from the statement in the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi.
Having united the body with the vital breath, one should project that breath into the *liṅga*.
Therefore, due to their inseparable connection, one should conceive of them as a unity. || 114 ||
Thus, from the statement of the Śuddhākhyatantra.

Having established and settled the subtle body in the form of vital breath within Rudra—the Liṅga whose nature is Rudra—one attains oneness with Paraśiva, who is Rudra in the form of the Liṅga. || 115 ||
Having become Rudra, one should worship Rudra; one who is not Rudra should not perform the practice of Rudra.
He who is connected with the body of the Prāṇaliṅga is Rudra; of this there is no doubt. || 116 ||
Thus, from the statement in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā.
The meaning is that they call oneness "sāmarasya" (equilibrium). [This will be explained] further below.
This Pāśupata vow bestows through austerity the fierce, eternal, ancient, desired, and vigorous [state].

The meaning of this is as follows: the *raudra* [liṅga] is of the nature of Rudra; it is eternal (*śāśvata*), indeed constant (*nitya*), ancient (*purāṇa*), primeval (*cirantana*), and powerful (*ūrja*, *ūrjita*). || 117 ||
This is the manifest *iṣṭaliṅga*, which directly wards off all that is undesirable.
The wise person should always wear it upon their body with focused attention. || 118 ||
Thus, according to the statement from the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, the meaning is that the *liṅga* is desired because it wards off what is undesirable.

"Through austerity [one attains] self-knowledge; austerity is the root"—from this statement of the *Brahmopaniṣad*, and "Inquire into Brahman through austerity"—from this statement of the *Taittirīya*, [the Lord] bestows liberation by means of virtuous practices such as the worship of Śiva; this is the meaning. "This is the vow," so it is said. (119)
In the Vātula-āgama, it is said that with an exceedingly steady mind, one [should serve] the Teacher of the World for as long as life lasts.
He who bears the liṅga of Śiva—this indeed is the supreme vow.

Because it has been stated thus, and according to the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* which says "the Vīraśaiva is one who observes the Great Vow," this vow—the vow of wearing the internal and external liṅga—is the Pāśupata, meaning the supreme Śaiva path. || 121 ||

In the subsequent section, he states the ancillary practice for its worship: "Fire is ash, wind is ash, water is ash, earth is ash, space is ash; indeed, all this is ash. The mind and these senses are ashes. Having taken up the ash with the words beginning with "fire," and having rubbed it over the limbs...
"One should touch [this]; this is the Pāśupata vow for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).
Thus, by means of the application of the external and internal liṅga, the rule for the wearing of ashes is declared for the Pāśupatas who worship Śiva, as indicated by the wearing of ashes.
It must be stated that the conduct of Śiva—such as the wearing of ashes and rudrākṣa beads and the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra—is to be practiced;
the meaning is that this Pāśupata vow is the supreme Śaiva path for the sake of liberating the bound soul (paśu) from its bonds (pāśa). || 122 ||
In the Vātulāgama, known as the *Tantrottarapradīpa*.
The Prāṇaliṅga, which is graspable by the mind, is both with parts and without parts.
"The Śruti declares that the mark [of the mind] is within the vital breaths. (123)
The entire great site of the desired liṅga is perceivable by the faculty of sight alone.
It constantly brings about the attainment of what is desired and the avoidance of what is undesired. || 124 ||
Iṣṭi is worship by which [the deity] is constantly desired and honored with reverence.
This is called the "chosen liṅga" (iṣṭaliṅga) by the teachers who worship the liṅga.
Whatever desired and vigorous fruit one seeks through austerity, from that [austerity] it is obtained.
Therefore, the Atharvaṇa Śruti declares that this is the desired liṅga.
In the ancient Gītās, it is stated that wives, sons, friends, and others should constantly wear the Śiva-liṅga;
"the wearing of the liṅga within them" is the doctrine of the Śruti, according to the words of the ancients in the Atharvaśiras.
The wearing of the Vīraśaiva liṅga has been clearly and unobstructedly declared. || 127 ||

Thus, it should be understood that this very Śruti is the root source for all the Purāṇas and Āgamas of Hari, Brahmā, Indra, the Suras, Asuras, the lords of Munis, and others, which establish the wearing of the Liṅga. || 128 ||

For this very reason, in the Skanda, Liṅga, Kaurma, Śaiva, and other Purāṇas that set forth the Pāśupata vow, relying upon the meaning of the Atharvaśiras, there are verses concerning Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and all the other gods, asuras, and lords of sages, such as: "Viṣṇu always worships a liṅga made of sapphire," and so forth.
The wearing of small liṅgas made of sapphire and other precious stones has been mentioned therein;

it should be examined there, as it is not written here for fear of prolixity. This very Pāśupata vow is called the Śirovrata because it is known from the Atharvaśiras, and it is also stated in the Muṇḍakopaniṣad.
In the conclusion of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, it is said: "One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the head-vow has been performed according to the rules. (129)
Regarding this matter, it is stated in the Sūtasamhitā: "O best of sages, I have [already] imparted to you the realization of Vedānta."
By those twice-born ones who have indeed performed the Pāśupata vow with devotion, [they attain the goal].
"Instruction should be given only to them; such is the teaching of the Vedas. || 130 ||

Thus, it has been stated that only those who observe the head-vow (śirovrata) known as Pāśupata and who bear the *liṅga* possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman; furthermore, the unity of purpose among the Pāśupata head-vow, the ultimate stage of life (*atyāśrama*), and the Śambhava vow has been declared.
And the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman has already been stated previously. || 131 ||
In the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi: "One who is always pure, wearing the liṅga, and endowed with sacred ash and rudrākṣas..."
The yogi who recites the five-syllabled mantra is remembered as a devotee of Śiva.
Thus, one who is endowed with such conduct is a Vīraśaiva, a practitioner of the Great Vow (mahāvratī). || 132 ||
It must be stated that he alone is qualified for the knowledge of Brahman.
Furthermore, those who say that this wearing of the marks is not prescribed in the Vedas; || 133 ||
That Brahmin who knows the four Vedas but does not know the Purāṇa according to its meaning;
Seeing him, he became afraid, thinking, "May this Veda not leap toward me. || 134 ||
From the statement of the Sūtasamhitā: "One should augment the Veda by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas."
The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He might lead me astray. (135)

In the Mahābhārata, according to the words of Vyāsa, the meaning of the cited scriptural passages must be understood in accordance with their elaboration as stated; thus, the wearing of the *liṅga* should be performed by all seekers of liberation, and so everything is both faultless and pleasing to the heart. || 136 ||
In the Brahmopaniṣad and in the Paramahaṃsa and other Upaniṣads.
In the heart, within consciousness, resides the supreme, most purifying sacred thread (yajñopavīta), which was innate to Prajāpati from the beginning.
Bestow upon him the foremost longevity and the pure sacred thread; may there be strength and splendor for him. || 137 ||
Having shaved his head including the top-knot, the wise man should discard the sacred thread.
One should hold that which is the imperishable Supreme Brahman to be the Sūtra. || 138 ||
They say that it is called a "sūtra" because it indicates; a sūtra is indeed the supreme state.
The Brahmin by whom that Sūtra is known is one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
By which all this is strung together, like clusters of jewels on a thread.
The yogi who perceives the reality of the knowledge of yoga should uphold that sūtra.
The wise man, established in the supreme yoga, should cast off the external thread.
Whosoever, being conscious, should uphold this Sūtra which is the very nature of Brahman. || 141 ||
By upholding this sūtra, one shall neither be defiled by food remnants nor become impure.
The Sūtra is internal for those who wear the sacred thread of knowledge.
They indeed are the knowers of the Sūtras in this world, and they are the ones who wear the sacred thread.
But those Brāhmaṇas and others who are authorized for Vedic ritual acts [should perform them].
This sutra is to be upheld by them, for it is indeed remembered as the constituent part of ritual action.
He whose topknot consists of knowledge and whose sacred thread likewise consists of that.
The knowers of Brahman understand that his entire status as a Brahmin belongs to him.
In the sixteenth chapter of the Laiṅgya [Tantra]:
"And the worlds are established upon it, like clusters of jewels on a thread."
That is to be known as the Sūtra, the wonderful form of the Lord. || 144 ||
When the cause arrived, Prakāśa said: "O bulls among sages, having summoned and seen the lord of sages, worship him."
Those proficient in the use of ashes and rudrākṣas [should wear] one made of crystal or stone.
The eternal linga consists of Śiva and Viṣṇu, and is the threefold thread.
The sacred thread is the supreme purifier, along with faith.
O you who are learned in the Vedas, worship Him upon the seat of His lotus-hand or upon a ritual pedestal.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Brahmā departed for Satyaloka.
But because it is interwoven, it is continuous even within all composite objects.
Because it indicates the Supreme Lord, the Sūtra is known as the Liṅga. || 148 ||
One should hold that which is the imperishable Supreme Brahman to be the Sūtra.
By wearing this sūtra, one shall become neither impure from remnants of food nor unclean. || 149 ||
By virtue of such scriptural authority as this, [the sacred thread] is called the *trivṛt* cord.

The meaning of this is as follows: the three—Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña—are the triad of individual souls (jīva) who identify with the three bodies known as the gross, subtle, and causal; or rather, the "jīva" refers to that which has the Sūtra as its covering, wherein the internal Supreme Self is veiled by the iṣṭaliṅga, prāṇaliṅga, and bhāvaliṅga.
The meaning is that it is the Great Liṅga, consisting of light, designated as "Sūtra" because it pervades everything like a thread through a cluster of jewels. || 150 ||
In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], it is stated: "Brahman has space as its body. || 151 ||
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Verily, from space alone these beings are born; into space they pass away; for space is greater than these, space is their ultimate resort. (152)
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "Upon that syllable in the highest heaven, all the gods have taken their seat. (1.2.153)

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, when Gārgī questioned Yājñavalkya: "That which is above the sky, O Yājñavalkya, or that which is below the earth, or that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—in what, then, is all that woven to and fro? Yājñavalkya replied to Gārgī: "In space alone, O Gārgī, is all that woven to and fro."
The meaning is that, because of such statements as "and what is woven through," the Sūtra is indeed the Jyotir-liṅga, whose nature is the all-pervading space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 154 ||
In this regard, in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, it says: "In the space of the Great Ether (*mahadākāśa*)."
Just as the space contained within a cosmic egg is not distinct [from space], so it is with the Self.
They know the Great Space (mahākāśa) to be the undivided Supreme Self. || 155 ||
Just as space is not divided within jars or within huts.
Likewise, the Self residing within eggs and within bodies is indeed not divided. || 156 ||
Free from the connection with limiting adjuncts, stainless, and consisting of pure consciousness.
The supreme ether is the supporting wall for the display of the world's manifold variety.
Consciousness alone is the supreme limit, whose essential nature is eternal bliss.
That which the sages, freed from all doubt, call the supreme ether.
The supreme ether is unmanifest, characterized by the bliss of awakening.
They say the Liṅga is composed of light, wherein yogins merge.
Inexpressible, incomparable, and beyond the sphere of speech and mind.
It is endowed with faces on all sides, consisting of the essence of existence, bliss, and consciousness.
Beyond time, beyond parts, and devoid of sequential yoga.
Established in the authority of one's own direct experience, it is the place of the rising of all lights. || 161 ||
The supreme Brahman, known as Śiva, is characterized by the ultimate space.
That without which the stability of the world does not exist is called the *liṅga* by the wise. (162)
Just as the luminaries shine individually within the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa).
In that same way, the cosmic eggs shine especially within the supreme ether. || 163 ||
Just as waves and the like are not distinct from the essential nature of the ocean.
Then this entire universe is not distinct from Śiva, the space of consciousness. || 164 ||

Based on such scriptural authorities, it must be stated whether the "thread" (sūtra) refers to the nature of the space of consciousness— the all-pervading, pure existence known as the partless *liṅga*—
or whether the *liṅga* itself, which is Brahman consisting of the threefold triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, is the "three-stranded thread" (*trivṛtsūtra*).
It must be stated. || 165 ||
In the *Yogatattvopaniṣad*: "There are three worlds, three Vedas, three junctions of the day, and three gods."
The three qualities reside in the three fires; all of them are established as having three syllables. || 166 ||
When a confusion of syllables occurs among the three, half a syllable is added.
By that all this is strung together; that is known as the supreme state. || 167 ||
From this Upaniṣadic statement, the meaning is that the trivṛt-sūtra is indeed the supreme Brahman itself as the liṅga.

By the word "and" (ca), the meaning is that it consists of the nature of Śiva and Śakti. This well-known supreme reality of Paramaśiva, the Liṅga, they—the seekers of refuge—know as the "threefold thread" (trivṛtsūtra);
this is the meaning of the term *yajñopavīta* here.

In the Purāṇas, it is well known that Nārāyaṇa is the Śiva-liṅga and the Śakti-pīṭha. According to the Vedic scripture, "Yajña is indeed Viṣṇu," the meaning is that the liṅga—which has specifically gone near (upa-ita) the pīṭha named Yajña-Viṣṇu—is the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread). Furthermore, "yajña" signifies worship (*pūjā*).
Therefore, the meaning is that the sacred thread (upavīta) is worthy of worship. || 168 ||
Likewise, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā and the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi of the Śaiva tradition, it is proclaimed: "That knowledge which is born from the Vedānta is designated as 'Vidyā'."
He who delights in that knowledge is called a hero. || 169 ||
This should be performed by the Śaivas and Māheśvaras, both internally and externally, in due sequence.
Śiva and Maheśvara do not differ from one another at all in this regard. || 170 ||
In whatever way they may differ, the Śaivas and the Māheśvaras are nonetheless not distinct.
Those men who take refuge in Śiva and are devoted to the sacrifice of knowledge are known as Śaivas. || 171 ||
They are known on earth as Māheśvaras, devoted to ritual sacrifices.
Therefore, the Śaivas should be inside, while the Māheśvaras should be outside.

Thus, according to the statements of the Purāṇas and Āgamas— such as "The Vīraśaivas are intent on the worship of the Jñānaliṅga situated in the center of the heart-lotus, while the Vīramāheśvaras are devoted to the worship of the Kriyāliṅga held in the center of the lotus-like hands"— the term *yajña* refers to worship, and the sacred thread (*upavīta*) consists of the worship of both action and knowledge.

The meaning is that the *liṅga* itself, whose essence is the Supreme Brahman, is the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Now, if it is argued that the three-stranded cord is merely a thread and that there is no fruit to be gained from wearing it—since even the four goals of life (dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa) would then belong only to those who wear rags, waistbands, or bracelets—[we reply: [this is not so].
The three-stranded thread, consisting of the three genders, is determined to be the Supreme Brahman. || 173 ||
In that very same [text]: "But those Brāhmaṇas and others who are authorized for Vedic ritual action..."
This sutra is to be upheld by them, for it is indeed remembered as a constituent part of ritual action.
In this context, the meaning is that the aphorism is a limb of action, i.e., an indicator of action.

In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, regarding the section on the marks of action (*kriyāliṅga*), it is stated: "All ritual actions, such as sacrifices and the like, are considered to be portions of the worship of the Liṅga."
Thus, that which is worshipped by the Siddhas is called the *kriyā-liṅga*. || 175 ||
Having abandoned all ritual activities, they were solely intent upon the worship of the Liṅga.
All yogins abide [in it]; therefore, the liṅga is preeminent. || 176 ||
Thus, the meaning is that the sign of action (kriyāliṅga) is the desired sign (iṣṭaliṅga).

In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*: "When there is a longing for the contemplation of the internal *liṅga*, no interest arises in the external; whether one is unable or indeed able to hold the *liṅga* within."
One should wear the external liṅga, being certain that it is of that very form. || 177 ||

Thus, because of the statement that "a longing for the external worship, meditation, and so forth of the chosen *iṣṭaliṅga* does not arise when there is an application of attention toward the internal *antarliṅga*," it is said: in what manner does the application of attention toward the internal *antarliṅga* come about? || 178 ||
In various Upaniṣads, such as the Brahmopaniṣad and others.
Making the self the lower fire-drill and the syllable Om the upper fire-drill,
"By the practice of churning through meditation, one may behold the God as if he were hidden. (179)

The meaning of this is as follows: having made the individual self (jīvātman)—which identifies with the three bodies and consists of the limbs and physical form—the lower fire-drill (adharāraṇi), and having made the Praṇava [the upper fire-drill]. || 180 ||
Nāda should be known as the liṅga, and bindu is declared to be the pīṭha.
The form endowed with sound (nāda) and the point (bindu) is here said to be in the shape of a liṅga.

According to this statement, having made the desired *liṅga*— which is the very nature of the syllable *oṃ* or *praṇava*— the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*) and the vertical fire-drill (*ūrdhvāraṇi*), through the practice of churning by means of meditation;

Because of the scriptural statement, "One should wear the external *liṅga* with the conviction that it is of that same form," through the practice of churning meditation upon His nature— which is eternal, perfect, and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss— one perceives the hidden God who resides within one's own self, just as fire is hidden within pieces of wood.
The meaning is that one should perceive Śiva as pure consciousness, whose nature is self-luminous and whose form is the partless liṅga. || 182 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*: "The wise one, through the churning of joy arising from the fire-drill of the Self..."
One should burn the entire web of bonds consisting of the world with the fire of knowledge. || 183 ||
In the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, in the section on the samādhi of Śiva-yoga,
it is proclaimed that the supreme Brahman is the Great Liṅga, while the vital breath is the individual soul (jīva).
Because of the contemplation of that single state of being, one is proclaimed as established in samādhi. || 184 ||
Just as fire does not manifest in the fire-drill wood without the act of friction, so it is in the case of the sign of action.
Likewise, without ritual action, Śiva, though abiding within, would not become manifest. (185)
In the sixth chapter of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"Having known that cause, which is to be attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, one is released from all fetters by knowing the God."
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire.
In the *Viśeṣārthaprakāśikā*: "By the repeated negation 'not this, not this,' that which remains is the supreme state."
Since it is impossible to deny its existence, be happy with the thought that "it exists. || 187 ||
Thus, by the negation of all categories of reality, the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of Brahman in its nature as pure consciousness is indeed Sāṃkhya-yoga.

According to the statement of the *Brahmopaniṣad*, "Consciousness abides in the heart," this very nature of the Supreme Self, which is to be attained through Sāṃkhya-yoga, [is realized] through the union with the power of the vital breath (*prāṇa-śakti*).
It should be called the *prāṇaliṅga*. || 188 ||
In the *Śivayogapradīpikā*, concerning Rājayoga, Sāṃkhyayoga, and Anantaryayoga.
Beyond this is a further secret, endowed with visible proof.
O friend of my vital breath, hear from me this yoga, which is established through my own experience. (189)
The eyes were then always half-closed, slightly opened.
He who perceives Brahman with the eye of the mind is the sovereign of yogis.
Between the moon and the sun, those two stars of steady radiance.
And having joined the two bindus, one should practice the Brahmatāraka.
One who is intent on the vision of Brahman within the external, internal, and intermediate marks.
Indeed, behold those whose natures are both seen and unseen! 192.
In that very place: "And the mind is an extreme secret, the great abode of the luminaries."
The site of the divine liṅga has been seen; now hear about its inner essence, which consists of one hundred thousand [parts].
Neither abiding within nor pervading without, its nature is immediate perception.
The space within the space is indeed that very internal focus. || 194 ||
He who proceeds with a mind absorbed in the *lakṣa* (the object) by means of the wind (prāṇa), with his gaze unflinching, shall become [liberated].
Now, this very [state] is Khecarī; by means of that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, he is indeed the Teacher of the World. || 195 ||
The space between the root of the palate and the dvādaśānta consists of the nature of the internal power (pratyakkalā).
Having focused the mind upon that light within one's own heart, gradually... [196]

Those self-controlled ones who, with an unblinking gaze fixed on the tip of the nose and an external vision directed toward the target, perceive with a hidden glance of contemplation upon Sadāśiva that immovable light which is the very nature of reality— devoid of externality within the heart— they alone have achieved their life's purpose in this world. (197)
The liṅga faces westward and has the shape of a fresh bangle.
Facing the east, look, look at this great wonder! || 198 ||
When water, light, the syllable Om, Brahman, the immortal, and the auspicious Self [are realized as one]...
That which the wise perceive is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Like the orb of the full moon, like a lamp of excellent jewels, like the midday sun, and like a flame of fire, it is eternal.
Like a flash of lightning, the wondrous Śiva-liṅga blazes within a hundred thousand leagues; beholding this very Self-liṅga before one's eyes, what is the use of other delusions of ritual action?
O limb, worship Him with the eight mental flowers beginning with non-violence.
Flowers, non-violence, restraint of the senses, compassion, forbearance, and what is called knowledge—these are [the requisites].
Through these very means—meditation, austerity, and truth—one should thus worship the perfected Linga within one's own self.

Having filled the mouth with air, having drawn up the apāna into the abode of the fire (the stomach), and having held it there while blocking the six openings of the hands with the thumbs and other fingers of both palms; thus [one should practice].
Through this path, the wise— whose minds are absorbed in the various sounds of the true *praṇava*— behold signs within the ears, the eyes, and the pair of nostrils.

Thus, by means of the six-faced mudrā, one should perform the contemplation of the light-liṅga (jyotirliṅga), which consists of the essence of nāda, bindu, and kalā, and is composed of consciousness (cinmaya). || 203 ||
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-shaped abode;

The meaning of the Vedic scripture, "Obeisance to the Lord of those possessing the mass of Indra’s matted hair," is as follows: the word *indra* is derived from the verbal root *idi*, meaning "supreme sovereignty."

Because of the phrase "due to the preeminence of the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvaraparatvāt*), and because the genitive case in the word *jaṭākalāpīnām* (of the masses of matted hair) indicates that the vow of wearing matted hair has the purpose of pleasing the Lord, the expression "their lord" (*teṣāṃ patiḥ*) denotes a unique relationship, specifically the particular relation of owner and owned.

Since such a relationship is understood as being the object of the intended meaning (*tātparya*)— as it is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*māna*)— this [text] has the injunction for the vow of wearing matted hair (*jaṭādhāraṇavrata*) with the aim of pleasing the Lord (*īśvaraprīti*) as its purport.
Nor should it be asked how this sentence can be considered Vedic in the absence of a recitation divided into word-order and phonetic analysis (*padakrama-vibhāga-pāṭha*).

it should be practiced by all without hindrance as being Vedic, just like the wearing of the sectarian mark (liṅgadhāraṇa).
