In the Mukutāgama,
it is stated that within all six supports (ādhāras), there is the six-syllable mantra beginning with the Praṇava.
Having established [the mind] and remaining constantly mindful, one should recite the auspicious five-syllabled mantra. || 35 ||
Alternatively, one should also visualize the jewel-lamp within the sixfold foundation.
Or else, in the form of the *liṅga*, [one should worship] in sequence within the pavilion of the support (*ādhāramaṇḍapa*).
Having recollected [the deity] in the form of light, one should mutter the six-syllabled mantra.

Based on such scriptural authority, one should understand that within the six supports (ādhāras), there are six kinds of liṅgas— beginning with Ācāra-liṅga and ending with Mahāliṅga— which consist of six syllables starting with *na* and ending with *oṃ*, respectively. || 37 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, in the section on the samādhi of Śiva-yoga, it says:
"One should visualize the lotuses within that take the form of the six cakras."
From the base up to the midpoint between the eyebrows, these constitute the abodes beginning with Brahmā. || 38 ||
Above the midpoint of the eyebrows, however, is a thousand-petaled lotus.
Therein, one should meditate upon a stainless lunar disc, and within that [disc].
One should know the subtle aperture; the wise call that the station of Kailāsa.
One should meditate upon Śambhu, the cause of all causes, as being situated therein.
Transcending all principles, it shines as the nature of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss.
Self-luminous, indefinable, and beyond the reach of speech and mind. || 41 ||
It is illuminated by the great power known as Umā, whose nature is consciousness.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Self in the form of a swan through the sense of "I am He."
The accomplishment of one-pointedness toward that [object] is considered the supreme samādhi. || 42 ||

According to the authority of this statement, the partless liṅga known as Sadāśiva—whose nature is that of the Paramahaṃsa and who is characterized by Śakti—is to be worshipped in the Brahma-randhra, which is situated above the six cakras. || 43 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, in the section on the conduct of realization (*bhāvācāra*), [it says]:
"The Great Lord is perfectly complete everywhere, both internally and externally."
The most excellent of scholars should meditate upon this for the sake of attaining supreme bliss. || 44 ||
In another text: "I worship my own *liṅga*, which resembles a jewel, situated within the lotus of the heart in the city of *māyā*."
Through the constant consecrations of the water of the pure mind from the river of faith, and with the flowers of meditative concentration, for the sake of non-rebirth.
The body is declared to be the temple; the living soul is the deity, Sadāśiva.
One should discard the withered garland of ignorance and worship with a sense of oneness.

In the *Laghujābāla*: "Avimukta is indeed Kurukṣetra, the place of sacrifice for the gods, the abode of Brahman for all beings. For when the vital breaths of a living being depart from here, Rudra reveals the liberating Brahman (*tārakaṃ brahma*), by which he becomes immortal and attains liberation."
In the second chapter of the Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa:
"Therefore, those seeking liberation should, with devotion, [resort] to Avimukta for the sake of knowledge."
Likewise, at the beginning and within oneself, it should be practiced in exactly that same way.
Mahādeva is to be meditated upon there; he is to be worshipped, without a doubt. || 48 ||
In that very work, the second section of the *Laghu-Jābāla*, it is said: "Then Atri asked Yājñavalkya:
'How may I know this infinite, unmanifest Self? Yājñavalkya replied: 'That infinite, unmanifest Self is to be worshipped in Avimukta; that [Self] is in Avimukta.'"

"He is established" means he is established in that which is the Unliberated (Avimukta). To prevent [misunderstanding], it says he is "established in the Vāraṇā," that is, in the middle of the nose. What is this Vāraṇā? What is the nose? It is called Vāraṇā because it wards off all defects produced by the senses; therefore, it is Vāraṇā.
Because it destroys all sins committed by the senses, it is called *nāśī*; and because its station is supreme,
that junction between the eyebrows and the nose is the junction of this world and the world beyond.

"It becomes a junction"—this junction, this twilight (*saṃdhyā*), the knowers of Brahman worship; that [junction] is to be worshipped as the Unliberated (*avimukta*); thus he explains the knowledge of the Unliberated. || 49 ||
In the Nādabindūpaniṣad:
"The forehead is between the eyebrows, and at the base of the nose."
One should know that the abode of immortality is that great sanctuary of Brahman.
Regarding this matter, the *Sūta-saṃhitā* states: "Śrīparvata is in the location of the head, while Kedāra is on the forehead."
Vārāṇasī is the great wisdom located between the eyebrows and the nose.
"The junction of the two eyebrows and the nose," so says the Jābāli Śruti. (51)
Regarding this matter, the Mānava Purāṇa states: "Where the junction of the two eyebrows and the nose is located, there Vārāṇasī is situated."
Therein lies the field of Avimuktaka, where Rudra is eternally present.
He is directly named Viśveśvara, in the form of the light of the Liṅga. || 52 ||

In the *Śāṅkarasaṃhitā*, in the latter part, within the section on the wearing of the *liṅga* (Liṅgadhāraṇaprakaraṇa), it is stated: "In the region of Avimukta, between the eyebrows and the nose, is the supreme self-liṅga known as Viśveśvara."
Great souls whose minds were attached to the nectar of meditation attained supreme liberation after meditating; others did likewise.
Some great souls, having worshipped within their hearts the Lord whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, as the *bhāvaliṅga*, [attain liberation].

Having attained liberation, with the movements of their minds dissolved into the Supreme Self and possessing a state of perfect fulfillment, they— being single-mindedly devoted— worshipped the subtle body called *prāṇa* in the region of the navel within the secret cave.
Some lords of sages, endowed with firm devotion, have attained that immutable and auspicious state;
others, ever devoted to yoga, [behold] the ancient one, blazing within the lotus of the heart and measuring a thumb's breadth.
Having contemplated Śiva, the immeasurable whose nature is the Liṅga, the noble ones attained dissolution within Him. || 56 ||
[He who meditates on Him] who vibrates within the center of the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the aperture of Brahma (brahmaraṃdhra), possessing the brilliance of ten million suns.
Those who perceive me with single-minded devotion are dear to me; they possess eternal liberation. || 57 ||
In the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇopaniṣad it is said:
"The Person, the size of a thumb, is the inner self; he is eternally seated in the hearts of all people."
In that very context:
"But when one perceives the reality of Brahman here as being joined with the reality of the self, by means of the simile of a lamp."
Having known the unborn, eternal God, who is purified of all principles, one is released from all bonds.

The meaning is that one should perceive within the center of the heart-lotus the reality of Brahman, which is of the nature of the Śiva-liṅga and is endowed with the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) like a lamp. || 60 ||
In that very same place.
He whose faces, heads, and necks are everywhere, who dwells in the secret cave of all beings.
That Blessed One is all-pervasive; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent. || 61 ||
In the *Kaivalyopaniṣad*: "I am subtler than the subtle; I alone am the truth. I am the Great One, this ancient universe.
I am the primeval Person, I am the Lord, I am golden, I am the ash of the form of Śiva.
(62) In the *Taittirīya*: "Brahman has space as its body, is the self of truth, rejoices in vital breath, and is blissful in mind."

"Venerate it as the nectar (amṛta) rich in peace, O Prācīnayogya"—thus it is stated that the power of the sky of consciousness (cidaṃbara-śakti) is to be venerated by those seeking liberation, insofar as it constitutes the body of Brahman. || 63 ||
In that very same place: "Who indeed could breathe, or who could live, if this space were not bliss?"

The meaning of this is as follows: If the power denoted by the term "ether" (*ākāśa*), whose nature is consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*), did not exist, then what living being in the world would perform movement such as exertion, or what living being would even perform mere locomotion?
For bliss is the cause of all activity through the medium of enthusiasm (*utsāha*).
The intention of the word "siddha" (established) is that it is logical for that which consists of all things to possess the nature of bliss. || 64 ||
Regarding this point, it is stated in the *Brahmagītā*: "Even though this supreme bliss, which is one's own self, exists for all beings..."
O gods, which man truly lives, or who indeed acts perpetually? (65)

In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], from the passage beginning with "This very space within the heart— in it is this person consisting of mind, immortal, golden" and ending with "Meditate on him as Prācīnayogya," the state of consisting of mind, the state of being immortal, and the state of being golden are described. (66)
In the Vājasaneyi [Upaniṣad]:
"This indeed is that great unborn Self, who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths; within the space in the heart He lies, the ruler of all. (67)

In the Chāndogya: Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, a small lotus-palace, and within that small [palace] is the ether; what is inside that is to be sought, and that indeed is to be desired to be understood. (6.8.1)
In the sixth chapter of the *Brahmagītā*: "O gods, this small abode which is here within this city of Brahman..."
In the center of that is a lotus, and within it is a small space.
That Hari, who is existence, consciousness, and bliss, is to be sought after by those desiring liberation. || 69 ||
In the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, it is stated:
"This body, illuminated by consciousness, is declared to be the temple of Śiva."
It consists of the thirty-six principles and has a lotus-pedestal made of beautiful flowers.
The Supreme Lord is light by virtue of having the nature of supreme space.
Dwelling in the cave of the space within the heart, he is perceived inside the bodies of embodied beings.
This is declared to be Śivapura, enveloped by the seven constituent elements (dhātus).
Here, the lotus of the heart is the dwelling, enchanting with its subtle etheric garment.
Therein resides the manifest reality, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Śiva is of the nature of eternally established luminosity, like the space reflected in water. || 73 ||
It is situated within the sphere of the intermediate space, free from all limiting adjuncts.
One should meditate upon Śiva, who consists of consciousness, as being limited, like the space within a jar. || 74 ||
Furthermore: just as a single lamp situated inside a jar appears as many through the numerous apertures of that jar,

even so, the single *prāṇaliṅga* abiding within one's own self in the center of the heart-lotus appears manifold through the gateways of the gross and subtle bodies, the senses, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and so forth.
It should be understood that the sixfold signs exist in many ways. || 75 ||

In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad]: "This very space within the heart—within it is this person consisting of mind, immortal, golden; that which hangs down between the palates like a nipple is the source of Indra. || 76 ||
In that very same [text].
The lord of mind, the lord of speech, the lord of sight, the lord of hearing, and the lord of discernment.

"Brahman has space as its body, its essence is truth, it delights in vital breath, its joy is the mind, it is enriched by peace, and it is immortal; thus, O Prācīnayogya, should you worship it. || 77 ||
In the Brahmopaniṣad it is said: "The supreme, most pure sacred thread abides in the consciousness within the heart."
According to the authority of such statements as found in the *Maitreyopaniṣad*— “The eternal, unborn, and independent one abides in his own glory;
by him this body has been established as if possessed of consciousness, and he impels it”— the object of worship in the *Dahara-vidyā* is that which resides within the center of the heart-lotus.
The Prāṇaliṅga, characterized by the supreme ether, consisting of light, and designated as the Supreme Self, is to be known as this very Liṅga of the Supreme Brahman,
existing in the form of sixfold Liṅgas within the gross body, the subtle body, the senses, the internal organ, and so forth.
It is said that there is a presence of the liṅga in all its limbs. || 79 ||

In the Aitareya Upaniṣad: "Which of these is that Self whom we worship? Which is that Self by which one sees, or by which one hears, or by which one smells odors, or by which one articulates speech, or by which one distinguishes between the savory and the unsavory? It is this which is called the heart and the mind."

"Understanding, knowledge, discernment, intelligence, vision, fortitude, thoughtfulness, intention, birth, memory, resolve, purpose, desire, and will—all these are names for discernment (vijñāna). All this has discernment as its guide; all this is established upon discernment."
"The world has wisdom as its eye; wisdom is its foundation; wisdom is Brahman"—thus, these very [qualities] constitute the sixfold marks within the heart and the other sense organs. || 80 ||

In the *Nārāyaṇa-vallī* of the *Taittirīya*, it is stated: "That very person (puruṣa), indeed, is fivefold and five-souled, by whom all this is woven together—the earth, the intermediate space, the heaven, the quarters, and everything;
this entire world. From this statement, [it follows that] the Supreme Brahman, known as the Self, abides within one's own self.
The single Mahāliṅga itself becomes five liṅgas—

namely Ācāra and the others— in accordance with the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta, within the five groups consisting of the five elements, the five senses, and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), across these sixfold categories of elements, senses, and internal organs.
The sixfold liṅgas, beginning with the Mahāliṅga, exist; this is the supreme state of Śiva, well-known from the Śruti, Purāṇas, and Āgamas. || 81 ||

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa, beginning with: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within— he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal," and so forth.
In the same way, he who dwells in the waters, he who dwells in fire, he who dwells in the wind, he who dwells in the intermediate space,

he who dwells in the sky, he who dwells in the sun, he who dwells in the quarters, he who dwells in the moon and stars, he who dwells in the ether, he who dwells in darkness, and he who dwells in light.

By such statements as "He who dwells in the vital breath," "He who dwells in speech," "He who dwells in the eye," "He who dwells in the ear," "He who dwells in the mind," "He who dwells in the skin," and "He who dwells in the semen," [it is shown that He dwells] within the five elements and so forth, both in the internal (ādhyātmika) and external (ādhibhautika) realms.
Having thus described the state of Śiva, the Supreme Self, as the inner controller of all; || 82 ||
In that very same place [it is said]: "The seen is the seer, the heard is the hearer, the thought is the thinker, the cognized is the cognizer;
there is no seer other than this, no hearer other than this, no thinker other than this, no cognizer other than this."

It must be stated that this Self, the inner controller, the immortal— namely, Śiva, the Supreme Self denoted by the word "immortal"— is established within the five elements, the sense organs, the internal organ, and so forth. || 83 ||

In the *Talavakāra Upaniṣad*: "Which god yokes the eye and the ear? That which is the hearer of the ear, the mind of the mind, the speaker of speech, and the breath of breath—that is the eye of the eye. Having transcended these, the wise become immortal after departing from this world; the eye does not go there, nor..."

"Speech speaks, but we do not know it; we do not understand it—what it might teach us. We have heard from those of old who explained it to us that it is something other than what is known, and even other than what is unknown. Know that alone to be Brahman, which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed; this [world] is not it."
That which they worship here—that which the mind does not think, but by which they say the mind is thought—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which they worship here;
that which one does not see with the eye, but by which the eyes see—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which they worship here; that which one does not hear with the ear, but by which...

"Know that very Brahman which is hearing and that which is heard; not this which they worship here. "Know that very Brahman which breathes by means of the vital breath (prāṇa) and by which the vital breath is led forth; not this which they worship here.
From these statements, [it follows that Brahman is] the witness within the six organs, the internal organ, and so forth.
It should be stated that consciousness itself manifests as the sixfold signs in each respective case;
thus, the sixfold signs are to be understood through direct perception.
Furthermore, it is only for those who possess direct knowledge of Brahman that there arises direct knowledge of the sixfold marks (ṣaḍvidhaliṅga);
and indeed, this very direct knowledge of the sixfold marks constitutes the integration of all the constituent parts of the mark.

In the Tāpanīya Upaniṣad: [He is] the seer of the eye, the seer of the ear, the seer of speech, the seer of the mind, the seer of the intellect, the seer of the vital breath— different from all and distinct from them, the witness of the eye,
the witness of the ear, the witness of speech, the witness of the mind.
It is the witness of the intellect, the witness of the vital breath, the witness of everything—thus [it is said]. || 85 ||

In the Āśvalāyanopaniṣad: "For he is the seer, the creator, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, the doer, the cognizer—the Puruṣa who is the self of consciousness. O dear one, he who knows that which is shadowless, bodiless, non-red, pure, and imperishable, is indeed omniscient."
He becomes all-pervasive; thus [he is] "all" (sarvī). 86.
In the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, in the section on Bhāvāgama, it is said: "The Great Lord is completely full everywhere, both within and without."
The most excellent of scholars should practice meditation for the sake of attaining supreme bliss. || 87 ||
Regarding this point, in the third chapter of the *Brahmagītā*, Śaṅkara, the self of all, says: "I am indeed the witness of everything."
O best of gods, in the absence of a witness, how does the world appear to the direct witness? (88)
For the entire world, including all things moving and stationary, is devoid of inherent luminosity.
And because of its insentience, this world possesses insentience through its manifestation. || 89 ||
Some declare that manifestation is produced from consciousness.
That would not be consistent at all; for if it were produced, it would necessarily be insentient.
It is generally accepted that only insentient things, such as jars and the like, possess the quality of being produced.
Consciousness itself would be the manifestation; it is not accepted as being productive. || 91 ||
Even for one who is eloquent, knowledge is not established by means of its appearing form.
If, because knowledge is unchanging, there were nevertheless a modification of that [knowledge] as well; || 92 ||
In that case, like milk and so forth, there would be no cognition at all.
Just as consciousness is not held to be the initiator of light. || 93 ||
Because it is not a substance and because it is accepted by others as being a quality (guṇa).
Cognition of an appearance that lacks a real form cannot be the producer [of a subsequent effect]. || 94 ||
Then, the cognition of the son of a barren woman would become the cause for the commencement of those respective [cognitions].
Cognition of that which appears as a form previously non-existent cannot be the producer [of that form]. || 95 ||
Because there is an absence of prior distinctions that did not previously exist for that which is non-existent.
Therefore, appearance is in no way produced by consciousness. (96)
O inhabitants of heaven, even knowledge does not possess the quality of being produced.
For, according to the reasoning already stated, the cognition of being produced is indeed a mere illusion. (97)
Likewise, O gods, regarding the fact that even perception is produced by error.
O best of gods, because it is knowledge and yet unproduced, that knowledge is eternal.
O gods, that knowledge which illuminates the world shines eternally by its own nature.
He alone is the witness of the world, the soul of all, known by the name Śaṅkara. || 99 ||
It is declared to be the illuminator of all; by it, this entire world [is illuminated].
Therefore, by means of the distinctions of form and so forth, a person perceives [it] as its own. || 100 ||
By means of this, he hears sounds and smells pleasant fragrances.
By this very means, a person always articulates speech. || 101 ||
By this, a person always discerns what is sweet and what is not sweet.
The final realization known as Śaṅkara has been praised in many ways by the wise.
In that very same [text].
All this is this Śambhu, whose characteristic is a mass of pure consciousness.
This wisdom of the Supreme Lord is the foundation of all things.
That very Brahman, known by such names as Śiva and Rudra, is nothing but pure consciousness.
In that very same [text].
That Brahman, which is the object of that knowledge, is existence, consciousness, bliss, and non-dual.
In this cave called saṃsāra, which is designated by such terms as "illusion" (māyā) and "ignorance" (ajñāna), || 104 ||
He who knows the Brahman deposited in that which is designated as the supreme ether (paramavyoman).
O best of gods, he attains all his desires in due order. || 105 ||
Having realized the nature of Brahman, one is undoubtedly liberated while living.
Even though this supreme bliss exists as their very own self for all beings, it is not realized by them. || 106 ||
O gods, which man truly lives, or who constantly exerts himself?
Therefore, Hara is the aesthetic flavor (rasa) manifesting within the minds of all souls.
By the power of her compassion, she brings joy to the individual soul (jīvātman) who is burdened with suffering. || 107 ||
In that very same [text].
This very Self, which shines by itself, is devoid of any other existence.
He alone is the direct inner controller (antaryāmī) of all, and no other.
And he who, though standing upon the earth, always remains within the earth.
Whom the gods do not know, even the earth is but his body.
He who is within, by whom this earth is pervaded, exists in the form of actionlessness.
For he alone is our direct inner controller (antaryāmin), the supreme immortal.
Standing within the waters, O gods, they do not know this one who is within the waters.
He who enters within that whose body is water—that is, the waters—[is the one who knows]. 111.
For this alone is our manifest inner controller, the supreme immortal.
In this way, O gods, [he is] the self of both Agni and the intermediate space.
And of everything preceded by air, whether sentient or insentient.
For he alone is our manifest inner controller, the supreme immortal.
He who has not seen the gods has seen them; he has heard this through his ear, even as it was heard.
And likewise, O gods, he is the non-thinker, the thinker, the knower, and the absolute one.
O believers, when Ravi, Soma, and Agni have perished, this [remains].
It shines solely by its own self-luminosity as the witness of the mind. || 115 ||
But when the activity of the mind is destroyed, O bulls among the gods, that [activity] ceases to exist.
By means of its own self-luminosity, it knows even the experience in deep sleep.
But the Lord himself is free from manifestation and disappearance.
The solitary Kevala always knows this entire universe as consisting of both existence and non-existence.
O best of gods, the entire object of knowledge consists of both existence and non-existence.
Drinking the [subtle] essence in the world of the well-performed deed, they have entered the cave of the heart, situated in the supreme, ultimate reality.
Those who know Brahman declare that shadow and light are the embodied soul and the one named Śaṅkara.
Having caused [the soul] to eat, Śiva causes the embodied one to enjoy the fruit of its karma.
Those two are contradicted by common experience; their distinction is merely figurative.
In the Sūtagītā:
"Understand that all this which appears is nothing but appearance."
One goes to the Lord of Gods, whose form is the assembly; there is no doubt about this. || 120 ||
In that regard, the fourth chapter [states]:
"All this that appears is the supreme state, whose nature is manifestation."
Perceiving [the truth] by means of the authority of Vedānta, one is liberated immediately.
In the first chapter of the Maitreyopaniṣad, it is stated: "He stands in his own majesty; by him this body is established through consciousness. || 122 ||

In that regard, in the fifth section: having mounted speech by means of wisdom, one attains all names through speech; having mounted the sense of smell by means of wisdom, one attains all odors through the sense of smell;
having mounted the eye by means of wisdom, one attains all forms through the eye; [and so on] by means of wisdom.

Having mounted the ear, one perceives all sounds through the ear by means of wisdom; having mounted the tongue, one perceives all tastes of food through the tongue by means of wisdom; having mounted the two hands, one performs all actions through the two hands by means of wisdom; and having mounted the body... by means of wisdom.

Through the body one experiences pleasure and pain; mounting upon the organ of generation by means of wisdom, through the organ of generation one obtains bliss, sexual enjoyment, and offspring; mounting upon the feet by means of wisdom, through the two feet one obtains everything.
"By wisdom alone one ascends to the intellect, and by wisdom alone one attains the objects of desire that are to be known through the intellect;
this wisdom is the supreme sovereign foundation of all things"—
from such statements in the *Sūtasamhitā* as authoritative evidence, [it follows that] all beings, senses, internal organs, and so forth, reside therein.
In that regard, these [senses] are presided over by the limited consciousness of Śiva (avacchinna-śivacaitanya). For this very reason, in ancient scriptural statements, it is said:

for the sense of smell, the sense of smell itself is the Ācāra-liṅga; for the tongue, the tongue itself is the Guru-liṅga; for the eye, the eye itself is the Śiva-liṅga; for the skin, the skin itself is the Cara-liṅga; and for the ear, the ear itself is [the Śiva-liṅga].
The Prasādaliṅga is said to be the very heart of the heart, which is indeed the Mahāliṅga.
This very knowledge of Brahman in six stages—this direct realization of Brahman in its six stages—is indeed the complete integration of all limbs and lingas. || 123 ||
Regarding this matter, which is to be personally realized, all the Vedas and entire scriptures are authoritative.
All the arguments of the Purāṇas culminate in this.
What is the use of speaking at length, my child? I have told you only the essential point.
Therefore, having understood this, become one who possesses knowledge of the six locations.
From such statements in the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā, it should be understood that all forms of Brahmavidyā culminate in the Ṣaṭsthalabrahmavidyā. || 126 ||

In the Kaivalyopaniṣad: "One who abides in the state beyond all stages of life, having restrained all the senses and bowed with devotion to his own guru, should contemplate within the pure and stainless lotus of the heart that which is luminous and free from sorrow. (127)
Inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite in form, auspicious, tranquil, immortal, the source of Brahman.
Then [he beheld] that one, all-pervading, wonderful, formless bliss of consciousness, devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
The supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly tranquil.
Having meditated, the Sage goes to the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness.
Having thus established that the Supreme Self, Paramaśiva, is the object of worship in the Dahara-vidyā by means of these and other passages;
That very self, its nature deluded by māyā, assumes a body and performs all actions.
That very same person, while awake, attains complete satisfaction through various enjoyments such as women, food, drink, and so forth.
And in a dream, the individual soul is the enjoyer of pleasure and pain within the world of the universe imagined by its own māyā.
At the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved and one is overcome by darkness, one attains the nature of bliss. || 131 ||
The phenomenal world consisting of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, which shines forth—
Having realized "I am that Brahman," one is liberated from all bonds. || 132 ||
Whatever may be the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoying within the three abodes;
I am Sadāśiva, the witness distinct from them, consisting of pure consciousness alone. || 133 ||
I am without hands or feet, yet possessed of inconceivable power; I see without eyes and hear without ears.
I perceive the form that is secluded, yet there is no knower; I am my own consciousness, eternally existing.
"By many Vedas I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas. (134)
Thus, a statement of Brahman intended to refer to its own inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) is found in the fourth chapter of the *Brahmagītā*:
"There exists a God, self-established, the witness of everything at all times."
He is the direct liberator from saṃsāra for those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence. || 135 ||
And by him, the minds of all were impelled with regularity.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) moves toward its object, the body exerts itself and speech also speaks. || 136 ||
The eye sees forms, and the ear likewise hears sound.
By which self all these [elements] are indeed impelled.
They proceed incessantly, each directed toward its own respective object.
And its capacity to set [the world] in motion is also due to illusion, not by way of its own inherent nature. || 138 ||
And the existence of the sense faculties is not considered to be intrinsic by nature.
O best of gods, it is as hot for him as a red-hot iron ball. || 139 ||
The Lord Maheśvara himself is superimposed upon both the ear and the self.
Having entered it, Hara bestows the state of being the sense of hearing upon the ear.
The Supreme Lord, having entered the mind which is superimposed upon the self, [presides over it].
Having entered it, Hara bestows the nature of hearing upon the ear.
The Supreme Lord, having entered the mind which is superimposed upon the self, [awakens it].
Established in sattva, his mind bestows [the fruit] according to the rule. || 142 ||
Having attained the state of speech for speech, Hara took away the vitality of the vital breath.
And likewise, Hara grants the eye by means of a specific rule.
But Maheśvara is the [source] of the other imagined sense-faculties.
And having assumed each respective form, he bestows [the fruit] according to the rule.
In that regard, there are the eye, speech, the mind, and whatever others there may be.
They do not go [into dissolution] within the Supreme Self, whose intrinsic nature is self-luminous.
That deity is other than what is known, and likewise other than what is unknown.
And likewise by speech, by mind, and by sight as well. || 146 ||
O best of gods, [this is true] even with the ear, the breath, or any other [sense organ].
It is impossible to make it an object of experience; this which I have spoken is indeed the truth.

By the authority of such scriptural statements as these, the sixfold signs (liṅgas) are indeed known through direct perception; thus, it is determined that the very consciousness of Śiva, whose nature is the Seer and who is distinct from all else, is the true sign (liṅga). || 148 ||
In the Sūtasamhitā, in the Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa, in the twenty-eighth chapter:
"Now, therefore, I shall explain the Śiva-liṅga in brief."
By the mere knowledge of which, a human being becomes liberated. || 149 ||
Śiva alone is the Liṅga; for the Liṅga is indeed that which makes known.
Everything is understood through Śiva; Śiva is not understood by anyone else.
For by this [means], O best of sages, that which is insentient is understood, not that which is sentient.
Śiva is certainly not insentient; he is directly characterized solely by self-luminosity. || 151 ||
If Śiva were not self-luminous, he would certainly not be Śiva.
Indeed, Śiva does not accept that walls and such things are non-self-luminous. (152)
O best of sages, when Śiva—who is characterized solely by self-luminosity—is not present, [the world does not shine].
Everything would then be unperceived, and consequently, entirely void. || 153 ||
Even the proof of emptiness is supreme; by this very [means], emptiness itself is established.
Indeed, it is entirely devoid of luminosity and characterized by emptiness. || 154 ||
Therefore, [he is] the direct manifestation of Śiva-with-Ambā, characterized solely by self-luminosity.
By that, all this is traversed; yet it itself is not traversed.
The virtuous Śruti declares that Maheśvara is self-luminous.
Therefore, Śiva, the illuminator of the entire universe, is self-luminous and is himself alone, absolute.
O bulls among the twice-born, that which I have described as the *liṅga* is itself to be worshipped, for it resides at the pinnacle of the Vedas.
Other lords of sages who know the Vedas declare that the linga of Śiva is the Śivalinga.
For that which is self-luminous, it is not logical [to require another means of manifestation]; therefore, Śambhu himself is the *liṅga*.
Some declare that the *liṅga* of Śiva is of many kinds from the perspective of conventional usage.
From the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no indicative mark (liṅga) for the Supreme Lord, who is self-luminous.
Some say that the supreme self-knowledge consisting of the realization of Vedānta is the *liṅga* of Śiva.
Others, moreover, declare that even the knowledge of Truth produced through reflection is the supreme sign [of the Self]. (159)
They describe Māyā as the *liṅga* of Śiva, visible within Śiva and grounded in the reality of Śiva.
Some say it is the mind of people; others, however, say it is the ego-sense, the intellect, and the mental faculty.
Some proclaim it to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while others proclaim the subtle body (*liṅga*) as the mark. || 160 ||
Some declare that the skin and other [elements] are the aggregate of the Supreme Lord. || 161 ||
They maintain that the elements such as sound are the gross elements of Maheśvara.
Some say that this entire world, beginning with the nether regions (pātāla), is the liṅga of Maheśa.
Whatever exists and whatever does not exist—all this, they declare, is the *liṅga* of Maheśvara.
For this one who is a supreme yogin of pure knowledge and is self-luminous, they say there is no external sign.
Whatever has been described as a *liṅga* of Śiva is in reality an insentient object; it cannot truly be a *liṅga*.
O you of pure intellect, for on this earth, knowledge alone is the *liṅga*.

Therefore, Maheśvara alone, whose nature is consciousness, is said to be the highest, being conditioned by various inert adjuncts; this is the meaning of the statement that he is the "indicator" (gamaka) of the Lord, while he himself remains established [as the self]. 164.
Others, who are most proficient in the knowledge of the *liṅga*, say that the *ālaya* is the *liṅga*.
That which is called the *ālaya* is indeed the support, the support of all, and the auspicious one. || 165 ||
Therefore, the Blessed Lord Śiva is the substratum of all imagined forms.
The Great God is without support, characterized by truth and consciousness. || 166 ||
O best of the twice-born, that which is the support of all has no support.
Just as no support whatsoever exists for space, so it is [with this]. || 167 ||
And the substratum turns back [the world] from Śiva, the Supreme Self.
"In its own majesty," says the Vedānta; it is a speaker of truth and is intrinsically valid. (168)
It is the established position that the Vedānta statements are the supreme authority.
Therefore, the Supreme Lord is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. || 169 ||
He is himself always the Liṅga; no other Liṅga exists for him.
Others, who are most proficient in the knowledge of the *liṅga*, say that the *liṅga* arises from the act of lying down (*layanāt*).
Nevertheless, the Lord Maheśvara himself is the Liṅga.
All this, as it dissolves, is dissolved into Brahman alone.
The Supreme Brahman does not dissolve, because its essential nature is eternally real.
In the latter part of the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā,
other experts in the Liṅga state that the Liṅga is the signifier.
It is understood by yogins because the root *gam* is seen to have the meaning of "knowing. (172)
In this way, the wise discern the Linga, which has the nature of pure consciousness alone.
And for this reason as well, it is established that [this belongs] to the Supreme Self. || 173 ||
And of the Lord in the form of a liṅga, the blue-throated wielder of the trident.
Then, in the manner described, Maheśvara took the form of a *liṅga*.
Thus it is sung among the principles of Vedānta by those most proficient in the knowledge of reality. || 174 ||
In the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad: "Him who is difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret place, seated in the cave of the heart, ancient..."
"Having known the Divine through the attainment of inner yoga, the wise man abandons both joy and sorrow."
That state which all the Vedas proclaim, and which all austerities declare;
Desiring that [goal], they practice the holy life; regarding that very thing, I shall speak in brief: it is this syllable "Om."
This very syllable is Brahman; this very syllable is the supreme.
Having known this very syllable, whatever one desires, that belongs to him.
This is the most excellent object of focus; this is the supreme object of focus.
Having understood this object of focus, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The meaning is: in the world of Śiva, which is designated by the term "Brahmaloka. || 175 ||
If it is asked how this is the object of focus, it is said:
[it is found] in the *Pūrvatāpanīya*, the *Uttaratāpanīya*, and the *Māṇḍūkya* Upaniṣads.

"Om"—this syllable is all this. Its further explanation is as follows: whatever has been, whatever is, and whatever will be—all that is indeed the syllable Om. And whatever else is beyond the three periods of time, that too is indeed the syllable Om. For all this is Brahman; this Self is Brahman. This very Self is Brahman. One should meditate upon this Self as "Om."

Having unified Brahman with the Self, and having unified the Self with Brahman through the syllable *oṃ*, and having experienced that single, imperishable, immortal, and fearless *oṃ*, one should then project this entire three-bodied universe upon it; then, thinking "this is indeed identical with that," one should dissolve it into that very essence with the syllable *oṃ*. Or rather, [one should dissolve] that [Self].

"One should unite this three-bodied self with the three-bodied Brahman"— this means that the support of this *praṇava* is precisely the oneness of the self and Brahman, whose nature is the state of equilibrium between the three marks (*liṅga*) and the three limbs (*aṅga*). || 176 ||
In the *Muṇḍaka*, the all-pervasiveness of Brahman is stated thus: "Brahman alone is this immortal [reality] in the east, behind, to the south, and to the north;
below and above, it is spread forth; Brahman alone is this entire universe, the most excellent. (177)
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: [He is] the manifestation of the qualities of all the senses, yet devoid of all the senses.
The Lord and Master of all, the refuge and friend of all. || 178 ||
Without hands or feet, he is swift; without a body, he grasps; without eyes, he sees; without ears, he hears.
He knows that which is to be known, yet there is no knower of him; they call him the foremost, the Great Puruṣa.
Subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, the Self is hidden in the secret cave of this living being.
Free from sorrow, he beholds that Lord of boundless power, the Greatness, through the clarity of his own nature. || 180 ||
In the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad:
"This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth."
But it is seen by those who perceive the subtle, with a foremost and subtle intellect. || 181 ||
By which one [perceives] form, taste, smell, sound, touch, and sexual union.
By this very [means] one knows; what remains here? || 182 ||
In the Nādabindūpaniṣad: "In this way, all beings [are contained] within the Self, like gems on a thread."
Steadfast in intellect, free from worldly prosperity, he is a knower of Brahman, established in Brahman. || 183 ||
Just as oil resides within sesame seeds, or as fragrance is inherent in a flower.
But in the body of a person, it exists both externally and internally. || 184 ||
In the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, in the section concerning the Kriyāgama, it is stated:
"Just as fire does not manifest in the fire-drill wood without friction."
Without ritual action, Śiva, though abiding within, would not become manifest. (185)
In the context of the realization of existence, the Great Lord is perfectly complete everywhere, both within and without.
The most excellent of scholars should practice meditation for the sake of attaining supreme bliss. || 186 ||
Just as a blind person does not see the objects situated before them at a place where knowledge has arrived.
Likewise, the embodied soul devoid of knowledge does not perceive Śiva abiding within itself.
Directly contemplating one's own essential nature as the form of Śiva, which is pure light.
Though possessing a body, the practitioner who is liberated while living is indeed bodiless.

On the authority of such scriptural statements as these, the single *prāṇaliṅga*, which consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*) and resides within the heart-lotus, becomes sixfold liṅgas through its respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)— namely, all the limbs, the sense organs, and the internal organ— as it pervades every limb; thus, it comes to possess the totality of the liṅgas of all the limbs.
In the *Śāṅkarasaṃhitā*, in the latter section, within the praise of the Vīramāheśvaras,
the Lord said: "Then, one who is devoted to the worship of Rudra should make his body consist of Rudra."
One who worships Rudra without being Rudra himself shall not partake in the fruit of that worship.
Having become Rudra, one should worship Rudra; one who is not Rudra should not worship Rudra.
He who possesses the connection between the vital breath (prāṇa), the liṅga, and the body is Rudra; of this there is no doubt. || 191 ||
O child, the deities preside over the organs within the body.
The internal [elements] are [known] through perception, and the external ones through enjoyment. || 192 ||
Objects indeed become offered, O Śikhivāhana.
He who returns what has been entrusted to him shall go to the Raurava hell.
To avoid those defects, one should regard the body as consisting of deities.
A person should meditate upon [the Self] as being of the nature of Rudra, joined with the elements, the senses, and so forth. || 194 ||
In the Śiva Purāṇa:
"The man who makes his own body an instrument for the worship of Śiva..."
In a very short time, that man becomes bodiless (videha). || 195 ||
In the *Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa*, it is said: "That which is the limb on the right is the solar person (*arkapuruṣa*); that is the mate of the Self. Since there are two of these, they form a pair;
for a pair is a productive couple. This very one who is Indra is this lunar person (*ikṣapuruṣa*) on the right, and he is to be meditated upon as Indrāṇī. This is who she is.

Based on the authority of scriptural statements such as "He is to be worshipped with sacrificial fees" (*dakṣiṇya etadvāmam*) and so forth, the relationship between Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*)—who possess the previously mentioned characteristics of the Linga and the Aṅga—is described here as that of husband and wife. || 196 ||

In the eighty-fourth chapter of the latter part of the Śāṅkara-saṃhitā, in the determination of the six stations (ṣaṭsthala-nirṇaya), it is said: "The Lord is the Liṅga and I am Satī; the self-ruling Master is united within the heart."
There is no worldly happiness; there is no supreme place of refuge. || 197 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, it is said: "Having known that the Liṅga, which consists of light, resides eternally within one's own heart at the site of the *aṅgaliṅga*..."
One should worship and constantly meditate upon him; one should know him as an *aṅgaliga*.
In that place of refuge, the body is to be known as the bearer of the *liṅga*, whose nature is knowledge; the consort is *Satī*, and the Lord is *Śiva*.
Whatever bliss exists in that immersion, he who possesses it is the one named Śaraṇa.
Thus, the status of Śiva—the nature of both the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*—as the husband of Satī has been declared. || 200 ||

In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "The Self alone is below, the Self is above, the Self is behind, the Self is in front, the Self is to the south, the Self is to the north—the Self indeed is all this. He who sees thus, who thinks thus, and who understands thus, rejoices in the Self, plays with the Self, and mates with the Self.
"He becomes self-blissful, he becomes his own ruler, and he attains freedom of movement in all worlds"—
thus, when the individual soul (jīvātman), whose form is the limb of Śiva, abides within its own self in that which is called the *liṅga*,
the heroic greatness (*vīramāhātmya*), there exists the bliss of the union of erotic play; he is the self-ruler, that living soul.
The meaning is that he becomes a self-ruler (svarāṭ), shining within his own refuge alone, thus delighting in his own self.
The meaning is that for such a person liberated while living, there is freedom of movement and conduct according to one's own will in all worlds.
Thus, the conjunction of all the limbs and the liṅga, as established by the Śruti, has been stated. || 201 ||
In the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad:
"He who knows this, hidden in the cave, O gentle one, unravels the knot of ignorance. (202)
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, regarding the physical liṅga of the devotee, it is stated: "Although Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, is the self of the entire universe..."
It shines forth especially within the lotus-heart of the devotees. || 203 ||
Although it is the self of all, it exists as something limited, just as [the sun] appears in reflections.
In that same way, Śaṅkara always manifests himself among his own devotees. || 204 ||
O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which shines eternally among your own [attendants].
The eternal Vedic revelation declares: "She is not terrible; she is the dispeller of evil. (205)
Among those who are pure, dispassionate, discerning, and great-souled.
Śiva dwells everywhere among those who bear the marks of Śiva.
For those who are endowed with constant contentment and whose karma has been shaken off by knowledge.
The Supreme Lord shines forth as the innermost essence of the devotees of Maheśvara.
In that place of the greatness of the Liṅga,
there is the Bodha-liṅga of Śiva, [worshipped] by one whose mind was awakened by Ruru.
That very Liṅga, the cause of all things, should be known as belonging to Śaṅkara. || 208 ||
The supreme, pure, stainless Liṅga is the eternal Brahman.
That which is designated as Śiva is pure consciousness alone, existence and bliss, unrestrained.
He is the cause of all worlds and even the cause of the Vedas.
It is the fulfillment of all reality and the crossing over of the ocean of birth.
Consisting of light and indescribable, it abides within the self of yogins.
How is it known that in the world there is no great teacher other than Compassion? (221)
Just as Śiva, although omnipresent, is held to possess a *liṅga*, so too is the *liṅga* desired [as the means of realization] in the Śivasūtras.
In the same way, the manifestation of Śiva-nature is held to occur precisely within those who are devoted.
In the *Yogasārasaṃgraha*,
having repeatedly recollected the knowledge residing in the mouth of the guru, which is of the nature of bliss, and having repeatedly heard the sun-colored resonance within the hollow of the heart;
Touching him again and again with his entire body, he touched the Lord residing in every limb; indeed, all the collections of his sense organs became focused on this single purpose.
In the observation of the moon,
one perceives the light of the self, the light of the mind, and the light of the eye.
He whose light is both external and internal—that light is called Śiva. || 214 ||
In the Śaiva Āgama, it is said that when there is direct perception (aparokṣānubhava) even of the bodily-liṅga of a devotee, that alone is known as the "intrinsic" (nija) liṅga. || 215 ||
In the *Śivayogapradīpikā*:
[The body] from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet is bound on the inside and outside by a covering of skin.
They say that the Self, which is of the nature of consciousness and immortal, is entirely of the nature of nectar.
In the Vāsiṣṭha,
one should contemplate that the entire world consists of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
He who remains with his desires stilled is happy, having the Veda as his armor.

In the sugar-cane juice, which is my own self, the lamp of yoga, there is no difference whether it takes the form of molasses or candied sugar; likewise, in me, whose essence is Brahman and whose flavor is bliss, there is no difference whether one is a Jambu, a Kola, a Kucika, a Nimba fruit, or a Kukola, nor between the body of Viriñca (Brahmā) or the form of a tree.
Likewise, O Lord, the God residing within the body does not bring about the welfare of men [according to the Bhāgavata].
Without propitiation, the omnipresent Supreme Lord is not [attained]. || 219 ||
In the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā:
"This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is indeed composed of both the Liṅga and the Aṅga."
Apart from the Liṅga and the Aṅga, there is nothing whatsoever anywhere. || 220 ||
In the *Sūktāvalī*, the *Toṭaka* meter:
Although the three worlds are filled with the nature of Śiva, the people have nevertheless not attained that state of Śiva-hood.
Through the vision of the Guru one attains the state of Śiva; from Śiva comes the Guru, and thus the Guru alone is the Guru. || 221 ||
In the *Vātulāgama*, in its northern section titled *Tantrottarapradīpa*, and in the *Anubhavasūtra*, it is stated:
"The one supreme *liṅga* alone is well-established within this body."
It shines forth in every direction through the nature of name, form, and action.
The *iṣṭaliṅga* is on the outer limb, while the *prāṇaliṅga* is likewise within.
The liṅga of existence is always well-established within this very limb of the Self.
The great liṅga is in the region of the heart; the one that bestows supreme grace is in the region of the ears.
The skin on the limbs is indeed a mobile liṅga, while the eyes on the limbs are the Śiva-liṅga.
The Guru-liṅga is on the part of the tongue, and likewise on the part of the nose.
Indeed, the emblem of right conduct is unwearied and firmly established.
Just as the subtle body (liṅga) is established sequentially within the components of the organs of perception.
Likewise, the Liṅga is established in the limbs of the organs of action in their respective order. || 226 ||
Of the ear, of speech, of sound, and likewise of all-pervading space;
The wise know her as the sovereign of the Lord, named Īśānā.
The sovereign mistress of the skin, hands, touch, and the winds, the divine embodiment of Īśvara.
Those ancient ones who know the traditional scriptures understand it as being designated by the term "Puruṣa. || 228 ||
Of the eye, of the foot, of form, and likewise of fire.
The wise declare that the presiding form is named Aghora.
Of the tongue, the generative organ, taste, and likewise of water;
The best of sages know the form of Īśvara to be the one called Vāmadeva.
Of the nose and of the anus, as well as of odor and of the earth.
They declare that the form of the Lord is called Sadyojāta.
The heart should be the locus of the voids whose nature consists of knowledge and action.
Because it is the substratum, because of its own purity, and because it consists of both knowledge and action. || 232 ||
But because it provides space for all the sense faculties.
It is called the "space of the heart" by those who are most wise. || 233 ||
In the gross body, [He exists] in a gross form; in the subtle body, in a subtle form.
For these cavities indeed abide as causes within the cause.
In all these three voids, the Liṅga is characterized by truth and the other [virtues].
Perfectly realized through the teacher's instruction, it shines forth in all directions.
Where this face of the Liṅga is seen by those with subtle vision.
For it is that which the Vedas, as well as austerities and religious observances, proclaim.
The heart [is the deity] of the heart, and the ear [is the deity] of the ear at all times.
From speech comes the quality of speech, from the skin the quality of skin, from the hand the hand, and from the eye the eye. || 237 ||
The foot [is the seat] of the foot, the tongue of the tongue, and the secret organ of the secret organ.
The nose is established as the nose, and the anus as the anus. || 238 ||
The experts in the Tantras of the Śiva-siddhānta call it the face of the talliṅga.
The nose of the olfactory organ, which is the emblem of right conduct, is said to be the mouth. || 239 ||
Likewise, the tongue becomes the tongue, and the face becomes the guru-liṅga.
And likewise, the eye of the eye shall become the face of the Śiva-liṅga.
The skin is said to be the mouth of the linga, which has the skin as its moving form.
The face is said to be the sign of grace, and the ear is said to be the sign of the sense of hearing. || 241 ||
In this way, the heart itself becomes the face of the Great Liṅga.
Thus the face of the Liṅga has been described; immediately thereafter, the well-known [face] follows.
And the classification of the hands for the six locations, beginning with Bhakta, is now demonstrated.
The existence of an object arises; from that existence, the emergence of cognition occurs. || 243 ||
From knowledge (jñāna) the mind (manas) is produced, and likewise from the mind arises the ego (ahaṃkṛti).
From that ego-sense arises the intellect (buddhi), and from the intellect arises the mind (citta). || 244 ||
A thing is begun by saying "it exists," and its absence is called non-existence.
The intellect always knows that [object], and the mind always thinks of that [object].
The ego-sense thinks "I am that," for it is the intellect that determines that [object].
The mind, by the very quality of its stability, holds that object with reverence.
One's own body is the hand of contemplation, intent upon the worship of the Great Liṅga.
Those who have reached the further shore of Vedānta declare this to be the very site of oneness. || 247 ||
The limb of space (vyomāṅga) is the hand of knowledge (jñānahasta), which is intent upon the worship of grace (prasāda).
Those proficient in the yoga of Śiva call this place a sanctuary.
He whose body is the wind, whose hand is the mind, and who delights in the worship of the mobile liṅgas.
Those who follow the dharma of Śiva say that Prāṇaliṅgisthala is Śiva himself in person.
A hand made of fire, devoted to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
The teachers, the Śiva-śāstrins, call this place Prasādisthala. || 250 ||
His body was water, his hand was intellect, and he was devoted to the worship of the Guru-liṅga.
The wise declare that this is indeed the very site of Māheśvara.
The earth-element, the hand of the mind, and that which delights in the worship of right conduct.
Those who know the Śiva-siddhānta call it Bhaktasthala.
The five-syllabled mantra is the supreme knowledge, while the six-syllabled mantra is indeed with Tārā.
She herself exists in eight ways, distinguished as gross, subtle, and so forth.
She is designated by the auspicious mantras, the essence of the mantra-mother (Mātṛkā), and the form of the Liṅga.
She eternally bestows auspiciousness and is established within all limbs. || 254 ||
The Supreme Goddess, known by the syllable *na*, is established in the *mūlādhāra*.
In the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the Śāmbhavī, known as the letter *ma*, is fully established. || 255 ||
In the great sacred site of Maṇipūra resides the Great Goddess known as Śikhā.
In the unstruck sound (anāhata), the energy of Śiva known as the letter Va is eternally established. || 256 ||
But in the state of purity, she who is called the letter Ya stands as the manifest Sovereign of the Universe.
The Great Goddess named Tārā is perfectly situated in the wheel of command (ājñācakra). || 257 ||
The letter *na* shall be that which is called Ācāra, and the letter *ma* is the sign of the Guru.
The syllable ŚI would be the fixed liṅga (sthavara-liṅga), and the syllable VĀ would be the mobile liṅga (cara-liṅga). || 258 ||
The syllable *ya* is called *prasāda*, and the *oṃkāra* is said to be *mahat*.
The sixth [syllable] would be the Savior (Tāra), and the letter Ya would be the fifth. || 259 ||
The fourth, however, should be the syllable *va*, while the third is the syllable *śi*.

[Thus, in the *Śivācārakathana*, which is an extraction of the essence of the conduct of the Vīramāheśvaras— the quintessence of the Vedas, Vedāntas, Śivāgamas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Gītās, Śāstras, and ancient sayings.]

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the True Nature of the Offering of the Liṅga," in the Uttarakhanda of the *Śrīmad-Vedāntasāra-Vīraśaiva-Cintāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Niṣṭhuraśrīman-Nañjanācārya.
Salutations to Śrī Śiva.
We shall explain the true nature of grace;
in the *Viśeṣārthaprakāśikā*, the venerable Guru said:
The limb is the individual soul (jīva), the supreme is the subtle body (liṅga), and their relationship is indeed identity (tādātmya).
The various forms of offering consist of the nature of those respective objects and the nature of clarity. || 1 ||
The manifestation of the nature of reality becomes the supreme grace for the living being.
And this offering is identity; such is the supreme state of Śiva.
This is the determination of the reality of these three: the world, the individual soul, and the Lord.
The three [types of] offerings consisting of food remnants are determined in their proper sequence. || 3 ||
The form of the world, beginning with the body, is residual and characterized by delusion.
Food would be its presiding deity, and the individual soul (jīva) characterized by transmigratory existence.
Grace is the Lord himself, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Having thus stated the essential nature, the specific distinction is now further explained.
He sees that body, yet he does not see that [very] body.
Another person sees those two, yet they both do not see him.
Thus, having taken as the subject matter the supreme reality, both external and internal.
The divine devotion consists in the unity of both knowledge and action.
The disciple said: [in verse]
To the Guru, the Greatly Compassionate One, who is serene and established in the states of Brahman within his own six locations;
Then the disciple, having bowed with supreme devotion and with palms joined in reverence, asked with restrained speech:
"O Guru, O ocean of the knowledge of Śiva, O you whose self is Śiva, regarding these determinations of the six stations (ṣaṭsthala) spoken by you..."
Out of compassion, you have known everything; whatever little I have reflected upon therein, please grant me your grace.
Furthermore, some say that food kept in a vessel is what is offered as prasāda to Śivā.
"It is indeed the leavings; that is what was consumed by you yourself. Tell me the truth of this, O Lord:
how is it that a single entity is divided into those three forms, O All-pervading One?"

Thus questioned, he who possesses the glory of unsurpassed bliss remained silent.
Having gazed for a long time at his disciple, who was self-luminous, the Lord Guru said to him: || 12 ||

The disciple said:
O Lord Guru, through your compassion, the means for realizing the categories [of existence] have been understood; now tell me the truth regarding the act of surrender here. The Guru said:

That portion of the food and other offerings which is contained in a vessel and being presented while situated within a bowl.

There is no distinctness in a single entity, because its intrinsic nature, name, object, quality, and so forth, are identical.
Although this is divided, when investigated according to the characteristics already stated, it is indeed indivisible.
The disciple said:
Whatever is perceived before one, appearing in the form of food and so forth, and placed within the vessel of Śiva;

The Guru said:
If it is of invisible form, then indeed it remains invisible even when contained within a vessel.

Among the entire multitude of objects offered to Śiva, that which is distinct must be what has not been offered.

The disciple said:

The disciple said:

The disciple said:

The Guru said:
Listen now to what is prohibited regarding the remains of food after eating; for this is indeed a common worldly saying: "It is called *ucchiṣṭa* (leftover). Thus spoke the disciple.

The Guru said:
There is no state of being leavings, nor any state of being forbidden, in the supreme, most pure direct grace.

If grace were to consist in the state of being a remnant or being prohibited, then grace would not exist at all;
and because it would be non-existent, there would be no sign of it, no guru, and no descent through the lineage.
The disciple said:

The Guru said:
The Veda teaches that one must first remove one's own defects and only thereafter is one worthy to enjoy the grace of Śiva;

Medicine should be taken for the sake of the disease, and likewise for the sake of the body's humors.
"This is the grace of Śiva that must be served"—this is the supreme state of the Śaivas. || 74 ||
Vṛtti: If that which has been consumed first, by way of one's own enjoyment, should be of a pleasing nature, it is also praiseworthy.

The disciple replied:
"Not so, O Lord; for some may have consumed the *liṅga* [food], yet remain defiled by their own tongue and senses."

To say that one portion among them is "leftover" while the remainder is not "leftover" is a false doctrine.
If it is all "leftover," then everything consumed by all the sense organs is likewise leftover.
If nothing remains as leavings, then everything has been consumed by all the sense organs without residue.
By those who are unconditioned, whose self, senses, elements, and bodies are signless, who are intent on their own welfare, yet still possessed of desire.
That which is seen, heard, touched, tasted, smelled, and even that which is known as "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa)—
all this is [perceived] by those who are beyond the senses, whose objects are not sensory, who are free from desire, and whose selves consist of the six locations.
That which has been eaten is indeed not considered leftover (ucchiṣṭa), nor forbidden, nor defiled.

Because the state of being born from a fragment is itself logically untenable.

Nor what has been eaten by oneself, nor what is left over, nor what remains in a vessel, nor what has been offered.

With supreme devotion, through actions performed according to one's own will, and with due ritual offerings.
"This indeed is the true greatness of the statement: 'This is the nature of the categories of existence. (101)
Whoever [recites] these eight verses on serene confidence with a mind intent on serene confidence...

Worship that Prasāda always in its form consisting of the six locations.

And likewise when a vessel or a container has been broken in many ways.

Vṛtti: Thus, having described the greatness of grace, the Greatly Compassionate Guru, being pleased, spoke of that very grace.

In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, within the *Śaiva Saṃhitā*, in the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini, Vyāsa says:

Thus, in the *Śivācārakathana*, which is an extraction of the essence of the conduct of the Vīramāheśvaras— the quintessence of the Vedas, Vedāntas, Śivāgamas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Gītā, Śāstras, and ancient utterances— [this concludes the section].
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The True Nature of Grace," in the Uttarakhanda of the *Śrīmad-Vedāntasāra-Vīraśaiva-Cintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Ācārya Añjaneya Niṣṭhūraśrīman.
Salutations to Śrī Śiva.

We shall declare the greatness of Vīraśaiva according to the Jābāla branch [of the Vedas]: "The wise Brāhmaṇas, whose minds are tranquil, eat what has been eaten by Rudra, drink what has been drunk by Rudra, and smell what has been smelled by Rudra."
They eat only the remains of offerings; one should consume only the remains of offerings. || 1 ||

The meaning of this has already been stated. Thus, by the very words of the Śruti, it is determined that those Brāhmaṇas who consume only the *nirmālya* of Śiva are tranquil-minded, wise, and distinguished;
whereas those who do not consume the *nirmālya* of Śiva are non-Brāhmaṇas.
The meaning is that they are unrefined people whose minds are not tranquil and who lack knowledge. || 2 ||
In another passage: "They consume only the remains of offerings; they are not outcasts (caṇḍāla), nor are they Pulkasas."

The intention here is this: even a *caṇḍāla* who has always enjoyed the grace of his own chosen *liṅga* does not remain a *caṇḍāla*, nor does he remain a *pulkasa*; rather, he alone is of noble birth, he alone is excellent, he alone is blessed, and he alone is a *brāhmaṇa*. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
Also in the Sāmavedopaniṣad: "Or even if a caṇḍāla should utter the word 'Śiva,' one should converse with him, dwell with him, lie down with him,
and eat with him."
"He should eat together. || 4 ||
Regarding this matter, in the *Padmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava, it is said:
"He in whose speech the auspicious name 'Śiva' proceeds..."
Indeed, the sin committed over seven lifetimes is reduced to ashes for him.
By speaking, by dwelling, and by entering again and again.
"He should eat together; he should eat together," so indeed says the Sāma-śruti. || 6 ||
In the *Śivarahasya*, it is said:
"O best of sages, even a dog-eater, through devotion to Śiva, becomes superior to the twice-born."
But a twice-born man devoid of devotion to Śiva is the lowest of outcasts.
Even a Caṇḍāla who constantly utters the word "Śiva" with joy [is purified].
One should speak words together with him, and one should always dwell together with him. || 8 ||
In the Āditya Purāṇa, within the Mānavīya Saṃhitā, chapter sixty-three, these are the words of Brahmā addressed to Nārada:
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even one born of the lowest caste;
A devotee of Śiva is always worthy of worship; he is the most excellent among all Brāhmaṇas.
Or even if one should be a barbarian, provided he is endowed with devotion to Bhava.
Neither one learned in the four Vedas nor a performer of sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma is equal to him.

In the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* of the Śaiva tradition, in the latter part (*uparibhāga*), within the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Upamanyu concerning the description of the conduct of devotion (*bhaktyācāra*), these are the words of Śiva addressed to the Goddess.
Likewise, in the first chapter of the Śivadharmottara:
Affection for my devotees and rejoicing in their worship.
Worshiping me personally with devotion and performing physical movements for my sake; (11)
Devotion to hearing my stories is manifested through changes in one's voice, eyes, and limbs.
May you always follow me, free from any deceit toward me.
These eightfold marks are present even in that barbarian.
He is a lord of brahmins, a sage, illustrious, an ascetic, and a scholar. || 13 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, in the section on devotion (*bhaktisthala*), and in another Purāṇa, it is said:
"Hearing [the name] of Śambhu, chanting [His praises], remembering [Him], and serving His feet..."
Worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender. || 41 ||
Thus, ninefold devotion has been proclaimed by the Lord Śambhu.
It is difficult for sinners to obtain in this world, but easy for those who perform meritorious deeds.
Whether in the lowliest or even the highest, wherever she may be, she is formidable.
In whom Śāmbhavī devotion exists, he is celebrated as a true devotee. || 16 ||
Devotion was firmly established even in that Mleccha who was the best among the twice-born.
One who knows the four Vedas is dear to me, but one devoid of devotion is not dear.
In the Śivarahasya, it is stated that there are four [metals]: bell-metal, silver, copper, and iron.
Just as the state of being gold [is restored] through the power of a specific medicinal elixir. || 18 ||
In the same way, indeed, a vessel such as a Śūdra and others [is purified] by means of that which consists of the Śiva-mantras.
Through the great savor of the wise, one attains the state of the Supreme Brahman. || 19 ||
For this Śūdra is indeed perfected by the Śiva-saṃskāra; he is truly a twice-born (dvija).
"He by whom a distinction is made between the Liṅgas shall go to the Raurava hell. || 20 ||
As stated in the *Liṅgasāra* and the *Śivarahasya*:
"Just as the waters of the city's streams and other sources attain oneness upon reaching the Gaṅgā..."
"By the power of initiation and yoga, even a Śūdra and others may attain the state of Śiva. || 22 ||
In the Bhṛgusaṃhitā:
"A Caṇḍāla is never at all [to be considered] as always present [in the body]."
The Śūdra-status of the Śūdra has indeed departed, whereas that of the Brāhmaṇa is otherwise.
In the Gāruḍapurāṇa, in the latter section (Uttara-bhāga),
[it describes] those who follow the lineage of succession and are distinguished by the wearing of the *liṅga*.
For those who possess knowledge and are devotees of Śiva, the status of being a Śūdra does not exist at all.
In the Vedic [tradition], there are the Namaka, Camaka, the five Brahma-mantras, and so forth.
Only they possess the qualification [for this] by virtue of the power of Śiva-initiation. || 24 ||
In the *Liṅgasāra*, it is said:
"Whether a woman, a man, a eunuch, an outcaste, or one born of a twice-born lineage,"
