One who has been born through the initiation of Śiva should not reflect upon his former birth.
But in the case of a well-established *liṅga*, the prior meditation does not apply in that same way.
As it is stated in the Śaiva Purāṇa: "Just as a lotus may exist in the mud, and just as fire exists within wood..."
Just as gold [is found] in stone, and a devotee is born from a family of outcasts. || 27 ||
In the second part of the Liṅgapurāṇa, it is stated:
"A liṅga made of wood, stone, metal, clay, or precious gems is consecrated."
Just as he is worthy of worship, so too should one born of a Caṇḍāla lineage be regarded with devotion. || 28 ||
In the Śivarahasya it is said:
"He is omniscient among all the Vedas and initiated into all sacrifices."
A dog-eater who worships the Liṅga destroys ten million great sins.
"From conversing with him, liberation will come, as well as the happiness of being a leader of the Gaṇas. || 29 ||
Likewise, in the Śivarahasya and the Liṅgasāra, it is said:
"One who knows all the auspicious times but does not wear the liṅga shall be like a caṇḍāla at all times."
But a worshiper of the Liṅga, even if he be an outcaste, excels ten million Brahmins.
In the Āditya Purāṇa, the Lord said:
Whether one stands on the path or not on the path, whether one is a fool or even a scholar.
"Indeed, if one should become my devotee, he is superior to all. || 31 ||
In the *Rahasya*, the Lord spoke these words to the Goddess:
"I do not dwell on Kailāsa, nor on Meru, nor on Mandara."
O Pārvatī, wherever my devotees abide, there I abide.
Or if a devotee of Śiva resides in a settlement of Caṇḍālas.
That row [of houses] would be the world of Śiva, and that house would be a temple of Śiva.
Even in the lands of Kīkaṭa, wherever there are people devoted to Maheśvara.
Even if one dwells there with only slight faith, it shall become equal to the sacred field of Kāśī.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"From seeing a devotee of Śiva, or even from conversing with him but once..."
O Nārada, the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice is obtained.
Thus, O Liṅgayas, [one attains] ten million minor offenses (upapātaka) and ten thousand killings of Brahmins (brahmahatyā).
The sight of a devotee of Śiva burns away all sins without exception.
In another text:
for the sake of purification from a great sin (mahāpātaka), one should go to the house of a devotee of Śiva.
One should beg for food as nectar; if that is not obtained, one should drink water.

By virtue of such authoritative statements from the Śrutis, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, the status of being twice-born (dvijatva) is well-established for all Vīraśaiva devotees, owing to their birth through initiation into Śiva (śivadīkṣā). || 38 ||
Therefore, it is said in the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā:
"Seeing that best of the twice-born performing the union of the Liṅga and the body, the Sun..."
"Having pierced through my mandala, this one shall depart for Śiva, moving from his station. || 39 ||
Thus, the statements of the Purāṇas are well-known.
In the Mahābhārata and elsewhere it is said:
"By birth one is born a Śūdra; by action one is called a twice-born (dvija)."
"A Brahmin who knows the meaning of the Vedic scriptures becomes a Brāhmaṇa who knows Brahman" (as in "he practices Brahman, thus he is a Brāhmaṇa"). || 40 ||
In another text:
those who have arisen from the *rudrapiṇḍa* and those who recite the sequence of the Vedas.
"Those who know the Śrī Rudra, which is to be recited as Brahman, they are remembered as true Brāhmaṇas. || 41 ||
This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, has originated from the *piṇḍa* of Rudra.
"Out of delusion alone, he does not recognize that he is the son of a courtesan, just like his father. || 42 ||
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the *Īśvaragītā*, and in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*, it is said: "The central *piṇḍa* situated between the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas bestows sons."
The remains of offerings to Śiva are declared in the Vedas; what more need be said? (43)

Thus, based on authoritative statements such as "the Rudra-piṇḍa is the grace (prasāda) of Śiva," it is determined that only those Brāhmaṇas who have received the piṇḍa born of the grace of Śiva are true devotees of Śiva.

For this very reason, although Viśvāmitra was born of a Kṣatriya, he attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa through austerity because he was a partial incarnation of Rudra; and although Paraśurāma was born of a Brāhmaṇa, he performed the duties of a Kṣatriya through his activities because he was a partial incarnation of Viṣṇu.
It is heard in the *Harivaṃśa* that [the conflict] was caused by the exchange of the *caru* offerings dedicated to Śiva and Viṣṇu performed by the sage Bhṛgu;

this has been stated previously. In the *Bhāgavata*, this same account is said to have been caused by the exchange of the *caru* and the sacrificial portions (*piṇḍa*) belonging to the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.

Because this is a Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, it has been stated somewhat cryptically; thus, the origin of the Brāhmaṇas is established as being from the Brāhmaṇa alone, since the birth of a Brāhmaṇa from anyone else is impossible.
Furthermore, Rudra's status as a Brāhmaṇa is heard in the Sāmaveda, in the Prapada-brāhmaṇa.
"You are a Brāhmaṇa among the gods, and I am a Brāhmaṇa among men; indeed, a Brāhmaṇa runs to a Brāhmaṇa for refuge—I run to you for refuge. || 45 ||
Regarding this matter, it is stated in the Parāśara Purāṇa:
"All the gods are of mixed origin, and Purandara is a vṛṣala."
The Grandfather (Brahmā) is indeed a Vaiśya, while Hari is the supreme Kṣatriya. || 46 ||
The Blessed One Rudra is a Brāhmaṇa, the most excellent among all.
For the state of being Brahman belongs to Rudra; his status as a Brāhmaṇa is not born of causes.
Indeed, in this world, a Brahmin always seeks refuge with a Brahmin.
One should take refuge in the Great Brahman, the Lord, and not in another. || 48 ||

In the *Vajrasūcī Upaniṣad*, having established the absence of Brahminhood through eight alternative arguments beginning with "If there is doubt regarding Brahminhood in the body," it is demonstrated that only one who possesses knowledge of the true nature of the Self is a Brahmin. Keeping all of this in mind:

In the *Vajrasūcī*, the teacher Paramahaṃsa, having stated the absence of Brahminhood within the body through eight alternative arguments beginning with "If there were doubt regarding Brahminhood in the body," concludes by citing the Sāman scripture: "Among the gods you are a Brahmin. Thus it is said that Śiva alone among the gods is the Brahmin, and his devotee among men is the Brahmin.
These and other such points have already been explained in detail previously. || 49 ||

In the *Yajurveda*, it is said: "He who sacrifices beyond his own deity falls away from his own deity; he does not reach the higher one, and he becomes worse off. The meaning of this is explained as follows: that Brahmin who, having passed over or bypassed his own deity, Śiva, worships another deity, indeed falls away.
Having become an offender against his own deity, that lowest of men does not attain the supreme goal; indeed, he becomes even more sinful, most certainly a sinner beyond measure. || 50 ||
In the Āditya Purāṇa, the Lord said:
"Those born of base conduct live in ways contrary to the world."
"Those who are the best among ten million knowers of the Vedas are permeated by my being. || 51 ||
In the Skanda Purāṇa and elsewhere it is said: "A Brahmin who upholds the four Vedas but is devoid of devotion to Śiva..."
Overburdened by the weight of the Vedas, he is indeed a donkey among Brahmins. || 52 ||
A Brahmin who upholds the four Vedas but is devoid of devotion to Śiva.
By giving him food, the donor shall go to hell. || 53 ||

Based on such scriptural authorities, it should be understood that only one who is born through the initiation (dīkṣā) of Śiva and is a devotee of Śiva is truly a Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas such as the Bhāgavata, Nārāyaṇa has stated, "The Brāhmaṇa is my deity"; the meaning is that the Brāhmaṇa is Lord Rudra, and only his devotees [are true Brāhmaṇas].
They become Brahmins. || 54 ||
Therefore, it was said by Nārāyaṇa in the Kālikākhaṇḍa, in the chapter on the liberation from Bhṛgu’s curse, in the words of Viṣṇu addressed to the residents of Vaikuṇṭha:
May all the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha hear my proclamation!
Whether he be well-behaved or ill-mannered, a devotee of Śiva is my lord. || 55 ||

On the basis of such scriptural authorities as these, because Rudra is a Brāhmaṇa, because he is the cause of the origin of Brāhmaṇas, and because he is to be worshipped by Brāhmaṇas, it is indeed proper that those who harbor hatred toward the devotees of Rudra should be excluded. || 56 ||
As it has been said: "That son who hates his father, one should know him to be of another's seed."
One who constantly hates Brahmins, know him to be one whose seed is elsewhere (impotent). || 57 ||

One should not examine his conduct, nor his lineage, nor likewise his religious observances.
O Nārada, he who is marked with the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) is indeed worthy of worship.
He who reviles devotees by deed, mind, or speech—
O Sage, there is no deliverance from hell for that deluded soul.
In the Kālikākhaṇḍa, Viṣṇu’s words to the Vaiṣṇavas:
"Those who hate the devotees of Śiva belonging to the stages of life of the student and the householder..."
Those who are ignorant regarding other forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) are heretics, and there are no others [of that kind]. || 60 ||
In the Āditya Purāṇa, within the description of the progression of the Kali Yuga, these are the words of Sanatkumāra addressed to Vyāsa.
They revile Mahādeva, the supreme liberator from saṃsāra.
And especially those Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to him in the Kali age. || 61 ||
In the Śivarahasya,
it is said that any person who performs evil deeds and reviles the devotees of Śiva even once [is reborn as a worm].

And for a hundred births he becomes lame, and for a hundred [births] he is born as a heretic.
An owl, a crow, a vulture, a snake, a pig, and a donkey.
One is born and indeed dies; no atonement whatsoever exists. || 65 ||
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Those who perform the ritual installation for Śiva-ascetics, hermits, or humans..."
Burnt by the fire of the Kumbhīpāka hell, they are born into low wombs.
In the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā:
[This applies] to those joined with the lowest of the low, to sinners, and to practitioners of malevolent magic.
The world of Yama shall never exist for those who wear the linga.
In that regard, whatever sin has been committed in another place during the time of sleep, such as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth—
Just as at the time of awakening, that [dream] itself becomes false.
In this way, great sin was committed by me in the past through the wearing of the sectarian mark.
Whatever exists goes to dissolution after the wearing of the *liṅga*. (69)
O Six-faced One, I do not see any Dharma equal to this.
In the Vedas, Tantras, and Purāṇas, I have declared this truth, this absolute truth. (70)
In that very same [text].
Thousands of killings of Brahmins and tens of thousands of killings of embryos.
Even while acting, those devoted to the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga* are not tainted. || 71 ||
In the Āditya Purāṇa, Brahmā speaks to Nārada:
"With the exception of those devoted to Śiva, the king is the punisher of all."
Furthermore, for those who are devotees of Śiva, Śiva alone is [the goal] and no other.
Neither Death, nor Dhātṛ, nor Yama, nor the messengers of Yama [have power over him]. || 72 ||
In the Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad:
"Those men who, upon seeing one who wears the sacred ash, revile him with their speech..."
The origin of these [castes] from a Śūdra should be inferred by the wise.
Those men who, upon seeing one who wears the sacred ash, inflict blows upon him;
And their birth from a Caṇḍāla, O Brahmin, should be inferred by the wise. || 74 ||
In the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā:
Therefore, having renounced everything, with one's whole being and at all times...
One should worship with great reverence the twice-born who is united with the limbs of the Liṅga.
It is rare to find in the three worlds one whose body is joined with the *prāṇaliṅga*.
For some, it becomes easily accessible due to merit performed in previous births.
By those whose minds were bowed in devotion, Śambhu was propitiated in former times.
Only by them can that meritorious soul be attained, who shares in the contact with the body of the Śiva-liṅga.
He who honors a twice-born man whose mind is absorbed in meditation upon the limbs of the Liṅga.
For him there is no further rebirth; this I have spoken as the truth, the absolute truth.
It is my conviction that any practice other than this is unrighteousness (adharma). || 78 ||
In the Skanda [Purāṇa], it is said that the Brahmin is the earth-god (bhūsura), and likewise, the mobile [deity] is the earth-ruddra (bhūrudra).
Between the two, the Suras and the Rudras, the Rudras alone are distinguished as superior. || 79 ||
In the Śivadharmottara, it is stated:
"A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) is superior to a thousand [householders] wearing the sacrificial thread."
One who has studied the Vedas is superior to thousands of celibate students.
One who maintains the sacred fire is superior to thousands of those who recite the Vedas.
A devotee of Śiva is superior to thousands of Agnihotris. || 81 ||
Animals are superior in intelligence to worms, insects, and moths.
Humans are superior even to animals; among them, the twice-born are the most excellent.
Among the twice-born, the Brahmins are superior; among the Brahmins, those whose intellects are fixed on sacrifice are superior.
Among those whose intellects are fixed on ritual sacrifices, the renunciants are superior. || 83 ||
Among them, the wise are superior; among the wise, those who worship Śaṅkara are the best.
Among them, O fortunate one, the most excellent are those who are united with my own body as their liṅga.
The man who possesses knowledge of the six stages (ṣaṭsthala) is superior even among those whose limbs are attached to the Liṅga.
Therefore, there is nothing superior to this in all three worlds in any way whatsoever.
"What is the use of saying much, my child? I am that very person; of this there is no doubt. (85)
In another text, the Lord spoke these words to the Goddess:
"Who indeed knows, in accordance with reality, the greatness of my devotees?"
"I know, you know, and Nandi or Guha knows as well. || 86 ||

Thus, in the *Śivācārakathana* (The Exposition of the Conduct of Śiva), which is an extraction of the essence of the ancient declarations from the Vedas, Vedānta, Śiva-Āgamas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Gītā, and Śāstras, and which is the core of the conduct of the heroic Māheśvaras.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vīraśaivism," in the Uttarakhanda of the *Śrīmad-Vedāntasāra-Vīraśaiva-Cintāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Annaṅga Niṣṭhūra Śrīman.
Salutations to Śrī Śiva.
We shall now describe the gift to a worthy recipient (*satpātra-dāna*) in the twenty-fifth chapter of the second part of the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Giving is said to be of three kinds: constant (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*)."
The fourth is declared to be Vimala, the most excellent among all gifts. || 1 ||
Whatever is given day after day to one who does not return the favor, [is called *nitya-dāna*].
That which is performed daily for a Brāhmaṇa should be done without aiming for any reward.
That which is placed in the hands of the learned for the purpose of pacifying speech;
This is designated by the virtuous as the unsurpassed occasional gift (naimittika-dāna).
That which is given for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty, or heaven;
But giving is declared by the sages who contemplate dharma to be that which is performed with desire. || 4 ||
If that which is given to those who know Brahman is for the purpose of pleasing Īśvara, [it is meritorious].
That gift, given with a mind endowed with devotion, is pure and auspicious.
Having encountered a worthy recipient, one should practice the duty of giving according to one's ability.
For whatever vessel shall arise, it will deliver everyone from all [suffering]. || 6 ||
In the Śivadharmapurāṇa:
"One worthy recipient consists of Veda; another worthy recipient consists of austerity."
Whichever vessel shall come here, that very vessel he will cause to cross over.
Of all worthy recipients, Maheśvara is the most preeminent recipient.
It is fourfold: the daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the optional (kāmya), and the pure (vimala). || 8 ||
A gift should be given to a worthy recipient; not even a particle should be given to one who is unworthy.
Indeed, it is given to a devotee of Śiva for the purpose of pleasing Hara.
That gift is declared to be stainless and the sole means for attaining liberation.
Therefore, having recognized one who is a most worthy recipient—a devotee of Śiva free from sin—[one should bestow it].
Everything should be given to him by one who desires inexhaustible fruit.
Because it protects one from falling into the exceedingly deep ocean of hell.
By virtue of the greatness of that bowl, even a tiny gift becomes inexhaustible.
Therefore, those who desire immeasurable fruit should always give to him. || 12 ||
In the Śivarahasya,
it is said that the worship of the teaching is superior to the worship of a virtuous recipient.
Therefore, one should honor the teaching without hesitation, by the command of Śiva.
Between the alms-bowl and the edict, the edict is indeed superior.
Therefore, one should first worship that Śiva in the form of his teaching alone. || 14 ||
The meaning is that the teaching bears the mark of Śiva; [this is from] the Vīrabhadrīya.
By worshipping Śivajña, the worshipper becomes Śiva himself.
One whose mind is free from stain should, for that very reason, revere the teaching of Śiva.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"But he who is a devotee of Maheśvara, though living solely by his birth [as a Brahmin]..."
Among all worthy recipients, he is the most excellent; what is given to him becomes inexhaustible.
And whoever bestows it upon another, bypassing a devotee of Śiva.
That gift shall be fruitless, and he shall fall into hell. || 17 ||
In the Śivadharmottara, it is said: "Whether one is unrestrained or restrained, or has reached any various state whatsoever,"
Whoever may be a devotee, they are the most excellent vessel, just like Śiva.
If even a dog-cooker (outcaste) is a devotee of Śiva, he attains the most excellent of births.
O Śivā, by the gift of his daughter and so forth, the donor shall be born in my lineage.
To me, even a dog-eater who is my devotee is dear, rather than one learned in the four Vedas who is not.
To him one should give, from him one should receive, and he indeed should be honored just as I am. (20)
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "O Skanda, my devotee is always dear to me, even if he is an outcaste."
There exists no superior vessel whatsoever greater than that.
In the Śivarahasya, it is said:
"The mind attains clarity by constantly worshipping the Great Lord (Maheśvara)."
One who is not of a family becomes endowed with a family by means of preceded salutation. || 22 ||
In the Śivadharmottara, it is said that upon seeing a devotee of Śiva approaching, those staying at home [should rise].
"All the medicinal herbs were playing, saying, 'We shall go to the supreme goal. || 23 ||
A devotee who has gone to the hermitage of Śiva at Vīrabhadra should worship a devotee of Śiva.
By offering a welcome and a seat, and by presenting water for the feet, the guest-offering (arghya), and salutations; || 24 ||
In the Śivadharmottara: Therefore, one should go out with palms joined in reverence to meet a guest who has arrived.
Rising to meet him, approaching him, welcoming him, offering a seat, and speaking kindly. || 25 ||
The water for washing the feet, followed by the guest, is like a seven-stepped ladder to heaven.
With a welcome, a seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, a bath, food, a bed, and so forth.
Therefore, one who desires infinite fruit should give with reverence. || 26 ||
In another treatise: rising to meet [the teacher], approaching him, saluting, and speaking kindly.
The seat, as well as food and drink, are said to be the seven steps. || 27 ||
Whatever fruit is obtained by feeding ten million twice-born Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, according to the Śivarahasya;
That fruit is obtained by a devotee of Śiva through the giving of alms. || 28 ||
In the *Śivadharmottara*,
it is said that the fruit which results from feeding ten million Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas—
By the mere gift of alms-food to a Śiva-yogin, that same fruit is obtained. || 29 ||
In the Laiṅgya [Tantra], it is said: "By means of seats, massage, bathing, clothing, grain, and the like for the body..."
He who honors a devotee of Śiva attains the supreme goal.
The words of Īśvara addressed to the Goddess in the Śiva Purāṇa.
And penance, sacrifice, recitation, and so forth, O lady of excellent hips, come to naught.
O beautiful woman, the oblation offered into the mouths of the devotees is never exhausted.
And so it is stated in the Vīrāgama:
"O lady of excellent hips, asceticism, sacrifices, recitations, and the like come to an end."
O beautiful lady, the oblation offered into the mouths of the heroes is never exhausted. || 32 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"But when food produced from grain, offered to Śiva, is being eaten by a devotee..."
For every single grain of boiled rice, the fruit that belongs to an Aśvamedha sacrifice is obtained. || 33 ||
In the Brahmapurāṇa, the words of Īśvara addressed to Brahmā:
The food offering placed before me has been accepted by me merely by its being seen.
O Lotus-born One, I consume the flavors from the tip of the tongue of my devotee.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"In whosever house a Śiva-yogin, being duly honored, accepts alms..."
By that, one delivers seven, and seven, and seven families.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa (Vṛtti): "I do not eat that which is offered by the sacrificer through the sacrificial spreads; rather, let that be offered and poured into my mouth by means of the fire-eater."
"Even from the food that enters the mouth of a moving creature as it wanders about, there is no such satisfaction for me, for my own karmic results remain unrestrained. (36)
In the Śiva Purāṇa:
"Because of their commonality of having hands, feet, and so forth, mortals possess the form of Rudra."
Thinking of them as if they were ordinary people, the wise do not recognize [their true nature] at all. || 37 ||
Contempt has been shown toward them by men of deluded minds.
Having destroyed longevity, prosperity, lineage, and virtue, they shall attain hell. || 38 ||
Having gone to the hermitage of Śiva at Vīrabhadra, the devotee should worship those who are devoted to Śiva.
By offering a welcome and a seat, and by presenting water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and salutations; || 39 ||
In the Śivadharmottara:
"That gift which is bestowed with faith upon a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rule..."
That should be known as having infinite fruit, or even as being merely the size of a sesame seed. || 40 ||
In the Śivadharmapurāṇa:

Since for those who are solely intent on the auspiciousness of meditative absorption (samādhi), rites such as cremation are prohibited, it is only appropriate for them to perform the activity of meditative absorption itself. || 1 ||

"For one who has desisted from all ritual actions and is devoted to the yoga of meditation..."

"The forest-dweller is a yogin; the mendicant is a renunciant who possesses the single mark."

The body, joined with the Śiva-liṅga, is a vessel of perpetual purity.
Even at the end of the body of a living being, it is devoid of the consecration by fire.
If the consecration by fire is omitted, the king perishes along with his kingdom.
Having made a cave, he filled the mouth of the cave with salt.
With song, instrumental music, and dance, and with perfumes, flowers, and lamps.
And the wise one should obtain the permission of the mobile devotees.
[He was surrounded] by disciples who were pure according to the four stages of life and who moved about observing excellent vows.
And immediately gathering his devotees together, he performed the rite of preparing a roll of sacred ash (vibhūti-vīṭikā).
Having installed it within the cave together with the Prāṇaliṅga.
Death occurs through anger, thieves, or by means of poison and water.
And one should place it together with a bilva fruit for the sake of the devotees and the living beings.
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, the latter part of the Śaiva Purāṇa,
within the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Upamanyu, during the praise of the devotees of Śiva, there is this speech of Upamanyu:
But that mortal who, having encountered death, beholds many omens of impending doom;
Devoted to the commencement of yoga, he should take refuge in a sacred field of Śiva.
Even while dwelling there, if this man remains firm-minded, [he will attain success].
One may even voluntarily relinquish one's life-breaths, even without being afflicted by diseases or other such ailments.
Having performed the prescribed fast and having offered his limbs as oblations into the fire of Śiva, he—
Or by casting one's own body into the sacred waters of Śiva and immersing oneself therein. || 17 ||
Whoever should renounce their life according to the procedure prescribed in the Śiva scriptures, [attains liberation].
He would be liberated immediately, and he would not be a suicide. || 18 ||
Or else, rendered helpless by disease and other afflictions, he takes refuge in a sacred field of Śiva.
If he should die [there], he too is liberated in this way; there is no doubt about this. || 19 ||
Nevertheless, death [by natural means] is praised, but not by means of fasting and the like.
For it is performed with a mind made steady by confidence in the scriptures. || 20 ||
Just as it is distinguished there, death likewise becomes increasingly superior in each successive stage.
Indeed, by virtue of cessation and other factors, the body dissolves into the elements.
Death by departing at will, especially in a sacred field of Śiva.
It is supreme, superior to all deaths, and bestows the yoga of the state beyond the mind (unmanāpada).
Having killed one who delights in reviling Śiva, or having been personally oppressed by him;
He who would renounce his life, which is so difficult to give up, is not born again.
He who was unable to kill one devoted to reviling Śiva died himself.
He shall be liberated immediately, together with twenty-one generations of his lineage.
He who would give up his life for the sake of Śiva, or indeed for the sake of a devotee of Śiva;
Either for the sake of Śiva’s conduct, or indeed for the sake of Śiva’s knowledge. || 25 ||
There is no other person standing on the path to liberation who is his equal.
Therefore, his liberation from the cycle of worldly existence is even swifter.
Or, having somehow relied upon one of these means;
Or if one who has attained the purification of the six paths according to the ritual rules should die; || 27 ||
One should not perform funeral rites for him here on earth, just as one would not for domestic animals.
Impurity would not at all attach [to him], especially in the case of his sons and others. || 28 ||
Now, if one also desires to perform a ritual act directed toward this [deity], [one should proceed as follows].
One should perform only what is auspicious and should gratify those who are devoted to Śiva. || 29 ||
His wealth shall belong to Śiva, provided that there exists a lineage belonging to Śiva.
If that [desire] does not exist, one should give it to Śiva; one should not give it to the lineage of bound souls (paśu).
Furthermore, if it is asked what kind of liberation belongs to the Vīraśaivas, it is said in reply:

Based on the scriptural statement, "His vital breaths do not depart; they are absorbed right here," it must be said that for Vīraśaivas, liberation consists precisely in the identity of one's own nature [with the Supreme]. || 31 ||
In the Kāmikāgama, it is said: "Śiva himself is indeed the liṅga, and the self alone, O dear one, becomes the body."
For the perfect union of those two, Śiva and the Self, is indeed their true conjunction.
For the union of the subtle body (liṅga) and the physical body (aṅga) is always a true yoga when it is performed correctly.
Union itself is liberation in the form of sāyujya; of this there is no doubt. || 33 ||
O Maheśvarī, for the Vīras, liberation is attained in a single birth.
And for other Śaivas, liberation occurs after three births.

Therefore, by virtue of the state of identity between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*, through the direct realization of the Supreme Lord—the mine of infinite auspicious qualities—there occurs for the devotees of Śiva the cessation of the bonds (*pāśa*). From that follows the absence of birth and so forth, and subsequently, the attainment of similarity of form (*sārūpya*) and union (*sāyujya*). || 35 ||

The Śvetāśvataras declare: "Having known the God, there is the severance of all bonds; when affliction is exhausted, there is the abandonment of birth and death. The meaning of this is: "God" (deva) is so called because he shines (dīvyati); having known—that is, having directly realized—Śiva, who is perfect bliss, there occurs the abandonment of all sins, which is to say, cessation.

The remainder refers to those whose afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted. The afflictions are ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to cling to life (*abhiniveśa*).

When these are exhausted, there is the abandonment of birth and death—the cessation of birth and mortality—which means liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). By the mention of this, the third [chapter] concerns the dissolution of the body.

The meaning of the phrase "possessing all sovereignty, absolute, with desires fulfilled" is as follows: through meditation upon that— that is, through the grace arising from uninterrupted meditation— one attains the third state,
namely the state of Rudra (the third in relation to Brahmā and Viṣṇu), at the time of the dissolution of the body.

When even the dissolution of the body has occurred, there is universal sovereignty (*viśvaiśvarya*). Mahādeva is the Lord of the Universe; his state is "universal sovereignty. He is absolute (*kevala*), one whose desires are fulfilled (*āptakāma*). "Absoluteness" means being non-dual (*advitīyatva*), and "fulfillment of desires" means having full desires (*pūrṇakāmatva*);
the intended meaning is that both of these qualities belong to him. Nor is this [state] adventitious (*āgantukatva*) to him.

The impermanence of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is a portion of the Lord (*īśvara*), arises because, when the division caused by dependence on bonds ceases, the manifestation of true sovereignty becomes possible. As it has been said: "But [the soul's nature] is concealed by the contemplation of the Supreme; from that [concealment] arise its bondage and its opposite. The meaning of this is: "by the contemplation of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*)."
Through the clarity resulting from prior meditation, one's obscured true nature becomes manifest; for what reason?

Because the bondage and liberation of this individual soul (jīva) proceed from that Supreme Lord. Thus, the intention of the Sūtra is that Paśupati—the Supreme Lord—is the one who effects the release of bound souls (paśu) from bondage, and there is no other. In this manner...
Liberation is indeed the attainment of the state of Śiva, characterized by the absolute cessation of bondage. || 36 ||
As it is said in the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad]:
"Having made the Self the lower fire-drill and the Praṇava the upper fire-drill..."
"By the practice of churning through meditation, the wise man burns away the fetter. || 37 ||
"Having known the Lord, they become immortal. In the *Atharvaśikhā*: "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon as the bringer of auspiciousness;

having abandoned everything else—thus ends the *Atharvaṇī Śikhā*. The meaning of "śivaṃkara" is "one who makes [the state of] Śiva"; this is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary focus. One who knows Brahman is indeed Brahman itself.

"It exists," and so forth, is indeed well-known. But what is this attainment of Śiva-hood? Is it identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) or a difference in attributes (*dharma-bheda*)? Not the first, because if there were non-difference—as in the oneness of two lumps of clay—there would follow the consequence of being subject to modification (*vikāritva*). Nor is it the case that distinct formless entities, such as time and space, possess oneness.
The second [position] is not tenable because it is sublated by scripture (*śruti*) through the context of awakening;
for a non-difference of attributes (*dharma-abheda*) in the form of a genus (*jāti*), like "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth, cannot be adventitious (*āgantuka*).

Although even in the form of an adjunct (*upādhi*), similarity (*sādṛśya*) consisting in the possession of common qualities—such as having true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*) and omniscience (*sarvajñatva*)—is possible.

If it is argued that nevertheless the conventional usage of "liberation" does not occur without identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*), it is replied: identity of essential nature itself is supreme liberation, and its impossibility in the case of embodied beings is not a fault, precisely because non-difference with the Great Space (*mahākāśa*) is possible for the spaces within jars and so forth. Thus...

Furthermore, liberation is not merely oneness with the Absolute (dharmaikya), because that would entail a return [to worldly existence], whereas states such as Sālokya and others are also established by Śruti. || 38 ||

"In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], it is said that one attains union with Brahman, equality of power (*sārṣṭitā*), and residence in the same world (*samānalokatā*); here, *sārṣṭitā* means equality of sovereignty. || 39 ||

If it is argued that, according to the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, "the passionless ones depart by way of the door of the sun," and therefore liberation by way of the solar door belongs only to renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*), we say no; for that [liberation] is prescribed for Vīraśaivas as well in their supporting scriptures (*upabṛṃhaṇa*). || 40 ||
For this very reason, it has been stated in the *Śāṅkarasaṃhitā*, in the latter section (*uparibhāga*), within the praise of the Vīramāheśvara:
Seeing that best of the twice-born performing the union of the liṅga and the body, Ravi [spoke].
Having pierced through my mandala, this one shall move from its place and go to Śiva. || 41 ||
From this statement: "Having mounted the chariot of the syllable Om, and having made Viṣṇu the charioteer..."
Seeking the state of the Brahma-world, he was intent upon the propitiation of Rudra.

From this statement of the *Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad*, certain Vīraśaivas maintain that [the soul] attains the world of Śiva, designated as the world of Brahmā, by way of the solar aperture; furthermore, there is no lack of evidence for the identity of their essential natures. || 42 ||

In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "Just as rivers flowing toward the ocean disappear into it, casting off their names and forms, even so the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high. He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman..."
According to the Śruti, "He becomes Brahman itself," it should not be argued that there is merely a conjunction between the ocean and the river and not an identity of essential nature;
for what is intended by the illustration is the usage of oneness due to the absence of the usage of distinct names and forms.
This is because the state of the absence of commonality of name and form is established by the force of the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Because there is no conjunction of selves with a partless essence, and because non-difference is established between the part and the whole— just as in the case of the space within a jar and the great space (mahākāśa)—
non-return is common to all four types of liberation; however, in the liberation of union (sāyujya), it occurs within the omnipresent Brahman.

There is no possibility at all of returning from the abode of the living; for this very reason, it must be stated that for the Vīramāheśvaras, liberation consists solely in oneness with Paraśiva, who transcends the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
Furthermore, the ancient teachers have declared that the liberation of the Vīramāheśvaras is independent.
It is stated in accordance with the conduct of taking refuge in both the ancient and the new [traditions].
In the *Anubhavasūtra*, it refers to both worlds: the objects pertaining to this life and the next.
Devotion remains, possessing its full majesty, even without coming and going.
Some [attain] the state of Śiva along with their vital breaths; some with their own bodies; some with their wives, their children, their houses, and their circle of kinsmen.
Some, having gradually established villages, regions, and their own retinues, as well as all other things, become themselves devoted and go to Śiva. || 45 ||
However, some devotees who possess attachment toward objects such as the vital breath (prāṇa) attain identity with Śiva along with those very objects.
Some, being skilled in detachment, abandon those sense objects and go of their own accord to the auspicious state. || 46 ||
In the Śivadharmottara, it is said:
"The primordial abode of Umāpati resembles ten million moons."
Endowed with all desires, it is pure, eternal, and inexhaustible. || 47 ||
Having attained this divine state, which is free from all afflictions.
They become omniscient, all-pervading, pure, and perfectly complete. || 48 ||
Performing their duties with complete purity, they are endowed with supreme sovereignty.
Both with bodies and without bodies, they always move about according to their own will.
Those men who have attained the supreme state are devoted to the yoga of knowledge.
For them there is no returning again to the terrible cycle of saṃsāra. || 50 ||

This is well known from such passages. Regarding this matter, the Śruti in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad states: "He who delights in the Self, plays with the Self, rejoices in the Self, and finds his companion in the Self, becomes a self-ruler (svarāj); for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds;
for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds. Here, "freedom of movement" refers to being a lord of the hosts (gaṇeśvara).
It occurs. || 51 ||
In the Āditya Purāṇa, the words of Dūrvāsas: "All the lords of the Gaṇas assume forms at their own will and act according to their own will."
The liberated ones rejoice together with Śiva and go to the state of Śiva.
Those who are the lords of Śambhu’s attendants do not return to the surface of the earth.
Having enjoyed pleasures according to their desires, they shall attain union with Śiva.

"All those who abide in the state of *sālokya* with Śiva at the time of the final end dissolve into the Self alone"—by this scriptural statement, it is clearly established that they attain oneness with Śiva right there. Furthermore: "Then the wise one, having shaken off both merit and sin, stainless, attains equality with the Puruṣa."

From the statement in the *Mantrōpaniṣad* regarding the liberation of Nandīśvara and others, it follows that their *sārṣṭi*—that is, their equality in sovereignty—is indeed attained. If it is argued that the attainment of the world of Brahmā through the gate of the sun belongs only to renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) and not to others, as stated in the passage "the *virajas* depart by way of the solar gate," we say no; for this applies to the *vīramāheśvaras* as well.
Because the renunciation of the knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*) consists in the knowledge of the identity between Brahman and the self through the union of the *liṅga* and the body,

and because the Śruti and Purāṇas record that householders such as Yājñavalkya and Janaka attained the renunciation of the knower through the knowledge of the identity between Brahman and the self, Vīraśaivism is the most excellent of all.

The attainment of the world of Śiva, which is designated as the Brahmaloka, occurs; for this very reason, it is taught that even for those in the householder stage among the four stages of life (āśramas), the practice of *samādhi* alone is prescribed for Vīraśaivas, according to the instruction: "one should cast the body into the Rasā. || 54 ||
In the *Viśeṣārthaprakāśikā*, in the chapter on the end of the body (*dehāvasāna*).
Now, therefore, [is the description] of the Śiva-yogins who possess the splendor of Brahman through the six stations (ṣaṭsthala).
I shall now explain in detail that specific duty which must be performed at the end of the body's life.
To those whose form is Brahman in its six stations, endowed with the six-limbed Liṅga.
There is no end to the body for those whose selves are not like those of ordinary people. 56.
The five-syllabled [Om] consists of the five elements; it is the Praṇava, the Person who is the self of the elements.
Through the state of being the self of the elements of the beings, the gross body is perceived.
The subtle body itself is the *liṅga* for yogins whose nature consists of the six stages.
The body is considered to consist of conduct and so forth, not of earth and other material elements.
Conduct is the earth; water is declared to be the Guru; fire is Śiva.
The wind itself, when it is in its state of clarity, is designated as space. || 59 ||
(Thus it is cited.)
The living being (jīva) is the great fire (mahānasa), the self of the elements (bhūtātman), for these who possess the six-fold state (ṣaṭsthala).
Here, the true meaning of the elements, beginning with earth, which constitute the limbs of the devotee and others, is being stated.
For those who practice virtue, the earth is the foundation; right conduct is water; wisdom is the teacher;
the supreme nectar of divine essence is the light; and Śiva is the purifying fire.
The vital breath moving externally and internally, as well as space itself, is clarity; indeed, the Great Soul of those possessing the six limbs is truly pure and devoid of body. 61.
For this one who is devoted to the non-duality of Śiva, there is neither destruction nor birth.
There is no other course, no other bondage, and no liberation.
Right here, everything truly dissolves into the state of the Existent by way of its identity with the Self.
Like the solidity of clarified butter, it is like the appearance of the phenomenal world in a dream.
He is the primordial form, with the earth and other elements serving merely as secondary indicators.
For that external body which was imagined is now nothing but this [remaining] one. || 64 ||
At the time of his passing, he should take refuge in a sacred field of Śiva.
The teachers have declared this to be commendable even for those belonging to all four stages of life (āśramas).
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic.
But he who, joined with the limb of the *liṅga*, takes refuge in a sacred field of Śiva, [attains the highest state]. || 66 ||
The Liṅga is Śiva, the body is the field (kṣetra), and their union is the substratum (āśraya).
Therefore, whoever is joined with both the external signs and the internal limbs [of yoga] becomes an Atyāśramin.
Abiding beyond the stages of life, knowing the proper time, and naturally possessed of a steady mind, he [attains] his own [state].
At the end, he shall abandon his body of his own accord, without being afflicted by diseases or other such ailments.
The first method is digging; the second consists of burning.
The third method of non-seeing is for those who wish to abandon their own bodies. (69)
There might be the existence of the self and space, and from that, the non-perception and the burning.
The state of wind and fire is digging; [the state] of earth and water is likewise. (70)
Non-perception is the supreme excellence, for there is no separation between the limbs and the body.
In the same way, burning is most excellent, like the union of fire and camphor.
In the absence of those two, the scriptures declare that digging is the best course of action.
Likewise, in a sacred field, at a holy site, during fire-offerings, and in recitation, meditation, and absorption. || 72 ||
In whatever state a being remains, within the stages of the path of the six stations;
In each such instance, one should abandon the body for the sake of attaining the state of right conduct and other virtues.
For the sake of proper conduct, for the sake of the guru, for the sake of Śiva, and for the sake of the spy.
The renunciation of the body is for the sake of [attaining] serenity; true renunciation is the offering of that [serenity].
The field is the liṅga of conduct, while the characteristic of the earth is the limb of the devotee.
For the Guru-liṅga is indeed a sacred ford (tīrtha), characterized by the water from the limbs of Maheśa. || 75 ||
The sacrificial fire (homa) should be the Śiva-liṅga, characterized by the fire of the limbs once it has been propitiated.
The *japa* is the *liṅga* known as *carā*, while the breath (*māruta*) is the *liṅga* of the vital force (*prāṇa*).
Dhyāna has serenity as its mark and the factors of refuge as its specific characteristic.
Samādhi is the Great Liṅga, the limb of unity, and the defining characteristic of the living soul.
Vṛtti: One who commits suicide by means such as digging, immersion, offering oblations into fire, or fasting is certainly not [a true ascetic].
By means of the methods taught in the Śiva scriptures, he should himself cast off the body and become Śiva. || 78 ||
Among these methods, this is indeed the most excellent, for it is a means that is easy and pleasant.
In the Unmanī-uttara-yoga, on the path of cessation (nivṛtti-mārga), there is the spontaneous casting off of the body. || 79 ||
Or else, even if one is afflicted by diseases and other ailments, one who possesses the union of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the *liṅga*, and the body—
At the end, he casts off the body and certainly becomes Śiva. || 80 ||
For sickness belongs only to the body, which is merely an external limiting adjunct.
This is the established position of those who know reality: that it does not belong to the pure consciousness within the body.
Though he knew the right time, he beheld the impending fall of his own body.
Having remained until the end of the ripening of his prārabdha karma, and having abandoned it, he becomes Śiva.
It is better to abandon the body by oneself through the ripening of one's own past actions.
The falling of one's own body is like the release of a ripe fruit from its stalk.
By whatever means possible, such as through illness or health, and for whatever reason whatsoever.
For one who is joined with the purification of the six paths and who is united with the body of the Liṅga of Prāṇa.
If his end had come with the dissolution of the body, no other ritual action would have been performed.
One should either bury that body in the earth or cast it into auspicious waters. || 85 ||
One should burn it in the fire of Rudra, or cast it away like a clod of earth in the wind.
Among these methods as well, digging is considered the best. (86)
It is similar to the prescription of non-perception by way of an intervening obstruction.
Having cast the vital breath (prāṇa) into the body, one should likewise cast the linga into that linga of these two.
Just as the initiation into Śiva was performed at the beginning, so indeed was it at the end.
The union of both body and sign, as well as the union of both vital breath and mantra.
When both the vital breath and the mantra have passed away, one should dig up both the body and the linga.
Just as a linga established upon the ground is not uprooted again.
Just as the *liṅga* established in the body is extracted at the end, so it is here. || 89 ||
When the vital breath has been cast into the subtle body (liṅga), one should cast that possessor of the subtle body (liṅgin) [into the supreme state].
Just as there would be a transgression if [the body] were separated while one is still living, so it is in this case. || 90 ||
He who is joined to the *liṅga* of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is called a *liṅgaprāṇin*.
From the burning of that very body, a great transgression would arise. || 91 ||
Just as there is no burning of what is already burnt, nor cooking of what is already cooked.
For one who has been consumed by the fire of the knowledge of Śiva, there is no further burning. || 92 ||
The body is external and composed of earth; indeed, that which is the physical mark (liṅga) is likewise composed of earth.
Therefore, both are of the nature of earth; hence, one must guard against even a minute vulnerability in that which is earthen.
The earth was shattered and submerged in water; the water was consumed by a great fire.
The light that has set into the wind dissolves into the wind within the ether. || 94 ||
The ether is within the self, and the self is within its own state, which is the supreme Śiva.
That which pertains to earth should be concealed in earth; that which pertains to water, however, in fire. || 95 ||
And that which belongs to each respective [element] exists within its own fiery essence by its very nature.
And even cremation in the fire of Rudra is better for those yogis who possess the yoga of the *liṅga* and the body. (96)
If, through the state of being separated from those two, nothing whatsoever remains, [then that is liberation].
If it remains, it is better to dig it up from the ground and cast it away. || 97 ||
Some may remain with only their limbs left, and some may remain with only their sexual organs left.
Where no remainder is seen, that is the unsurpassed injunction.
Vṛtti: Even when the body has been burnt, the remainder of the limbs is finally cast upon the earth or into the water.
Therefore, the rule of relinquishment is more powerful because it effects a state without remainder and does not permit further formation.
Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, [that state one attains].
The knower of reality, constantly permeated by the state of being, attains exactly that.
He who is awakened at the time of death, whether by himself or even by being enlightened by a friend;
Meditating upon the one Śiva, he goes to the supreme state. || 101 ||
When one meditates on the form whose nature is Śiva, one is liberated from the vital breaths.
Then he attains the state of Śiva; there is no other way—so says the Śruti.
Whether at a sacred ford, in the house of a Caṇḍāla, or even if one has lost consciousness;
One should thus abandon the body; through knowledge alone, one is liberated.
Now, the characteristic of meditative absorption (samādhi) is stated in the Makuṭāgama:
Whether in a house, a temple, a pond, or on the bank of a river.
In a flower garden, in the middle of a village, in a forest, or on a mountain retreat. || 104 ||
One should arrange them for the purpose of depositing in eight locations.
The first [part] is long and extended, with a single step of the staircase. || 105 ||
One should make the second [part] long, and likewise raise it by two feet.
One should conceive of the third [face] as being three-quarters of a unit in length and width.
It is square, five-footed, and likewise broad.
A square of nine compartments is prescribed; and in its center, with great care, [one should proceed]. || 107 ||
Having constructed a three-stepped altar to its south, in that direction.
And it should be dug in the shape of a triangle, with three feet, long and extensive. || 108 ||
Exalted manliness is to be understood as that which is diligently applied therein.
Having established him within the interior of the cave, endowed with the lotus posture (padmāsana). || 109 ||
And having filled the area up to the heart with ashes, likewise upon that [he should place the remaining ashes].
Having filled the remaining part with ashes and joined it with a bilva leaf.
Thereafter, one should fill it with earth and likewise have an altar constructed.
In the Ādityapurāṇa:
"He who is perfected through the purificatory rites of Śiva and is devoted to the worship of Śiva..."
In that [state], ordinary defects such as birth-impurity (sūtaka) and the like do not apply. || 111 ||
The man who regards a twice-born person devoted to Śiva as if he were a mortal, [incurs great sin].
He falls into the Taptakumbha hell for an inexhaustible period of time. || 112 ||
Those who perform the ritual action cause [beings] to go to the auspicious hermitage of Śiva.
Burnt by the fire of the Kumbhīpāka hell, they are born into low births.
In this [treatise] which illuminates the specific meaning,
one should not perform funeral rites for him here, just as one would not for bound souls (paśus).
There is no corpse for him, because [otherwise] impurities such as birth-impurity would cling to him. || 114 ||
Nor is there any rite such as the Śrāddha, nor the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), nor the libation of water.
One should not perform the Pārvaṇa and other rites for a yogin who has become one with Śiva.
Now, if it is desired to perform a ritual action even with reference to him as well;
One should perform only what is auspicious and satisfy those who are devoted to Śiva. || 116 ||
And every year, on his behalf, one should feed devotees of Śiva.
For the food that is given to devotees is indeed as if given directly to Śiva himself. || 117 ||

O Śambhu, may You assume this body of mine in the form of a pillar of light, manifesting Your own intense splendor on all sides— slowly, slowly, like the moon and fire— to be beheld directly by the eye as Your very Liṅga.
If, at the conclusion of my prārabdha karma, this boon is granted to me through Your compassion and great mercy, so be it. || 118 ||

[Thus, in the *Śivācārakathana*, which is an extraction of the essence of the conduct of the Vīramāheśvaras— the quintessence of the Vedas, Vedāntas, Śiva-Āgamas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Gītā, Śāstras, and ancient sayings.]

In the *Śrīmad-Vedāntasāra-Vīraśaiva-Cintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Añjanācārya, the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Final Rites of the Vīramāheśvaras," in the Uttarakhanda, is complete. Śrī.
Śrī.
